Most of us devoted Sunday morning to the Cathedral. Founded in 1211, with its great twin towers, and its three exquisite recessed portals "containing about 530 statues," it is, in some respects, "perhaps The most beautiful structure produced in the Middle Ages," though its dignity and beauty are considerably obscured by the inferior surrounding property, which ought ought to be incontinently swept away. Immediately in front of the Cathedral there is an equestrian statue of Joan of Arc. The work- manship is good and there is inspiration in the upturned eyes of "the predestined maid " ; but the statue is entirely dwarfed by the majesty of the great western front and seemed to most of us distinctly out of place. Inside the Cathedral there is another statue of this 'brave peasant girl, who was killed as a witch in the fifteenth century and has just been canonized in the twentieth.
" Far in front the cross stands ready and. the cracklin,, faggots burn, While the crackling mobs of yesterday in silence awe return . To glean up the scattered ashes int.) History's golden urn."

All morning the great fane was filled with -worshippers, and I was privileged to gaze upon a solemn vision of stern priests and acolytes, and, in the midst of them, a plump and kindly and white-haired old man who was robed from head to foot in scarlet, and

water flowing sadly from a rusty iron pipeiand a melancholy-looking grotto with some seats and tables just in front of it, where we could purchase "bock " and sundry " sirops" to appease our thirst—such was this budding Spa. A fat,bald-headed, garrulous old French- man did his best to make things "go," and two or three French peasant women seconded his labours with a zeal that was worthy of a better cause, whilst a wheezy gramophone occasionally contributed to the entertainment of the patrons of the place; but we all agreed that it was the funniest attempt at a Spa that we had ever seen.

Afterwards we strolled down through a straggling village, peeped into a musty church, plucked an,occasional grape from the abounding vines which covered the flat land that lay between it and the railway, and slowly sauntered back towards the Station. The vines were not Mall What I had pictured them. I had dreamt of a sort of more- impressive hop-garden; but the plants were only a foot or two in height, and were attached to sticks, like dwarf chrysanthe- mums. The grapes were mostly green and very small and sweet, and, as all the vine- yards were unfenced, we could pluck them, as we passed, with nobody to say us nay, and salve our consciences by remembering how One of old had plucked the ears of corn one golden Sabbath day in Galilee. div.head: GOVERNMENT PALACE AND PARK, NANCY.
div.p: THE GOVERNMENT PALACE AND PARK, NANCY.

turned out to be none other than the "Cardinal." The ceremony, which I wit- nessed from afar, as I found out afterwards, was, indeed, the Cardinal's Mass. The beauty of the altar lights, the genuflexions of the dazzling company who stood before them, the moving music, and then the sound of the compelling bell, the solemn stillness, the great company all bowed in reverent awe before the Host, and the ascending incense, gradually filling all the place, combined to make a deep impression on me; and I must confess that I am always thrilled with a vague sense of worship at this crowning feature in the ceremonial of the Roman Church.

Afterwards the Cardinal proceeded to an enclosure in the Dave and sat in state, amid a crowd of dignitaries, listening intently to an obviously powerful sermon from an intellectual, clean-shaven, striking, black- robed priest. I could not follow it except in fleeting snatches, but the sermon seemed to be extremely earnest, eloquent and practical. And, presently, the service over, I could see the plump, red-robed and rubicund old man proceeding slowly through the crowded church, extending, as he went, his plump and kindly fingers, with a gracious smile, to certain favoured females and a host of proud and happy children, and disappearing, finally, amid an atniosphere of mingled-condescen- sion and benignity, beyond the side doors leading to the Palace. I felt a sort of love for the old fellow, but I wish he had not been so ludicrouSly like the Abbot in the famous legend, which has given to Rheims a fame more universal, perhaps, than even Joan of Arc. Such is the power of poetry! I subsequently looked at all the leading features of the huge interior,and was especially delighted with the great rose windows and the gem-like beauty of the ancient glass, and then, accompanied by Mr. Shawcross, I

climbed up one of the twin towers, and, scrambled all about the roofs, and visited the belfry, and gazed at the gigantic gar- goyles, and the figure of the Centaur poised above them all, and, from the highest point to cIP hich we were permitted to ascend,looked out across the city, with its pleasant streets and.squares, to/the open plain near Betheny, where we could dimly see the pylons which had guided the sky-travellers on their venturous excursions in the air.

At the Cathedral doors I saw the only beggars I was doomed to meet in all my journey; and, after lunch, I went to see the wonderful Cathedral Treasury, with all its vessels of incalculable value and miraculous association—a curious contrast to the poverty outside, a contrast which might give the cynic some occasion to • blaspheme. I was also able to obtain a fleeting glimpse of the Palace, with its Chapel, and the famous Hall in which the Coronation Banquets once were held. A voiture took me thence to the Station, where I joined some members of our party who were going out to Rilly-a- Montagne, a pretty little place some miles from Rheims, to see the vineyatds. Here we spent three golden hours or so amid the vines which clad the sunny slopes,and rambled on into a pleasant wood which crowned a hill that overlooks the distant city; and, lying there upon the soft sward by a sort of quarry, I did my best to defend the cause of Tariff Reform against the attacks of my good friend, Mr. Shawcross, and to prove to him that Rheims Cathedral was not rooted in an empty fable,iii spite of all the crimes and follies perpetrated in its Founder's name. Between my arguments I kept a sharp look out for the "dirigible,"which was to ascend,we had been told, that afternoon. One of our party, indeed, asserted that he had seen it hovering over Rheims in the early morning, but none of us contrived to see it now.

We had observed a notice board, on our way to the wood, which indicated that there was a ferruginous "source," or iron spring, of ,some kind somewhere in its near recesses, and eventually we found the spring, and came once more upon the rest of our com- panions. A sort of doll's house built by the proprietor, some rude birch huts, reminding one of Indian wigwams, on the grassy margin of a sort of tiny duckpool, which was dignified by the imposing name of "The Black Village on the border of the Lake'," a jet of

architect who had read a delightful paper at the recent Town Planning Conference in Southport, and had come out specially from Paris to meet us, joined us at the Station,and very pleasant was the chat we had with him outside a little wayside cafe, in the soft light of the setting sun, before we started back for Rheims. Ho dined with us at our Hotel (our civic comrades of the previous day had dined with us the night before), and we spent a pleasant social hour or two before he had to leave to catch the train back to the capital. But the great cathedral haunted me (" a dream in stone," our good friend M. Rey had called it in his charming after-dinner speech) ; and when, a little before midnight, I stole out quietly, before I went to bed, to gaze up onc3 again at ihose twin towers, which loomed so solemnly against the stars, it was not without amuse- ment that I found three other members of the party, in the darkness, surreptitiously engaged on the same errand. We were up by six o'clock, and, at about a quarter to seven, Mr. Aldridge having got the whole of his municipal chickens, with all their miscellaneous impedimenta, under his protecting wing, we left the Grand Hotel, glanced once more wistfully at the Cathedral, rattled through the white and half-deserted streets, with their endless vistas of Venetian shutters, passed the gilded monument to 31arshal Drouet-d'Erlon,a soldier son of this delightful city, and so on across the leafy Promenades into the Station, where, at ten past seven o'clock, we all set out upon bur long day's journey to the capital of Whrtemburg. The country, in the main, was not particu- larly interesting or picturesque—low vine- clad plains, and smooth canals, with Noah's Ark-like trees along their cool green banks; great areas of somewhat scanty-looking grain, much still unharvested, with frequent teams of brown, broad-chested, mild-eyed oxen, ploughing in the unfenced fields, or yoked to the great country carts; and here and there a solitary gravestone in the middle of some lonely farm. A few of our enlightened company played Bridge all day and seemed, to half resent the zeal of the enthusiasts who, ever and anon, broke in upon them in their soul-devouring game to tell them they were passing some old church, or ancient city, or especially attrac- tiVe bit of scenery; a few discussed the vital problems which had brought us hither and the deeper questions which go right down to the roots of our civilization; and some of us, from time to time, stepped out upon the long, low platforms of the busy stations, to note with eager eyes the passing crowd of country folk, and now and then to patronize the genial peasant women;who were anxious to beguile the tedium of the long day's journey by their baskets of ripe peaches, luscious pears or sweet green bunches of delicious grapes. - Amidst these manifold distractions, I essayed from time to time to snatch a hasty glimpse at my omniscient Baedeker, and gathered that, on leaving Rheims, we had rapidly ascended the valley of thefl Vesle to St. Hilaire, and crossed the broad plains of the Haute Champagae; and, to the left of Sillery, the vines of which are vel.y famous, passed the mighty Camp de Chalons, which covers nearly thirty thousand acres, was established as a military centre by the third Napoleon in 1857, and is still used for military manceuvres. Then, crossing the Rhine and Marne Canal,we reached Chalons- sur-Marne, a town of 28,000 inhabitants, the headquarters of the Sixth Army Corps, the seat of a bishop, and, last but not least, an important centre of the champagne trade. Here, in 451, the conquering Attila and his triumphant Huns wtre crushed by the Romans, Franks and Visigoths in one of the "fifteen decisive battles of the world," which checked Attila's "mighty attempt to found a new Anti-Christian dynasty upon the wreck of the temporal power of Rome." The history of ChOlons-sur-Marne has been indeed eventful, and, in the last century it was occupied by foreign armies on not less than three occasions. It boasts a fine Cathedral, a noble church of Notre Dame, the Forth Ste Croix, an uncompleted arc de triomphe, and

opposite to the Hotel de Ville, a statue of PresidentrCarnot. We crossed the Marne, and rode through the small town of Vitry- le-Frangois, and following the Rhine and Marne Canal, which runs to In, near Strassburg, came, at last to Bar-le-Dix, a town of over 17,000 inhabitants, which stands upon the river Meuse and the adjacent heights There is a fine War Monument just by the Station, and the usual interesting churches. The ancient capital of the Dukes of Bar, and the chief town in the department of the Meuse, it gave asylum for three years to poor Prince Charlie.

- The Canal now passes through a tunnel two and a half miles long, while the railway pierces the low hills between the valleys of the Seine and Meuse, and bears you on through Commery, with its old castle, now a barracks, notable, in these days, for its " Madeleines," a sort of sweet cake which, at Mr. Aldridge's kind invitation, most of us were glad to sample. Then on across the two arms of the Meuse, and through a tunnel to the valley of the bright Moselle, a name with manifold- associations. And then through Poul, the bishopric of which was founded by an Irish Monk, St. Mansuy, a town which boasts two churches—the first St. Gengoult, the other beautiful St. Etienne —the towers and beautiful fatade of which are plainly visible from the train. And now we cross canal and river, each of which, a little further on, runs parallel with the rail- way. At Liverdun the former dips beneath the town and crosses the Moselle by a great bridge, and here the scenery assumes a picturesqueness which is new to us; and so we pass into the valley of the Meurthe. I never saw so many famous rivers in a single day before. At last we sight the iron work of Champigneulles, and, in the distance catch a glimpse of Nancy; and there, about eleven o'clock, we slowed down silently within the busy Station, busier than usual because of the attractions of the Nancy Exhibition, which was in full swing. Here we were cordially received, upon alighting, by a tall and gentlemanly French- man with a short black beard, a sallow face, a merry manner and a great black tie, so big as to suggest to some one in our party that we might appropriately christen him "The Undertaker." He was the keeper of the city archives, and

"A merrier man, Within the limits of becoming mirth," I have not recently set eyes upon, his black tie notwithstanding. With many kind words and delicate attentions, he led us through the green square opposite the Station, with its ''statue to the statesman, Thiers, and down the long Rue Stanislas, across the noble Place which bears the same distinguished namei, to the HOtel de Ville. We were taken through the main apartments,the ceil- ings beautified with naked nymphs and goddessess, and, after glancing through the windows with unbounded admiration, for right in front of us was one of the loveliest city scenes in Europe, we were glad to turn .to the well-filled table which had been pro- vided for this hungry troop of English travellers. The Deputy Mayor, a brisk and business-like and gentlemanly fellow, bade us welcome, and invited us to help our- selves ; and we were nothing loth to drink of the delightful ;Tines of this delightful country, and to taste the " Macarons de Nancy "which are one of the specialities of the place. Some graceful complimentary speeches followed,and we then set out to view the glories of the great Place Stanislas. It was laid out in the middle of the eighteenth century. At the end of it there stands the beautiful .116 tel de Ville. Upon the East you see the Episcopal Palace; upon the West the Theatre; and, facing the Town Hall, in either corner, two immense bronze fountains, whilst between them rises in its majesty the great Porte Stanislas, one of the seven gates of Nancy. In the middle of the square a noble monument commemorates the virtues of old Stanislaus Leszczynski, ex- King of Poland, and the last of the Dukes of Lorraine. Proceeding through the Arc de Trionzphe,you come into an oblong tree-filled space whioh is known as the Place de la Carriere,and this in turn conducts you to the charming Hemicycle, with the Palais du Gouvernement at the end of it, exactly oppo- site to the Hotel de Ville. Directly to the right,we found the sylvan park,La Pepiniere, a paradise of verdant trees,and sunny glades, and many-coloured flowers, and noble monu- ments.

In France they honour-those who do good work for town or country and one of the continual statues which we passed com- memorated the work of Here, the great Nancy architect to whom these leading features of the .town were largely due. Directly to the left of the Palace is the Church of St. Epure, which boasts a lofty spire, and further on you come to the Place Carnot, with the University to the left of it, and, at the entrance to the green Cours Leopold, a statue to the murdered President. The Cours Leopold, is called a square in Baedeker, but,if I were an Irishman, I should, I think, describe it as an oblong square, for that views up the situation. In the centre, there is a statue of Marshal Drouot, and, at the end, another of the seven triumphal arches which are one of the chief li glories of the city.

1-- Returning, we walked past the Town Hall once again, glanced hastily inside the Cathedral, which was very disappoint- ing after Rheims, and wandered slowly through the busy streets and back to all the bustle of the Station. Here we bade a hearty Au revoir to; our good friends, the Deputy Mayor, "The Under- taker," and their genial associates, and we left their lovely city with a sigh. Two hours were all we had to give to it and it deserved at least two days! The train sped, on with us, and now we caught, upon the right, a distant vision of the Vosges, and presently, pulled up at Luneville, a town of 24,000 inhabitants, "which still retains a flavour of decayed grandeur and was once the residence of the Dukes of Lorraine." Here the last of them, the mighty Stanislaus,whose memory broods over Nancy like an autumn cloud,, passed from a troublous world in 1776, and here his heart was cherished in the leading church. There is a stately Chateau .too, a barracks now, and, in the grounds, a statue to our boyhood's friend, the great French writer, Erck mann.

Soon after two, we passed through Igney- Avricourt, the French frontier station, dis- mounted curiously, and got into the train again, all gaping through the windows in the hope of being able to detect the actual boundary line. One has heard of the man who wanted to hoist a flag on the Notth Pole (it is a pity Dr. Cook neglected this pre- caution!) ' • but, to me, at any rate, the boundary line between France and Germany was as invisible as the Pole. However, we must have crossed it, for, at half-past two, we come into• another station called Deutsch Ar ricourt, and were at once aware of an unusual bustle and a general air of business. The whole surroundings seemed quite differ- ent from those which we had left a few minutes before. France, somehow, beautiful and attractive as it is, had given me a melancholy sense of a decaying nation. I was saddened by the thought that, once,'

those pleasant lands belonged to her, and that, even in my time, they had seen the tramp of armies and echoed to the roar of German guns. Now, Alsace and a portion of Lorraine belonged to the all-conquering Teuton. The names above the rooms at the Station were German names; the language spoken was German; the officials looked like German soldiers. Of course the money was German, and, of course (this is one of the objections to Tariff Reform), we had to haul our luggage from the rack, and trudge with all the patience we could muster to the large and crowded room where busy Customs officers were swiftly over hauling it. I must admit, however, that the examination was exceedingly perfunctory, and,unless you had a bag as big as a coffin say, they usually passed it without troubling you to open it ; and I got the magic chalk mark on my two portmanteaus with the mini- mum of time and trouble, and was able to peep at the approaches to the Station, and to saunter quietly around it, and secure the inevitable picture postcard ere we had to get into the train again—of course, a German train. The German time is 55 minutes in advance of the French—a fact which has its own significance, and by the simple process of altering our watches we" killed " an hour without the slightest inconvenience. Thus easy would it be for all of us to save it if our rulers only had the sense to pass the Daylight Saving Bill! (To be continueq).

div.head: WOMEN'S CIRCLE. OPENING OF THE BRIDGE-STRET
div.p: WOMEN'S CIRCLE. OPENING OF THE BRIDGE-STRET
CLUB.

The Warrington Women's Circle is making con- siderable progress in its excellent work and Saturday witressed the opening of the commodious new club premises in Bridge-street. This red letter event was celebrated by a Workers' Circle in the afternoon, and a social gathering for members and friends at night. The place was very brightly_ decorated with choice flowers provided by Mrs. Rylands and Miss M. Broad- bent. Mrs A. H. Crosfield presided at the earlier meeting and it was a great disappointment that die weather kept so many away, but the audience included Mr. A. H. Crosfield. Many letters of apology were received; but only those of Mrs. Armitage and Mrs. Rylands, members of Execu: ive Committee,were read. Mi:s PARKER-BROWN, rew Superintendent of the Christian Deac mess Mission, formerly Federation Secretary, offered prayer, Mrs., CROSFIELD, who had a cordial reception, said it was with mingled feelings of pleasure and misgiving that she had accepted the Presidency of the Circle, for although she greatly appreciated the houour that had been conferred upon her, and would do all in her power to help the Circle in every possible way, she could not forget that she must suffer by comparison with her kind and able predecessor. She could never hope to fill her post as President nor perform the duties in the able manner in which Mrs. Dodds, with her energy, zeal and self-sacrifice, had done. She was proud to he associated with her and with . the workers who had devoted their time and talents to that admirable work, end they would all be glad to join with her in thanking Mrs. Letheren for the admirable work she had done for, and the good judgment she had exercised on behalf of the Circle. (Applause). After all, there was no work so important as that which helped women to lead richer and fuller lives. They vv, re living in an age of con- stant progress, and aiming at a higher stindard of life. The olqect of this Circle was to help women to attain that higher standard and they had only to look at the record of the past year to realize how Warringten women had appreciated the formation of the Circle. (Hear, hear). It was wonderful what results had been obtained in one year, and with but very slender resources. They had over 200 effective members; they had established a variety of classes, and they had obtained, opened, and furnished, a club room, for which their thanks were largely due to Mr. Carter for his very effective assistence. (Applause). But thete were other results not putilished in the report which a society of mutual help like that could not fail to obtain, and which were often more p,ecious them those they had referred to. But, although they were glad of what had been done, far more still remained to be accomplished. There were hundreds of women and girls who would he 'happier for the aid of the Circle, and that was why she had no hesitation in asking generous friends to help them. They would he especially grateful to those who, by giving them annual subscriptioLs, would help theta to ley their plans for the future, and, as the saying went, "cut their coat according to their cloth," but any donation would he welcome. 1 hose who could not give mcney could give their talents and energies to further a cause which could not fail to be a blessing to so many in the town. (Applause). Miss LISCI, BnoACBENT, of the Manchester Women's Hostel, spoke on recreation and emphasized the close link between prayer and recreation. The two were, she said, so far from opposed that they were interwoven. Prayer resulted in recreation. She made some practical suggestions, one being that parties of girls should visit museums and other place s of interest with informed workers and have their interest aroused by having the objects explained. We understand that this idea will to carried out in connection with Miss War.ipg:scla s.

MISS BESSIE DurroN said -she hael.lately read that the most effective points upon the political platform were those that were tibged with a little vulgarity. What vos ti,e most effective point on the platform of practical religions work ? Was it persuasiveness? Trmt ? Enthusiasm? Whatever it might be it was not apologetics. The poet laureate of Warrington in his beautiful acmstic in the Women's Circle, had shown that there was no need for it to apologize for its exist- ence since it met a'manifest need. And now here they were that day in their new room, and a strikingly efficient room it was—inirespect of space, light, ventila- tion, comfortable seats, pisno, and fitments generally. They had in a town like Warrington a great deal of smoke, hut a gcod measure of prosperity too and a variety of intei exts. Into that town( ame Mrs. Letheren and what interested Ler was the reople, and especi4lly the womanhood of IVarrington, and she set out to see what she could do for the improvement of their lot. Should she work with- out encouragement, unattended, unequipped, or even with oht half the cheer and sympathy such an enterprise should enlist? Many asked only to have a good time for themselve.. They looked for some con- venient crossing to that ether side where, like the priest and Levite, they could pass by the poor Samaritan. And bow well worth while such work was! SLe bad heard from many in after days of heavy toil and sickness that they were still cheered and helped now darker days bad come with the re:nembrance of the influence and holy cheer which helped them to he good and dreT them near to God. 'Ulose.already at work wore worth joining, worthy of co-operation aid self-denial on their part. (Applause). It had been so ardently yet so wisely commenced that there was a credit in joining and helping in any va* such a work as this. (Applause). Miss Florence Brown contributed two 8,11°3. Mrs. Jackson Holmes accorupaaied. To a was then served by invitation of the Exemitive Committm.

Mrs. DODDS proposed and Mrs. HARVEY' COOK seconded a vote of thanks to the speakers and all who bad helped and Miss EARKER-BROWN added some remarks on the use fulness of a magazine which the Circle proposes starting in the New Year.
EVENING MEETING.
MRS. A. ii. CROSFIELD ON THE OBJECTS OF
rHE CIRCIAL

A highly successful social gathering for members and friends brought the day's proceedings to a close. Mrs. R 3 lands presided over a large attendance, amongst those present being Mr. A. H. Creek) hl, M.P., and Mrs. Crostleld; Mr. and Mrs C. B. Parker, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. C. Jackson-Holmes, Miss Parker-Brown, Mrs. Gladding and Miss Waring. An admirable music ii programme had been arranged by Mrs. Jackson-Holmes and there was also some interesting speech-making. Mrs. RYLANDS warmly commended the excallent work of the Circle in providing wholesome recreation. Tl:ere was no reason why it should not be supported by all classes and denominations, for it was carrie 1 on entirely en undenominational and non-political lines. She hoped that in a rhea time the results of the work would be so gratifying that all sections of the corn- mnnity would be delighted to join in it. (Applause). Miss Ada Jones (te cher of fancy eork claz-s) then presented Mrs. Crostleld with a handsome photo frame which she had worked,and Mrs.Crostleld returned cordial thanks for the gift. Mrs. Crtosrietaa then delivered a neat little speecb on the work of the Circle. She said :—Ladies and gentlemen and kind friends of the Circle. Wo are here to inaugurate the new Club Room, and to open the second session of the Warrington Women's Circle. The word Circle seems to me a very happy and appropriate description of our association, because it embraces so wide a sphere of a hat is useful and pleasant for women in this workaday 'world of ours. (Hear, hear.) If ong considers the number of subjects that are taught, and the variety of culture that is offered to our members, one can see at a glance how very wide that sphere is. Let us take to he;in with the nursing, cooking and sewing classes. In th 3 division of the world's work nursing in a special degree falls to women; it is at the same time our duty and our privilege to help those who are in sickness ani distress. As for cooking, we all know how much More comfortable a home ca a be

made by even an elementary knowledge of the culinary art. For after all, ladies and gentlemen, it is an art in its /way. (Hen-, bear.) Economy, as we all know, is too often not the strongest point in English house- holds, and cooking is not the least important because of the immense amount of waste that it teaches, us to avoid. Let us take sewing next. Dress appeals to all because however simple, it can be made tasteful and pretty by anyone who has a little knowledge of sewing and dressm sk ng. I Then the Circle does not naglect either physical development or recreation. Tnere are evenings devoted to games and drill. Nowadays when one hears so much about the security, or, if you will, the danger of the nation, is it mat right that we should not neglect our girls' physical development? (Hear, hear.) As for music, I dare say that most of you know that my late ancestors—laughter—a few thousand years ago put music along with athletics in the very forefront of their s stem of training. The to went hand in hand, just as I am delighted to know they go band in hand in this Circle. We are all of us proud of the musical talent and culture there is in Warrington, and, lam so glad that this Circle plays its part and takes its share in that development (Applause.) But by far the in ast imaortant is the moral and spiritual si le. We have our de7otlooal services on the Sunday, and there is at all times in the Cirele a pure and healthy moral tone. On all sides nowadays we hear, and very rightly hear, of the impas t- eine of people breathing flesh air, and living in healthy surround!nes ; is it cot just as necessary, or even more necessary, for them to live in a healthy and pure mental atmosphere? How pleasant to know that a girl away from home, lonely fled among strangers, instead of spending her Sunday afternoon in loa,,linns or in less protit4ble surroundings, can fi.:d in our Circle good friends and a warm welcome. (Applause.) And that welcome, 13dir-s and gentlemen, is extended to all. Our Circle admits all who believe in God's good work, irrespective of religious or political opinions. We are non-sectarian and non-political. You see sittirg here this evening many friends who represent quite a variety of political opinions. You even see Conservatives mil Libern's sitting side by side,•and quite in harmony too. (Hear, hear, and laughter). Our Circle sincerely believes in co-operatien, and we hope to work ii friendly alliance Rich all the societies who are doing goad work in the town. And that is why, ladies and gentlemen, just becausa we a-k everybody to join us, whatever their views, that I think we may fairly look to our friends to give us their help. Of course, I am appealing chiefly to women, becau e there is work in this Circle which can only be really well done by them. We da not perhaps realise how great our influence is in this world. It is on the training of the women of to-day that the national character of tha future is dependent. Thee is room for all and work for all in the Circle; we each of us have a duty to per- form which no one else can. "Others may do our work, but no one e!se can perform our duty." There- fore, to him that knoweth to .do good, and doeth it not to him it is sin. Se let us all join the maks, and let all who can help take their part., remembering that in helping others we will help ourselves. Lot us march bravely forward,

"Languor not in our Learts, Wtakness not in our words, Wear irmss not on cur brows." (Applause). Miss PAIZNER-BROWS said that God had given to her the pi ivilege of sat,ing a great deal of wrk amongst women. With their splendid organization she felt that they of the Warrirgton Women's Circle had a tremendous future. She wanted to ask the members if they had rosily thought what an important factor they might be in the future of the town and if they rea!ized what a privilege and responsibility was thei, s. What was w.nted everywhere to-day was that women should hive a deeper realization of their possibilities and opportunities. She har3ly agreed with the ides of regii•ding the s scial ani spiritual sides of their work as separate sal distinct, becanse all scoial work should be spiritual. If the spiritual work was maintained in the spirit of prayer and dependence upon God the social part would fall into the right D ,acing and acting could not have a plane in girls' cluhs if the work was to he on spiritual lines. They must set their faces like a flint against anything that woul.d mar or hinder young lives, remembering that their limitations were their weak sisters and that what might he right for tome would lead others into temptation and must therefore be avoided. She prayed with all her heart that the Circle might ke such a power that many a life would be the nobler and the better for it. (Applause). Mrs. GI-ADDING reminded the audience that they had met on historic ground. [tight opposite that building was the place where John Howard Ik-e4—a man whoe name was written high on onr country's roll of honour, a man who literally fulfilled Carist's command by visit- ing the perple who were sick and in prison and saved them from horrors we could scarcely realise in these happier days. Just about where the cluh building stood, there once lived a nun who in a little watch- maker's shop thought and worked until he hsd found out something that made him a riJh man and made his name bnd this town known throughout England. Then they were met right between the places where the famous Acldsmies stood. They had the Old Academy in Bridge-street rtad the second Academy was in Butter- market-street. Thera ought to he something in the law of ass sciation to lead them to live up to those memories and she hoped that in the work of the Circle eff.,rts would be made to create and foster in the young people an interest in the past of our country in which Warrington took no insignificant share. She was surpised to find among women end young girls so much indifference and apathy concerning the men wh) once lived in this town and who bought for us privileges which we should value highly. The speaker also referred to Mrs. Barbauld, the Warrington poetess, a great and no: le woman who made the best of her opportunities and who united to a charming personality rot ntal gifts of a high order and a rare aid intelligent piety. Soe taught some of thel boys who afterwards attained foremost places in our nation's Wstory. The poet Wordsworth said he wished he could only have written the lines which Mrs. Barbsuld wrote towards the end of her long and somewhat shadowed life:

Life! we've' been long together Through pleasant and through charrly weath3r ; 'Tis hard to put when friends are dolt-; Perhaps 'twill cost a sigh, a tear : Then steal away, give little warning, Moos.) thine own time; • Sly " Good night " but in s)rae brighter clime
Bid me" Good moiming."

Coneinning Mrs. GL.tDDING ra'd the Circle should have the support of every right- minded caizon of Warrington, of everyone who had the interests of the good 'old tows at heart. Some of them were straining every nerve to realize the ideal of a City Beautiful. The ideal of the Women's Circle was not so much a City Beautiful as every home in the city teantiful. It w.is in the homes of the city that the men were being born and trainei who were to beco:re the citizens of the future. The Circle claimed the htlp not only of the citizens of the town, but of the Christians, no matter what their Cburvh or sect might be. They were all working towards the same supreme end. (App'ause). The musical programme was pleasantly varied and most appreciatively received. An instrumental

quartette party (Nfrs. Htviour, Mrs. Jackson Ho Mr. H. Hon.], and Mr. Joh;mon played "Atlegri) (Mozart) and "Andante and Rondo" (Mozart) with taste and skill. A cornet duet was effectively int prated by Mrs. Willett sad Mr. W.Rutter, aid a -ttio for two violins and piano, "Prayer" (Schubert), was given with expreszion by Mrs. Haviour, Mrs, Willett and Mrs. Jackson Mimes. Miss Violet 13 -owa, a promis- ing young vozalist with a sweat and powerful soprano voice, sang a bright gipsy song and "When the heart is yonng"in artistic style aid WAS cordially enc,orei• Mrs. Jicks332 Holmes played the piaucforte accomp3ni" ments.

Mrs. C. E. PARKER., in moving a comprehensive vote' of thanks to the speikers, Mrs. Jackson-ldolrnes, and the artistes, said Mrs. A. H. Crosfield had proved a wortht successor to Mrs. Dodds in the pretidency. They %cot" all agree that the wisest thief,' Mr. Cr >sfield ever did was when he broaght to Warrington a la ly so cultured, broad-min-led and altogether charming as Mrs. Crosfield was (Applause). Mrs.Rylands had shown great sympatilT with the work of the Circle and without her promise of help they would have felt very d.ffilent at ta'ileg smh 3a important step as to acquire the new pramises. Mist WARING secondel and the vote was pa sad with enthusiasm.

div.head: Warrington Swamp the Rangers.
div.p: Warrington Swamp the Rangers.

The worst of weather conditions attended the match between L\ arrington and Broughton Rangers on Satur- day, for rain fell the whole time, and at one period there was a deluge which almost blotted the players from sight. There was no cessation of play, and the 4,000 spectators who braved tho elements witnessed an interesting and exciting game. Warrington were at full strength, Frawley for the first time appearing in Bradshaw's place at right wing. The Rangers were in an awkward predicament, for besides having to provide a couple of the Cumberland vangulrd in the game with Yorkshire, their back division was j•endered exception- ally weak by the injuries received by Hogg, Harris and Barr. Teams

Warrington : Tilley. back; Fish, Diokenson,Taylor and Frawley, three-qnarters ; Brookesand Jenkins, half- backs; Neill, O'Malley, Thomas, Boardman, Shugars and Belton, forwards. Broughton Rangers: Barlow, back Sankey. Harry James and Lear, three-quarters; Wright and Loft- house, half-becks; Darlison, Beetham, Wylie, Winskiil Heyes and Ruddick, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes ; touch judges, Messrs, A. Lee (Leigh) and W. Cross (Preston). Warrington won the toss and started with the elements in their favour. The Ringers made a strong opening and just inside the borne half Lof thous() got the ball away smartly to Lear, who ran well before passing inside to C. James. The latter was well placed and scored a capital try near the posts but missed an easy goal kick. This was a staggerer for the locals, and it was no wonder to Bad, on dropping out from half-way, that Warrington immediately swarmed round the railway goal. The ball was passed out, and Taylor cleverly eluded Barlow and dodged in under the posts, but Fish, like James, was unable to make the goal. Broughton again effected a raid on the Warrington line and it required all Tilley's skill to thwart the visitors. Fish came to the rescue, and a tricky run and kick landed the " Wirepullers" once more aggressive. Harry tried to repulse the attacking force, hut all to no purpose, for the forwards were playing a desperate game, and after Fish had made a brilliant effort to cross, Brooks, Jenkins, Dickenson and Taylor handled in quick succession, and Frawley ran speedily to the line, where Barlow and James challenged him, and he was forced back into the open before he could ground. However, the bajl was speedily worked away, and Dickenson, plying his foot to the sphere, dribbled through and

placed Warrington in front. The goal kick was a failure. The game continued to be well fought, anp after Fish had shown up well on the left, Frawley was again to the fore with a good effort, but his pass to O'Malley was ruled forward. The attack was main- tained, and after Brooks and Neill had tried to break down the defence the Warringtonians indulged in a round of passing, the ball being finally transferred to Fish, who beat Rados in great stOe and scored a try. Thomas missed the goal shot. Warrington still forced matters at the pavilion end, and Frawley was arnost over after a sharp sprint. At half-time Warrington had a lead of three tries (nine points), to Broughton Rangers one try (three paints). Thomas re-started and the visitors had advantage of the breeze, but it was Warrington who pressed at the start, for the forwards, lel by O'Malley end Thomas, immediately got to the railway (rid, where Brooke failed to accept a pass from Neill with a clear course. Dickenson had a penalty shot at goal and an additional two points were recorded. No sooner had the game been restarted than the spectators were roused to a hih pitch of enthusiasm, for Brooks warted a move- ment at centre field, which ended in Dickenson placing the ball in Fish's hands on the half-way lido. Taree of the R angers were easily trio!. el, and hen Barlow was speedily left in the rear, Fish placing thi ball behind the posts for Thomas to place a goal. It was a magui- cent try and the scorer earned all the applause wlfch greeted his effort. The Rangers played up pluckily,and following some faulty work by the home hack division the Broughton forwards made commendable he adwov, which had its reward with a try to Beetham at the corner. James took the kick and landed a flue goal. The Wirepullers caused the • Rangers to fall back, and , after Thomas bad led the way Shugais rushed over with , a try near the posts and Fish added the goal. Boardman next led the home forwards in another rush, but Barlow effected some good saves. From one capital clearance the Warrington hacks were liv•king in judgment, and Lear raced over for a try, which James improved upon. A speedy retaliation was forthcoming, for the game was rushed to the Rangers' quarters, where Jenkins scored after an effective dribble. Broughton failed to withstand anotherattack, and this time O'Malley scored at the corner; the goal-kick being a failure. Result : Warrington, three goals seven tries (27 points) ; Broughton Rangers, two goals three tries (13 points). WIGAN'S DOWNFALL AT RUNCORN.

Close on 3,000 spectators assemblei at Runcorn to witness the above match. The visitors brought a strong team, Green playing in place of Jenkins. Runcorn were still without Jolley and Harrison. Walker started for Runcorn against the wind, but the visitors were soon on tbo attack, their powerful kicking gaining them much ground. Runcorn were penalised, and Leytbam landed a splendid goal. Shortly afterwards the same player had annther shot at goal without success. Half- time score—Wigan 1 goal (2 points), Runoorn nil. After the interval Runcorn gave a much better display, attacking with vigour. The visitors were penalised, and Padbury brought the scare even with a somewhat lucky goal. Following this, Runcorn gave a spirited display, their forwards dribbling to the Wigan end, where Walker crosssd the line, Butterworth even- tually grounding the ball for Moran to add a goal. Wigan attacked desperately in the last few minutes. Result—Runcorn 2 goals and 1 try (7 points), Wigan 1 goal (2 points). Teams and officials : Runcorn —Riohardson, back; Flanagan, Moran, Butterworth, and Unswortb, three-quarter backs; White and Watton, half backs; Padbury, Walker, Kennedy, Wood, Langley, and McDonald, forwards. Wigan—Sharrock, back; Leytham, Green' Price, and Miller, three-quarter backs; Thomas and Jones, half backs; Blears, Whittaker, Francis, Cheatham, Ramsdale, and Silcock, forwards.
Referee, Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton. Touch judges Messrs. F. Turner, Warrington, and E. J. Hannaford Si. Helens.
SALFORD v. WIDNES.

These teams met at the Willows, Weaste, when the game was only of a very poor description. Rain fell throughout and this no doubt affected the play, How- ever, after the gam3 had been in progress five minutes Radcliffe scored, for Mesley to add the goal points whilst shortly afterwards Adams succeeded in again, crossing the Widnes line, but Alesley failed to add the extra goal points. Crossing over with a lead of eight points, tte visitors were the first to attack, and Mosley had great difficulty in clearing his lines. Buckler started a dribble by the home forwards, and this led up to Raffcliffe scoring after really flue work by Adams, W. Thomas failing. Towards the close Widnes attacked, and Colgrave scored, for Daintith to add the goal points. Result : Salford 1 goal 3 tries (II points), Widnes 1 goal 1 try (5 points). Teams ; Salford—Mesley, full back ; Cooke, W. Thomas Adams, and Radcliffe, three-quarter backs; Preston and Johns, half-backs ; D. Rees, Buckler, E. Thomas, Curzon, Morten, and E. Rees, forwards. Widnes—Jones, full back; Reid, Lamb2rt, Taylor, and Dainteth, three-quarter backs ; Lalley aid O'Brien, half-backs; G. Aspey, S. Aspey, Johnson, Rigby, and Colgrave, forwards. At the top of the League once more ! The last time they reached this exalted position, Warrington were ,tleposed in the course of a few I—ours, but they should lead the way for a more respectable pariod this tima. After a study of the fixtures I don't see any reason Why Warrii.gton should not still be leaders when the New Year dawns. Such matches away as Oldham, %.Wakefield and Leigh spell danger, but I think the Wirepullers ought to get at least four points out of a Possible six. The home engagements are of a Promising character, and should be productive of raaxinium points on each occasion. It is a long cry to the League Championship, but no club is bettEr Placed than Warrington at present, and if the players Ret their hearts on it I feel sure they can secure a Ilaw laonour for the club and themselves.

On current form Warrington ought to come some- hero near repeating their big performance at Barrow last season. The Furness men have made no advance ;11,Id with the present dry weather holding out warrington should be seen at their best. They must make the game as open as possible and a big balance of Points is sure to follow.

~The selected team is exactly as last week, viz. : !Hey full back; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Prawley, three-quarters; Brooks and Jenkins, half- backs; Thomas, Shugars, Boardman, O'Neill, 'Malley and Belton, forwards.

t. Tho' A" team has a good home fixture with pbernberton, for whom " Bucky " Green and i'reharne are expected to play. Warrington's side „18 a strong one, viz.: Mclntyre, full back; Smith, ,vartwright, Lander and Bradshaw, threequarters ; v3/41°31 and Daintith, half backs; Bradshaw, Gibbs, Chesters, Worrall and P. Boardman, forwards.

44,1-en the Lancashire Cup-ties there should be some games. The ultimate winners I expect to be 17igaril Leigh, Swinton and Oldham. Though Runcorn leat Wigan last Saturday, I don't fancy them doing Lge same with Oldham, who are in my opinion the "%ost powerful team in the League to-day.
The County Match between Lanes and Yorks takes tee at Hull next Thursday. Lanes, for whom ugars is playing, should just about secure the erdict by extra cleverness behind.

i Last Saturday was one of the worst football days kaginable and the deluge of rain in the second half 11,1°Iliething quite out of the ordinary. The 26 players ,ePresenting. Warrington and Broughton Rangers ;'pt hard at it, however, and remarkable to relate 2r53' gave a display which never flagged in interest _l' one moment. As a rule wet weather means ambling football with a paucity of scoring—for :stance the Leigh match on the opening day! On turday the crowd at Wilderspool was treated to a ,el 7 lively game in which no less than 40 points Lere scored in the eighty minutes. Warrington were Ponsible for 27 out of the 40 points and thus 'co, red more than two to one against the Rangers. It Igould be said for the latter that they were weak in rll back division, such men as Hogg, Harris and ,o'l* being absentees. The forwards gave a capital `,41191ay, and some of the juniors behind did credit to wneir selectors. They were all triers, and on a day 'len scientific play is almost impossible energy °tints for nearly as much as skill.

r. The Rangers had the temerity to score first - Ze'ocl try too. After this barring occasional bursts Iter a loose ball, there was only one team in it. ;arrington played with dash and judgment. At times Ze handling of the wet ball was quite good, and the r,s_nning and punting of the backs outclassed the perienced men on the other side. Individually 40 or two men had a great day. Fish scored two 4°l his most brilliant tries and ran with wonderful 43eed on the heavy ground. On each occasion he Oded the Broughton full back with the ease which spoke - fishy " genius. Tilley too, gave a great I,lVitty at full 'back and few men could have sur- rased him under the circumstances. Among the "rwarde O'Malley was more prominent than usual v. got the final try—his first for Warrington—by " good following up which is a feature of his play,

Though Warrington continue to win matches there is much dissatisfaction with the back play of the team. • And not without reason. The combination is not by any means up to the mark. The passing is too methodical and too frequently drives the wing man to touch. Warrington had a reputation not long ago for resourceful handling, but they seem to be g .ing back to methods which were condemed imme- diately- the 13 aside game was introduced. How seldom we see the Warrington backs try the inside pass or the dummy? Yet they know all these moves and can carry them out if they want to do so.

The fault begins at the base of the scrum, where Brooks and Jenkins are not so effective as they were last season. Brooks has not shown a spark of that brilliancy which made him the half back of the year in 1908. The two halves have got into a stereo- typed method. For instance, if instead of running with the ball every time, Jenkins were to throw straight out to Brooks standing a bit wide the outside half would have more room and opportunities to shiiie. J. Thomas of Wigan shows how well this plan can be turned into account. A variation of method is required and there should be no hesitation about trying experi- Ments. The team which takes the trouble to think will come out top in N.U. football.

I would like to give a hint to Taylor. He has apparently not realised that he is less speedy than of yore and is spoiling a good deal of his centre play by running too far with the ball. Once he has beaten his man he should put his wing in possession as quickly as possible and let speed do the rest. Instead Taylor frequently tries to beat half the team and gets collared. Mmy a good opening goes a-begging in this way. Once the centre has cut through he should let the ball go unless his wing is covered. It is sheer folly for him to attempt more, and especially so when he lacks the speed. Both our centres are slower than they should be, but I will give Dickenson the credit of knowing how far to go. He makes two openings to Taylor's one with equal opportunities. The one thing in which he has fallen aw.ly is tackling. It is not often now, that we see- Dickenson breaking up the opposing three-quarter line in the way which used to earn him fame. There is too much going for the pass and missing the man with the ball, for my liking.

Frawley made his debut with the senior team on Saturday, and did little which aroused enthusiasm. He 'Could not have appeared under worse conditions, and the way Taylor neglected him was enough to make any man feel out of the picture. Once or twice

when the ball did come to Frawley he seemed too starved to do much with it. I saw him play some fine games with the Kangaroos and I feel sure that when he has got his football legs back again he will dis- tinguish himself in the Warrington jersey.

The "A." team continued its winning career at Broughton. where the young Rangers—hitherto undefeated—were put through their paces by a superior side. Warrington won 11 -2, which can be counted a very gool performance in weather which militated against,skilful football.

Played at St. Helens in boisterous weather, before a good attendance. Prescott stirted against the wind and rain, and Bland knocking on St. Helens took up an attacking position on the Dewsbury line. Dewsbury were penalised for obstruction, and Creevey failed to land a goal. After Wade and Bland had failed to cross for Dewsbury, St. Helens forwards combinei, and from a dribhle to the line Mavity scored. Turtill took the place kick, and landed a goal. The visitors livened up after this reverse, and from some neat passing between their hacks Everson cross-kicked to Wade who eluded Creevey and dashed over at the corner. Stringer kicked a grand goal from the touch line. Half-time score : St. Helens 1 goal 1 try (5 points), Dewsbury, 1 goal, 1 try (5 points). Brayshaw started the second portion with the wind at his back, and St. Helens early on had to defend. ' St. Helens forwards rallied, and a dribble to the line took place, Bradley eventually crossing. C. Creevey failed to improve from an easy position. Dewsbury asserted themselves, and Wade scored his .second try for the visitors. Stringer made a poor attempt to convert. With honours even both sides attacked desperately, but without avail. Result :—St. Helens 1 goal « tries (8 points), Dewsbury, 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points). Teams and officials :

St. Helens—H. S. Turtill, back; C. Creevey, "Matt" Creevey, James Greenwood, aad J. Flanagan, three- quarter backs ; F. Trenwith and H. Greenwood, half hacks ; Briers, Bradley, Prescott, Helsby, Mavity, and Pope, forwards. Dewsbury—Gerratty, buck; Wade, Blald, Stringer, and Rhodes. three-qnarter backs ; Bra37shaw and Everson, half backs; Smith, Kilburn, Edwards, Abbott, Garnett, and Hammill, forwards. Referee. Mr. H. Edmondson, Bradford. Touch judges, Messrs. 4. Priestley (Broughton) and T. Foulkes (St. Helens).

WARRINGTON " A " V. BROUGHTON RANGERS "A.'— These teams met at Broughton on Saturday in miser- able weather. Warrington were always superior, and in the first half scored through the medium of Bradshaw, who put on the finishing touch to a smart round of passing. Turning round Smith scored and later on Warrington added another try, which Mclntyre goaled. Broughton Rangers rallied, and Swambo placed a goal. Final :—Wrrrington, one goal three tries (It points) ; Broughton Rangers, one goal (two points).

PEARSON AND KNOWLES v. TEIATTO HEATH. Played at Wilddrspool-road on Saturday last. P. & K. won the toss and Worrall kicked off for the visitors. Asdton for P. S; K. made a grand return. A scrimmage on the visitors 25 line ended in Tbatto Heath touching down. • Some grand play by the visitors' backs took the game to the home team's line. Smart passing by Spencer and Tickle (who made a grand run and kicked over the fullbacks head) should have resulted in some- thing tangible for P. S; K. but they were obstructed when a score seemed certain. P. &K. were awarded a free kick. Spencer made an attempt at goal but failed. Half-time :—No score. Heath resumed for the home team and at owe P. &K. attacked but met a sound defence from the next scrimmage. P. and K. were penalised for off side play. Jones made a fine attempt at goal for the visitors, the ball hitting the oross-bar and bouncing into play. Hockenhall kicked away and a race for the ball between Jones (T. H.) and Tickle (P. It K.) ended in favour of the home team. Result :—No score. To-day P. & K. meet Stockton Heath at Stockton Heath. Referee: Mr. Acton, of Widnes.

RYLANDS' RECS. V. ST. HELENS WHITE ROSE.— What with the rain, the wind and the muddy ground Rylands Recs. and St. Helens White Rose bad their their work out out on Saturday last on the ground of the latter to play at all, but however, a good match ensued. Rylands' bad to play uphill and against the wind and rain dur ng the first half. Soon after the start Furness for the visitors got bold of the ball and ran threiquarters of the length of the field but was pushed into touch when only 5 yards off the line. From a scrumrnageGallop,for Rylands kicked the bill, followed it up, and got whit was thought by the spectators to be a try, but it was disallowed. Half- time : Rylands' Rees, nil ; St. Helens, nil. On turning round Floyd (Rylands) from a pack dropped a beautiful goal. Furness again had hard lines fOr after dribbling the ball a considerable length of the field he was unable to "gather" and lost it close to the line. White Rose were penalised and Floyd kicked a goal. As soon as the ball came out Horrocks got bold of it and after • a desperate run secured a try, which was converted by Floyd. Result : Rylands' Recs, 9 points; St. Helens,nil.
STOCKTON HEATH V. WIDNES WII IT E STAR.—The above match was played at Widnes on Saturday in stormy weather. The home team won, defeating Stockton Heath by 10 points to 5 points.

SUTTON COMMERCIAL V. WARRINGTON ALBION.— The Albions journeyed to Sutton on Saturday and had to admit defeat after a hard-fought game. The visitors had the advantage of the wind in the flist half. Sutton at once got into the Albion's quarters through Fildes, Makin saving splendidly from a hard drive by Bradley. Warrington then made play on the right and forced two abortive cqrners. Thomas made a good attempt to lower the home goal. The home forwards then took the gome to the other end, where Dilworth made a smart nlearance". Hardy shot in splendidly, Makin again coming to the rescue. With the wind Warrington were often dangerous, but the home defence was sound Richardson shot over the tar. From a good position Whitfield made a tricky run without making any pro- gress. Makin again saved well from Fades and Nolan when hard pressed. Half-time :--Sutton, nil; Warring- ton Albion, nil. In the second half Sutton penetrated the defence once And won by one goal to nil.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The last word in ventriloquism has evidently not been said yet. Coram, the ventriloquist from the Alhambra, who tops the bill at the Hippodrome this week is original from beginning to end of a most laughable performance. The repartee between him- self and his doll is quite the smartest we have heatd in this line, and the rapidity of the talk is a great tribute to Coram's wonderful ventriloquial powers. "You must positively hear Coram," as the bills say. The night we attended this week was certainly a merry one. A lady in the circle saw the funny aide of Takio's " imataysongs," and every time he uttered the word in his peculiar nasal drawl this lady went into shrieks of laughter. As Takio proceeded with those inimitable mimicries of his, the laughter grew louder and longer until even the artiste was infected by the mirth, and the poor lady was almost exhausted with her paroxysms. Needless to say the audience enjoyed the turn in the circle as much as the one on the stage. Arayama, a typical small nimble Jap, created a sensation with his exploits on the tight wire, and bamboo trick which he challenges the world to imitate. Briefly he walks up two smooth vertical 12 foot bamboo poles with nothing but hand and toe grip, and then moves about the stage like a Man on stilts. It is an astonishing feat. EscoUrt creates a good impression with some clever conjuring and sleight of hand tricks to a running vocal and orchestral accompaniment. With a bottle and plate he rivals Cinquevalli as a juggler. Charles Santon's speciality is double- voiced singing, baritone and soprano. While not a very attrae tive accomplishment his singing is sufficiently remarkable to earn applause. A couple of good novelty songs in humorous character are sub- mitted by Fred Lincoln, who keeps his audience in an audible titter. Lily Arthur, comedienne, and Blanco White and Miss Clifford, vaudeville artistes and dancers, contribute turns which do not rank above the ordinary. The Palace pictures are of never-failing interest, and the orchestral work under Mr. Widdop maintains its usual high standa d.

div.head: ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTH.
div.p: ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTH.

One is always sorry when one of the old guard disappears, and the news that .Bobby Walker and the Heart of Midlothian club are friends again is very welcome. WO should have keenly regretted the dropping out of Walker from the game he has played, and still plays after all these "years so well. Walker is slow nowadays, maybe; but is there such an artist? his influ- ence in any team cannot be estimated. Walker's football is a splendid lesson to all youngsters; it is a fine art, deeply thought out, the work of the master. The cunning of the man is colossal. I was, discussing Walker's play with an old Inter- national the other day, and the question cropped up whether cleverness entirely compensated for lack of speed. A good, fast man is most times to be preferred ta a footballer who is slow but intensely clever; but Walker occupies a position c.sf splendid isolation; I do not know that there is any forward exactly like him. He may not be able to run very fast, you cannot expect him to be as sprightly as he used to be, but Walker's Presence can still make a whole forward line. In ether days Sandy McMahon used to play for Celtic; he was very slow, as the old-timer knows, but he was absolutel3;, a great man. With
le "gECoNic 11-/,17.

Campbell, who afterwards played with Aston Villa, he made one of the finest wings that ever did duty for Scotland. And we have Peter Somers, whom Blackburn people were so sorry to lose, a -tremendous player, but without any speed at all. Then there is Alexander Turnbull, of Manchester United, who amply jcgs along, but whose subtlety is wonderful. In some ways his understanding with Meredith recalls the as- sociation of Bassett and -Geddes. The latter, like Turnbull, seemed to understand to a nicety what to expect from the right wing; how many times has Geddes turned the celebrated Bassett cross- shot as it was whizzed in from the corner flag into a goal? Those were great days at West Bromwich.

Two (irent Half-Backs. It is very difficult to understand why it is that such an accomplibed footballer as James Turn- bull, who leads the Cupholders, finds it so hard to preserve an even temper. I have never known a case where a man has been sent off the field two Saturdays running. I am afraid Turn- bull will be kept out of the game for some time when his conduct comes before the Football Association. One is always sorry for a player who is sent off; oftener than not he 4s really a good fellow, and from what I know of Turnbull lam sure he is very much in the doldrums. It was quite an achievement for Manchester United to win at Dramall-lane. Candidly, I did not think they were equal to the task, for it has boon very plain in recent matches that the Cue- holders are scarcely playing so well as at this
rrz \CI-9 1-e

time last season. I wonder 'whether us game will help the members of the Englivh Selectiot: Committee. One is specially interested to sec whether Charles Roberts is asked .to represent his county this season instead of Wedlock, of Bristol City. Somehow, Roberta has scarcely been at his best in representative matches. whereas the little .wonder of the West Countr, revels in an International. The play of Weel• lock and Roberts has always caused a difference of opinion, but I think it ..will be (0:1 ceded that, ati a footballer pure and sirn,h, Roberts is the -superior of Wedlock, though ith- latter for his inches is unique in the .way he cat. break up combination. In a set test I think I should stand' on Wedlock, ,but for all that Roberts remains one of the finest centre -half backs the game has ever known, and, like hi:: great rival, is scrupulously fair. A Ray of Sunshine at Phimstead

The man who expected that Woolwich Arsenal would defeat Everton, though the game v: # played. at Plumstead, must have been absolut..-.:, opposed to the idea that thCre is such a thing a: "form." And yet Woolwich, despite the hug( crop of goals that hae been reaped at their ex pense, were successful. I am sure that mast have surprised themselves. Well, I L. their victory will do them a power of good; 1: outlook at Plumstead is pretty well as bad as n can be—a lean purse and a very Uncertain tean make for serious trouble. But, I say, Evert,n. will have to pull themselves together; they seen. to have gone back in a very extraordinary way. A young player about whose capabilities not : great aPal is known—one Thompson, who cam.

to the notice of the Woolwich ofilcirt!s as a pro mising• centre-half—led the Woolwich forwarch in this game, and he had the distinction o scoring the goal which gave his club their much needed victory. From what I have been told. however. Thompson has still to complete MI football lessons. Still, he has begun very well.

Glossop Doing Well. Burnley is very much like Barnsley—it is the burying-place of reputations. I do not know twc centres so dreaded by teams fighting for promo- tion as these places are. Some of the very best sides have come a cropper at Barnsley and Turf Moor.' and Fulham people, if they only knew, would not be so distressed by the defeat of their team a week ago. I do not suppose for one moment that Burnley have any idea of getting back to the First Division, but they can certc•tmly do this—they can stop others winning this tiis- tinct'on. The race for a place in the premier League, as it ever was, is delightful topsy-tur- vydom. Hull are kccping their head in front, but an upheaval is likely any week-end. Glo's- sop, for instance, are well on their toes, as some would say; if they maintain their present form—certainly if they continue to play as they did against Manchester. City—they are bound to go to the first place. Time Glossop team, with- out & doubt, is one of the surprises of the sea- son. At different times, notably-when a place was won in the First Division, the Glossop officials have had a happy knack of getting bold of rood players; Glosson brousaht out. Goddard. of Liverpool, Irvine Thornley, of Manchester City, and Herbert Burgess. of the Manchester United. And "Punch" McEwan was one of the players who helped the Dorlcihire club into the First Division.
