div.head: PLAY'S THE THING.
div.p: THE PLAY'S THE THING.
BY JOSEPH HATTON,
ituihor of "By Order of the Czar," "The Princess Masaroil, " "The Banishment of Jessoißlythe," "When Greek Meets Greek,"

"Walk up, walk up! Be in time!" bawled the :.iown, in a hoarse voice. He had been clowning, outside and inside that very show, night and day during the whole fair-time, and this was the last day of the Statute carnival. Oil lamps and heavy dips illuminated the exterior of the theatre. The clown -needed great lung power. He had to contend with a menagerie and its brass band, a living waxwork, the speaking trumpets of rival impresarios, and many other com- peting and complicated noises. But he was of a persevering and hopeful nature. "Be in time!" he cried. "Be in time!" And to emphasise his earnest invitation, he beat his drum and banged his cymbals. "Comedy, tragedy, and farce, by the most renowned company of his Majesty's servants, who have played before the Court, and hope again to entertain the King and his friends, including many of the test crowned heads of Europe! Be in time! Walk up! Three- pence will admit you to comfortable seats, each with a 'velvet cushion. For the last time, this evening, in three acts, The Murder of the Banker of Eastcheap,' one of the greatest and most moral plays of the century!" "You may say that, sir," remarked an elderly gentleman of the company, stepping forward from the rest of the players, who were promenading the high platform by which the theatre was entered. "Gnilty creatures, sitting at a play, have been so moved, saith the Bard of all Time, that they have presently confessed their malefactions." "Therefore, be in time!" said the clown; and it seemed to Dick Jeffery that he pointed his white finger at him; not only pointed at him, but lobked him straight in the eye. "Young men and maidens, and hoary-headed sinners, all the good, the bad, the virtuous, an.-1 the evildoer be in time!"

Dick Jeffery felt that., however the clown modified the invitation, it was levelled at him. He tried to avoid the jester, whose chalked, face, with its red patches, seemed to grow until it filled the market- place ' • and his. voice drowned all others, as he yelled: "The last time, to-night! Perhaps the last time on earth! Walk tip, walk up! The Murder ti 7 the Banker of Eastcheap,' a drama in three act-, founded upon fact; an entertainment and a moral! ' Then it seemed to Dick as if the speaker stooped down to him, and whispered: "If you are afraid to be seen walking up the steps and crossing this outer stage, there is a side-door, and reserved seats at sixpence; nobody need see you." But the truth was the clown, as a parting shot for the better dressed of the crowd, only said: "Ladies and gentlemen, you who are too modest to mount these steps--may you never have to mount any more terrible—there is a side door round the corner, where you may find special seats at sixpence; though all the seats are alike, inasmuch as you can Fee and hear from every part of the spacious theatre. Ile in time! The great moral sensation is about to begin. Three acts of tragic and immortal truth. Walk up! Walk up! Or pass round to the. side door! "

The motley company paraded to and fro in their costumes, some of which rather betokened the classic than the modern drama. The elderly artist who had spoken was evidently the banker who was to be murdered. The leading lady was fat, fair, and over forty; and wore a headdress of feathers hardly eclipsed by the fashions of our own day, and she was hooped as severely as Queen Elizabeth at a State function. The hero of the play was dressed in the extreme fashion of the time.

"Ladies and gentlemen," said the elderly actor, addressing the crowd, "the company will execute one cotillion before retiring behind the green curtain of the stage to prepare for the representa- tion of one of the most thrilling tragedies of real life ' that has ever been presented to an English audience." Whereupon, offering his hand to the leading lady, while the clown played his pipes and beat his drum, he and the rest of the troupe of comedians trod a graceful measure and then retired, watched with straining eyes by Dick Jeffery, who, apart from having drunk more than was good for him at the fair, was racked by remorse for a crime he had not yet committed. "You can learn the character of our theatre from witnesses all around you. There was a servant. man at this Statute fair to-day who was hired by a would-be master: Now, Hodge had not obtained a written character. So his would-be employer waitea until the evening for Hodge to get one. That would-be master was a bad man; not bad by force of evil companions, same as the young man in this play, but bad by birth and inclination, so it was good for Hodge that he had a respite before taking the fastening penny. When the evening came, the would-be employer said: Well, good fellow, Hodge, have you got your character? ' ' No,' replied Hodge, grinning, ' but I've gotten yourn ; and you're not the master for me! ' "

The crowd laughed heartily at this humorous tribute to the local wit, and the clown, taking up a speaking-trumpet and laying aside his drum, bellowed: "Friends, one and all, this Theatre Royal has long ago obtained its written character, and yours is 'inscribed across the history of the ages, as a community of taste, students of the arts and patrons of the drama. Then, once more, and for the very last time, let me urge you to be in time. Be in time! Threepence will admit, you to one of the most intellectual and moral entertainments that has ever visited this ancient and renowned borough of Reading-on-the-Thames."

There was now a general response to the merry man's eloquent invitation. All the time, it seemed to Dick' that the clown was only saying to him : "Don't be afraid! Come in by the side-door! Nobody will see you. The great drama of The Murder of the Banker of Eastcheap! ' The curtain is rising, the actors are on the scene."

Then, all at once, everything else appeared to vanish, except this one show and this one clown. The actor, himself, and the moon comprised the audience and players. But the clown stooped over the railing that divided him from the rest of the market-place, and said: "No, you are mistaken; the fair is in full swing ; don't you hear the music? That is not the moon. It is the lamp of ' the high and mighty Soboenski, magician to all the crowned heads of Europe, but more particularly to his Supreme Majesty the Emperor of Morocco. Come! Fear nothing! Just round the corner, the side-door reserved for the aristocracy and the intimate friends of Jonathan Wild!"
Dick shook himself, rubbed his eyes, and sneaked round to the side door.
"Very drunk," remarked a townsman. "Like fathpr like son; and I can say tliat4for I knowed his father."

Dick Jeffery was a clerk in the mercantile house of Barnaby Dakin Fryer. He was only three-and- twenty. When first he went up to London he was a gentle, quiet, and honest youngster, but by-and- bye he fell in with Mistress Nannie Lightfoot, one of the most fascinating of Jonathan Wild's petti- coat allies. Dick's downfall was rapid. Ho enlisted Into Wild's corps of gallants of the road, even condescended on occasion to pick a pocket; was kept up to his nefarious work by the exigent demands of his mistress, and was presently dismissed by his master, not on account of dishonesty, but because his dissipated life brought disgrace on the house and was a bad example to the other clerks. At the same time the dear old gentleman, out of regard for the lad's father, made him an allowance, until such time as he reformed or could find other employment, and by personal effort and otherwise tried to wean him from his evil courses. He even went so far as to plead with Mistress Lightfoot, and Jonathan Wild himself had undertaken to help Master Fryer in breaking the lad away from his evil companions. Jonathan Wild, as you know, was a humorist. It is true he jested with serious things. He was a humorist all the same. In his picture there is, in pose and staff, a suggestion of the old-world Punch of the first and most lasting of melodrama. Wild's truncheon was a silver bilton, with a crown on the top. It was made in his own atelier, in the Old Bailey. London thought it wat a legal symbol of office. Wild had other humorous symbols. He was thief-taker and thief-maker. It was his humour to be both bandit and justice. He knock, d people about, metaphorically, with as little con • punction as Punch in the old original show. His humour was so grim that, when Fielding sat down to write the life of the Macchiavelli of Thieves, he could only make it a peg for his own subtle jesting. Ti) Jonathan, the greatest joke of all was the gallows, lie gave it pet names. Never a month passed that he did not have someone hanaed. Most

)f his victims were the rebellious of his own gangs. If his subjects did not deal fairly by him in the aistribution of their plunder, he indicted and hanged theta. There was no difficulty about it. lie was so very humorous that he kept a set of suborned witnesses, who swore whatever he required them to swear, and in one of the departments of his Old Bailey house a company of artiet3 replaced old plate marks with new ones, re-set jewellery, broke up precious stones, and forged every kind of document.

Dick . had • betrayed the secrets of Fryers' counting-house and strong-room sufficiently , to enable certain of Wild's experts to remove sundry valuable securities. Now, Wild was regarded by some of the wealthiest and most eminent persons in the realm as a safe medium for the recovery of lost and stolen goods. The front part of his house in the Old Bailey was indeed kept as an office for the purposes of this agency. Now and then Wild would obtain the restoration of .property that was difficult to dispose of, and on several occasions hq had actually restored jewels, and even money, by which astute policy he managed for a long time to establish confidence with the public, while he enforced discipline among his servants by threats of the gallows and the frequent application of that triangular weapon. He had shewn Dick Jeffery a document, signed by his master, in which Barnaby Dakin Fryer besought Jonathan Wild to hand the young man over to Justice, and gave Wild such apparent evidence of the lad's infidelities and ne- farious deeds as would warrant his immediate arrest. The document was couched in terms of bitter regret ; and, in conclusion; the writer confessed that it were better Dick were dead than live to commit crimes that should make his name infamous for all time. .

If Dick had been clever he might have doubted Lime genuineness of this document. But he was not clever, and, moreover, he was weakened, physically and mentally, by the unwholesome life he bad been leading; and during a well-timed debauch of wine, Wild forecast in grim detail the old man's death.

"lie would slay you," he said. "Take the hull by the horns, or rather, Fryer by the throat. Life's a battle, especially yours. The soldier kills his man to prevent his man killing him." "Kill poor old Fryer I " said Dick "who never said an unkind word to me! My father, had he lived, would have flayed me alivd had I deceived him as I have deceived his friend, dear old Master Fryer." "Dear old scoundrel! A known backslider! I could have him shot as a traitor, a scheming jacobite. "
"No! You jest ? " "Do I ever j est ? " "Sometimes," said the lad. Jonathan grinned and filled up the lad's glass. "When do I jest ? " "When Jack Ketch has one of your enemies by the neck."
"You are not one of my enemies, and curse me to all Eternity if I mean old Fryer to hang you, my lad!"

"He loves me," said Dick, with maudlin conceit, "loves the very ground I walk on, as Nannie does. Fryer hang me!" "He has warned - Nannie against you, and if I were not your friend, as it is my duty to be, you would be in Newgate at his suit this very minute." "On your oath ? " "On the oath we have both sworn, to be true to each other. Now listen. To-day you will go by coach to Reading. At night you will be seen at the Nag's Head. To-morrow you will visit your friends. The Statute fair is being held. It will be a natural thing for you to be there. Go to the shows, buy fairings for your sweethearts. say, 'don't say your love is confined to Nannie. At sun- set you will slip away to the Bath-road a f3w hundred yards beyond the Green Man Tavern. There you will find my horse and Larry Be t, the Maim You will ride like the deuce. On the road you will find relays of horses. See how care fin l lam of you. You and the Rufiler will be at the Black Horse in town by eleven o'clock. At twelve you will be in the library of that arch traitor, your malignant master; and if it should become necessary, which it will not, you will have a host of witnesses to prove that you were at Reading at the time it will be said old Fryer gave up the ghost and his cash-box. You must needs be punctual, for Master Barnaby Dakin Fryer propoges to leave at daylight for Dover on a mission to Paris. He means to carry with him a valise or casket of gold and notes for the King's service. Larry Best will be your ally; but; if necessary, he may be your executioner. Don't start boy, the good General takes precautions and Best is my most trusted Lieutenant and ydu my most promising subaltern." "You said Master Fryer was a Jacobite." "I say so still. The King's service is a blind. Either way makes good our game. Furthermore—. this in your private ear—he has papers that are compromising both to you and me." "To you? "
"It i wolf against wolf between hint and me— he a Jacobite, I an agent of the King's Govern- ment."
"I don't understand ? "
"You are too trusting. To you old Fryer is an honest and loyal man. Yet he has your head in the hangman's noose, and would have m:ne there too." "Is he so vile?"

"Judge for yourself," said Jonathan, handing him the document he had previously only quoted. "Judge for yourself. You ought to know his handwriting." "As Alen as my own." "Very well; read." Dick took the forged paper, examined it, turned it over, saw the familiar seal of the house of Barnaby Dakin Fryer, and noted, as he thought, the unmistakable signature. Then read the indict- ment of himself, addressed: "To Master Wild, in confidence and privacy." At this crucial moment Wild signalled his janitor and confidant, Maseer Quilt, and, the door opening, there entered Mistrees Nannie Lightfoot in all her glory of silks and perfumes, laughing eyes and radiant complexion. "He'll do it, Nannie," said Wild, greeting her. "A lad of mettle, I'll warrant you. No more harass for money, no more stint for well-earned pleasures ; Banelagh, Vauxhall, the Mint--" "Ali, my beauty!" exclaimed Nannie. "I was longing to see you." And she gave the lad a hearty hug. "Tell him, Nannie, for none knows so well, that Jonathan Wild is only the enemy of the wealthy and the tyrannical ; that his troop of gallants only relieve the idle rich of their ill-gotten gold and the avaricious merchant of his easy gains. By the powers, if old Fryer of Eastcheap was no worse than his neighbours in this respect his hypocrisy deserves death! Aye, his hypocrisy," he repeated, in answer to a questioning look from Dick. "Have you not seen it yourself? To the deuce with such pretended friends, who smile and smile and tie the rope round your neck all the time." Then Quilt entered with two bottles of wine, and a servant followed with a tray of other dainty refreshment.

"We see no other callers, Quilt, until our present company quits." "Now, Nannie, my belle of belles and Dick's devoted, I drink to you, and success to Dick's great adventure. At the moment Dick hasn't a penny to bless himself with. Have you, Dick ?" "I'm as poor as a church mouse," said the lad, with a grim smile. "To-morrow you shall be as wealthy as an Archbishop. Here's to you, my brave son of Fortune!'

"And to our next merry meeting!" said Nannie, and they all three touched glasses and tossed off the inspiring liquor. After a gay hour or two Dick made his prepara- tions for a visit to his native town of Reading.

It was a great thing now and then for Wild to really establish beyond all doubt a genuine alibi, and his good faith having been questioned in a late important matter he meant to kill two birds with one stone in Dick's person. It was his intention to have Dick duly arrested for the crime be had instigated, if only for the purpose of securing his acquittal on the undoubtable evidence that, while the murder was being perpetrated Dick was among his friends at Reading, for nothing, be knew, would be easier than to get over the discrepancy of an hour or so when plenty of evidence would be forth- coming that Dick was on a visit to his native town, at fair-time, on the night when his master was robbed and done to death in the back parlour of Eastcheap.

Dick smelt the sawdust of the show and the orange peel, and heard the fiddles, hit still seemed to be alone, lie had sneaked in at the side-door and paid his sixpence, and found himself on a form all by himself. Although the booth was more than half-full he around and saw, in his confused fancy, only a grey warm mist, illuminated by a ring of sweating candles. Once he thought there were eyes in the mist. and once there were tears in his own.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909

This ocCurred when the fiddles played the tar of "My Lodging is on the Cold Ground," which was a song his mother used to sing when he was a little fellow and said his prayers by her knee at nights; and somehow the words now seemed to dance in his memory. "Matthew. Mark. L tki and John, God bless the bed that I lie on." • • As the last wor4s danced out of his memory he was sitting by the Thames at hay-time, with a girl to whom he swore undying love. Then he was alloat.on the river in a skiff that took him Over weirs and through locks without impediment., and he was drifting out to sea, to he rescued by a pirate ship, which they called Jonathan Wild, and the captain had a skull and cross-bones painted on his blouse. Then once more he heard the fiddles, and was conscious of a row of lighted •candles in front of .him and a green curtain, and he said: "I knew where I am. It is the play." And, sure enough, at the moment the curtai9 went up on the first. scene of the dramatic story. It represented a room, not too well furnished, but intended to be the home of a siren of the gay world of London. The lady was that ample beauty whom Dick had seen on the platform outside, but to him she was Nannie Lightfoot. He rubbed his eyes and looked around him; still the same mysterious void, though he heard voices. The siren was looking from a window, and beckoning to someone, and there entered—who, but himself? . . . Though he was sitting there between the footlights and the auditorium, there he was on the stage, to all intents and purposes—gay, bright, well dressed. Then followed a short love scene, in which Dick was the successful of a hundred lovers. At the close other persons entered, and the curtain came down on a scene of riot and debauchery, so far as such gay life could be presented by a limited company of players and a not too numerous collection of stage properties. The next scene was more to the purpose of the play. It needed plenty of imagination on the part of the audience to realise that it was the private room of a great merchant, with maps, cabinets and strong boxes, and, at the moment, evidence that its owner was packing for a journey. Dick's fancy supplied every deficiency. Was not the room perfectly familiar to him ? Who knew it so well? It was his master's private office in Eastcheap 1 • • • At first he did not see the face of the old gentleman, who was stooping over a valise that was open on the table; but, hearing footsteps, the traveller half-turned his face as if listening. Then Dick saw that the actor was no mimic representa- tion of life, tut his master, dear old Barnaby Dakin Fryer. . . . Nor had the old man been deceived. There entered, crouching from behind with a knife in his hand, the criminal who was to rob him, not only of his money but of his life. It was Dick himself! Dick, with a murderous expression on his face! Dick, about to leap at the throat of the man who had been his best, friend!

Dick, in the play, crept towards his master. Dick, in the audience, tried to exclaim "Back, villain! Desist! They'll hang you. Oh, for Heaven's sake, dye not your hands with blood!" But no sound came from his lips. Then he endeavoured to rush upon the stage, but he could not move. . . . A tran in the next seat leant over and asked him if he was ill. Dick had unconsciously groaned as one in pain. But a cry of "Order! sent the man back to his place, and the play went on. . . . All suddenly the old man saw his assailant; but before he could challenge him the murderer stabbed him to death. In his dying moments the victim murmured: "May God forgive you, as I do!" "Why did you denounce me?" demanded the assassin.
"I never did. I loved you as a father." "You nought my death through Jonathan Will?"

"I never sought anything that was not for your good." Upon which the old man breathed his last,:and the murderer fell, sobbing, upon his corpse. It seemed to the audience as the curtain went down, that the player's mobs were repeated in the front row of the pit, as in truth they were. A rush of tears had come to Dick's relief.

"You are sick," said his kindly neighbour, once more coming to his assistance. "I shall be better soon," the young man said, and relapsed again into semiconsciousness. "It's the play that's upsa him," remarked the kindly neighbour. "Had too much wino, that's what's the matter with him," commented more than one of the bystanders. Then there was a cry of "Order!" and "Turn him out!" as the curtain rose again to the grue- some scraping of fiddles. . . . And now came the last scene of all. It was Tyburn, with Dick in the cart standing by his own coffin, and the clergy- man exhorting him for the list time to repentance. There was, however, an accessory group that only one of the audience saw. It was Dick's father and mother and the sweetheart of his youthful days, before ever he knew Nannie Lightfoot. They were kneeling at the foot of the Fatal Tree. . . . When the executioner adjusted the rope round the neck of Dick in the cart, Dick in the auditorium staggered to his feet, with a wild scream that com- pleted the terrible realism of the scene. "Save him! . . Mercy! . . . For his mother's sake! . . . Mercy Mercy ! " As Dick fell forward towards the stage one of the fiddlers, who had played the old tune of the mad Lover, caught him in his arms. He was dead. Tuc Eno. 1 •
THE LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAMSHIP CO.

The report of the directors—Mr. Henry Mao Ivor (chairman), Mr. Walter L. Nichels (vice-chairman), Sir R. Williams Bulk°ley. Bart., Mr. Thomas B. Barlow, Colonel Henry Platt, C. 8., and Mr. William H. Dodd— of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company, to be presented at the 20th ordinary general meeting, to be held on Tuesday, 2nd November, states that although the weather during the season was not favourable, and with the exception of a fortnight in August, left much to be desired, the company's steamers have on the whole been well patronised. For the further extension and development of the business in North Wales, the company purchased an additional small steamer at the commencement of the season. This steamer was named the St. Trillo, and has been regularly employed from June until the beginning of October with very satisfactory results. After deduct- ing the sum of £5,885 2s. 7d. for depreciation, the amount available for dividend and other purposes, including the balance brought forward from last season, is £5,468 19s. 2d., out of which the directors recommend the payment of a dividend of 6 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, carrying forward a balance of £1,616 19s. 2d. The directors retiring by rotation are Mr. W. L. Nickels and Colonel Henry Platt, C. 8., who are eligible for re-election. The retiring auditors, Messrs. Chalmers, Wade and Co., are also eligible for re-appointment.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
SLUM AREAS AND THE DEATH RATE.

The final meeting of the Warrington Town Council for the municipal year was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), presiding. There were also present :—The Deputy. Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Aldermen A. Bennett, T. Burton and James Evans; Councillors T. Birtles, J. Broadhurst, T. Chantler, J. G. Craik, E. Cunnington, J. Dickenson, J. Halliwell, J. Hawthorn, G. C. Howard, P. T. Lashford, J. T. Locker, H. Roberts, W. Rogers, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. Fulton-Smith, 0, Toole, G. N. Vernon, J. Wilkinson, and W. J. Wilson; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), A. r. Halliway (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Deas (water engineer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), F. V. L. Mathias (tlectrical engineer), J. M. Murray (director of [educa- tion), F. G. Ruddock (borough analyst) and Dr. J. C. Hibbert (medical officer).

CORPORATIONS AND TiIEIR, LEGAL BATTLES. The MANOR said : It may be convenient hero to report, that I and the Tot% Clerk attended the autumn general meeting of the Association of Municipal Cor- porations, and that the motion in which I proposed that all Corporations ought to contribute to the legal expense in all cases in which there is a common interest, as, for instance, the two recent cases concerning the dismissal of married women teachers, was passed unani- mously.

The Mayon also said : I luxe pleasure in reporting that, after paying all expenses in connection with the King's visit (including several items which were not properly chargeable against my salary, I have handed a cheque to the Borough Tre tsurer for the balance amounting to £B9 10s. 7d. STREET IMPROVEMENT CONINIITTEE.

At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Light- ing Committee the Chairman (Alderman Bennett) presented his report on the Continental Town Planning Tour. It was resolved that the thanks of this Com- mittee be given to Mr. Alderman Bennett for his valuable and instructive report. The question of the purchase of the property at the corner of Wharf-street wrs again considered, and it was resolved, that the same be not purchased. Alderman BENNETT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, took occasion to enter a protest against- the committee's policy with regard to Knutsford-road. He bad objected to the sale of land there on several occasions hut he bad been defeated. Councillor CRATE seconded.

Councillor BROADHURST asked when the report of Alderman James Evans as to the street lighting of Sankey Bridges would be considered by the committee. Alderman BENNKrr replied that it had been decided to wait until the new committee had been appointed when the whole of the question of the lighting of the into. The would be gone The minutes were agreed to. • NOTIFICATION OF BIRTHS ACT.

Alderwan JAMES EVANS, in proposing the adoptson .of the minutes of the Health Committee, alluded to the resolution that the Town Clerk take the necessary steps with a view to the adoption of the Notification a Births Act, 1907. He said they did not at present know what the cost to the town would be; but the medical profession thought they ought to have some remuneration which was not allowed under the Act. Every birth was to he registered within 24 hours.

div.head: OUR SLUM AREAS.
div.p: OUR SLUM AREAS.

At a meeting of the Health Committee the report of the special sul.-committee appointed by the Paving and Sewerage, Sanitary Works,and the Health Committees to consider the conditiun of common courts and yards in the borough was submitted and the consideration thereof deferred ur the next meeting. The report stated that steps s ould at once be taken to remedy the evils arising out of badly paved and ventilated courts and yards in the town. There could be little doubt that the conditions undt r which the dwellers in those courts live were reTonsible to a very great extent for the high death-rate. The present state of the courts was due to a variety of causes—unsatisfac- tory condition of the pavements and insanitary and ill- ventilated property. It would undoubtedly take con- siderable time, but with the active co-operation of the owners of property, improved conditions would be obtained.

Alderman JAMES EVANS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that in 1907 the Medical Officer gave a startling report about one or two questions affecting directly the health of the town, and he also referred to the slum area in which the death rate was 53.1 and the birth rate 511, so that they were" about a child and a half " better off for all those born in the slum area in Warrington. The general death rate of the town was 15.7. if it were not for the terribly high death rate of the slum area in all probability the death rate would compare favourably with any town in Lancashire. The high death rates among the slum dwellers were undoubtedly aggravated by the conditions under which they lived. These slum dwellings were, as a rule, badly ventilated, and even the so-called fresh air Admitted into the rooms was for the most put taken from an enclosed and badly ventilated court in which wore situ tted the pail closets and ashplacee. It was most important, therefore, that those courts be kept in as sanitary a condition as possible ; th,t the paving, scavenging and cleansing be carefully attended to. At present the paving was often either absent or defective and, therefore, the proper scavenging of the surface was difficult. The condition of the pail closets was also very unsatisfactory, liquid filth in very many instances escaping from the pailplaces on to the surface of the adjacent ground which wes often unpaved and undra,ined. Although there were many evils in connection with these c)mmon -courts and yards which could be dealt with hem Vme to time by the Health Committee, still that cpmmittee could only attack a part of the work. It was esential that these courts be in the first place properly paved, and then they could be effectually cleansed and scavenged. It was also essential that the present system of removing the pails and emptying the ashtubs and of cleansing the pail and ashplacesa !considered in order to obtain a more frequent removal of the excreta and other refuse and to ensure a more systematic and thorough cleansing of the pail and ashplaces. The present system by which one department had control of the scavenging of the courts and works independently of another department, which deals with the cleansing of the closets and ashplaces., was unsatisfactory. The closer co-operation, therefore, of the Paving and Sewerage Committee and the Sanitary Works Committee with the Health Committee was essential if the present con- ditions were to be remedied. Hence the need of the Joint Committee. The Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee were doing an excellent work in hurrying on with the paving of now streets. The Street Improve- ment'Committee were practically helpless apart hem the two committees to which he had referred. Since 1907 the Health Committee had closed 50 insanitary houses but the death rate was still about equal to what it was then. _ -
- Alderman BURTON seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor HAWTHORN said the Committee had been rather tardy in presenting the report. It was nearly two years since the medical officer made his complaint as to the bad condition of the slums. He (the speaker) hoped there would be no further delay in carrying out much needed work. The report disclosed a very lament- able state of affairs in the slum areas of the town. It showed that many of the sanitary conveniences were insanitary and they would never reduce the death-rate of Warrington to a satisfactory figure until they dealt effectively with the slum areas in the old parts of the town which were out of keeping with m ode rn require- ments.

Alderman BENNETT said be was pleased the committee were now at any rate alive to the absolute- necessity of dealing drastically with the question of slum areas. One of the things that impressed him most in visiting Continental towns was that there wera practi- cally no slums. He went to three or four large Ger- man towns and did not see any areas that he could call slum areas in the sense of which they spoke of slum areas in Warrington. In 11Innich they took the deputa- tion to a district which they called a slum district and it was quite as good as Church-street. Councillor ROBERTS also expresed gratification that the Health Committee was turning its attention to the serious conditions of health which obtained in certain parts of the town. A death rate of 53 per 1.000 in any part of Warrington was a scandal and a disgrace and a condition of things for which the Council as a whole was responsible. There was no satisfaction in finding that they were "one and a half children to the good "in slum areas, with a birth rate of 54 par 1,001 That birth rate ought to be a magnificent asset to the future of the town but if it was accompanied in the same district by a death rate of 53, it was a condition of things which must make the heart of a man ache if he was interested in the welfare of the poorest of his fellow-townsmen, and make him do all be could to ameliorate a state of things which bad existed far too long. He would like to know if anything had been done to call the attention of the Paving and Sewerage and Sanitary Works Committees to their part of the responsibility. He believed that if a schedule were sent from time to time to the Riving and Sewerage Committee of the particular locali- ties suffering from these frightful and abominahl conditions that committee would do its duty in cern pelling landlords of the property, or in doing it them- selves if the responsibility fell upon the town, to abolish their participation in the horrible state of affairs. If it was necessary for the comfort and cleanli- ness of the people and the prevention of disease that the pail closets should be emptied twice or thrice or half-a-dozen times a week it ought to be done. I.le cordially supported the Health Committee's forward movement and hoped it would be pressed to a success- ful issue. Councillor SKF.LI. AND said the Watch Committee ought to join with other committees in investigating the causes of the slum conditions.
The MAYOR : It is no part of the duty of the Watch Committee. You have your sanitary inspectors. Councillor SKELLAND said many good houses wets

made into slum dwellings through the improvidence of the people who lived in them. Alderman BURTON said the Watch Committees in Germany had power to intervene and if landlords or tenants declined to carry out the demands of the authority, the police stepped in and the work was done for them.

The MAYOR.: But it is not the law in England. Alderman BURTON: Thene get the law altered. (Laughter.) Alderman JAMES EVANS in reply, said he believed the Health Committee did not possess the powers they ought to possess. The committee wanted to have power to do something with the person who was with- out aspiration, inspiration or desire for cleanliness and good conditions. He could take them to places in the town where the Corporation had provided ashb ns and yet the ashes were thrown on the ground. The whole question bristled with difficulties from beginning to end, and one hardly knew what was the best method to adopt.

div.head: TIIE SMOKE NUISANCE.
div.p: TIIE SMOKE NUISANCE.
At a meeting of thellealth Committee the formation of a "Smoke Abatement League," which will seek to promote a strong national movement for furthering smoke abatement, was reported.. . . .

Aldermen JAmis EVANS said that at the Conference recently held at Sheffield it was pointed out that there W5B a considerable difference in the conditions obtain- ing in the South and North of EnglaPA respectively, which made it somewhat difficult to take combined action. It was, however, hopei to devise a scheme in which both sections could join and the now organisa- tion would seek to apply itself particularly to the con- ditions which existed in the northern counties.

Alderman BENNETT said he was grateful to Alderman James Evans for the interest he had taken in the ques- tion Of smoke abatement. It was a distinctly forward step to know that the opinion had been expressed that some outside aothority was required to stimulate the municipalities to their duty. Most of the evils they suffered from weodue to ignorance rather than to any other cause. The most satisfactory solution would probably be to appoint government inspectors instead of local inspectors. He knew the local officials tried to do their duty, but they met with the utmost possible discouragement in a town whore there were so many industries affected, and it was difficult for them to act, entirely in the interests of smoke abatement. Allusion was made to the decaying of the trees at the Cemetery on the town side, in consequence, the Alder- man alleged, of the fumes from the chimneys, and the speaker said that if something was not done to stop the smoke nuisance all the trees at that end of the Cemetery would die, and what applied to the Cemetery would apply to all parts of the town ultimately. Councillor ROBERTS said that Alderman Bennett in his zeal for smoke abatement was hardly fair to the conditions which obtained in law. The curious anomaly about the treatment dealt out to various manufacturers -he would not say where but in many towns—was that the principal offenders were protected by the law; their particular class of manufacture was exempted. In Warrington it was not the inspectors who were at fault, but it was the fact that the greatest part of the smoke was turned out in connection with industries which were exempted by law from the regulations which governed other manufacturers. There would not he any material improvement by the appoint- ment, of Government Inspectors and all that they could do would be to harrass the manufacturer who turned out the least amount of smoke. The proper course to take, if it were considered desirable to do so. was to agitate for the alteration of the law, making it equitable all round. Alderman JAMES EVANS replied on the discussion and said that a great deal of smoke was allowed by law, but the inspectors were faithfully carrying out their duties. They complained to the manager of the works and sometimes they did not get quite as much redress as thi-y should get. Only last week he said to Mr. Flood "See the head of the firm and point out quietly that the law is being broken and doubtless the matter will be remedied." He (the Alderman) believed the manufacturers of Warrington were doing their best to create as little smoke as possible, without interfer- ing with the industries of the town. The minutes were approved. SLAUGHTER-HOUSE LMPROVENIENTS.

The Medical Officer, at a meeting of the Health Committee, submitted a list of slaughter-houses where the committee's suggAsted improvements had not been carried out, and the Town Clerk was instructed to take steps to enforce the tame.

THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. At another meeting of the HealthlCommittee a letter was readlfrom the Local Government Eoard asking what steps the committee were taking with regard to various matters mentioned in the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health, and the 'Town Clerk was requested to reply thereto. NO BANDS TN THE CEMETERY.

The Cemetery Committee had resolved that in future no bands be allowed to play in the Cemetery. Alderman BENNETT asked whether the resolution would apply to military bands ? Councillor CRAIK who moved the adoption of the minutes, said it was only on very rare occasions that a band asked permission to play and it had generally been the Salvation Army band. The playing interfered with tho services that were being held in different parts of the Cemetery at the same time and the committee were of opinion that it should not'continue. The resolution would not apply to military funerals, for in those cases the band did not play in the Cemetery, and the only music was the sounding of the " Last Post " by the boglers. Another point which influenced the committee was that if one or two bands were allowed to play, others would probably be making application. Cluncillor DICKENSON : Why should we give the privilege to military bands mid refuse it to others ? Councillor CRAIK : The military band only plays to the cemetery gate. it is customary for bugles to sound the " Last Post " but the resolution of the committee will not apply to that. Councillor WILKINSON: How many bands do play in the cemetery? _ _ -

Councillor C-RAIK : It is very rarely that a band does play—probably three or four times a year. Councillor WILKINSON said the resolution might be the whim of some member of the committee. Coun- cillor Craik made special- reference to the Salvation Army band. Councillor CRAIK : I said they playei oftenest. Councillor WILKINSON: I don't think the committee should go out of their way to take exception. Councillor CRA IK : It had never been allowed until

recently and it was the unanimous feeling of the com- mittee—not the whim of anyone—that it should be stopped. Alderman EVANS : Has any complaint been made to the committee with regard to the band? Councillor CRAM: Not to the committee but to the Registrar. Councillor DICKENSON : B 7 whom? Councillor CRAIK : By the clergy who have been taking funerals in different parts of the cemetery. Councillor BIRTLES observed that when a band went into the Cemetery a large crowd generally followed and did damage by trampling on the flower beds. There was no question of any one band. The minutes wore approved. BEAUTIFYING AN ISLAND. At a meeting of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee it was resolved that the head gardener be authorised to incur expenditure to the amount of £2O for the planting of trees, &c., on the island adjacent.to Victoria Park.

Councillor BROADHURST asked whether the expense was to be incurred for profit or for beauty? A VOICE: For bent. Councillor BROADIIURST said that they had a recrea- tion ground at Sankey Bridges but at present the roadway leading to it was in such a bal state that the children going to the ground had to wade through water eight inches deep. If £lO could be spent on that road- way instead of on an old island on which nobody could play, it would be of far greater utility. Alderman JAMES EVAN.; raid the matter was one for the Open Spaces Committee. Councillor BIRTLES said there were some old build- ings and dead trees on the island which were an eyesore and would be removed. The island might be made one of the beauty spots of Warrington. Alderman BURTON said the approac to the rearm- - tier] Rroun I at Snitey Bridges was in a disgraceful condition but be had been informed that they had no power to deal with it. The minutes were approve& THE PRICE OF GAS. The minutes of the Gas Committee stated that the engineer reported that all the slot meters (about 10.000) had been altered to give the additional 5 cubic feet of gas per Id. Councillor WILKINSON said there wait a clerical error in the minute. The additional gas allowed would be la proportion to the reduction in the price and it would be about five feet. It would only refer to those slot meters within the borough.

OUT OF ORDER. When the minutes of the Water Committee were sub- mitted Councillor BROADHURST said be wished to drew attention to certain remarks of Mr. It. T. Fairclough The MAYOR: It is out of order. The TOWN CLERK : It is not on the minutes. FIRE BRIGADE COMPLIMENTED. Several members spoke in complimentary terms of the smartness with which the Fire Brigade had turned out to recent fires, Councillor Toole stating that on the occasion of the outbreak on Conncillor Cunnington's premises (near the Horse and Jockey) the brigade was on ths scene within 71 minutes of the alarm being given.

div.p: THE RECENT STREET FATALITY.
THE BATHS.

In the eighteenth century, people said that Scrofula could be cured "by the touch of a king's finger." But they took good care never to put it to the proof! To-day, many. things are supposed .to cure that most common of all complaints—lndigestion—but we like proof. Within twelve months it developed into severe stomach trouble. I could neither eat nos drink anything without stomach pains. I felt so heavy I could sleep at any time, anywhere. I had no life in me. I went to a hospital and they wanted to keep me in, my stomach was in such a bad state. The pain was like a continual screw, screw, screwing of the stomach, with awful agony that made me sweat, until my stomach threw up the food. I lost 24 lbs. in weight. Then I got a bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup, and have been without pain and vomiting from the time I took the third dose. I can work now, for I have no Indigestion! Mother Seigel's Syrup has cured me."

I was so completely run down that I couldn't do any work. I had medical advice, but with no good result. But I felt ever so much better after using only half a bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup 1 After one bottle, I was completely cured. Day after day, by publishing letters from men and women who have been cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup, the Proprietors of this family remedy arc piling up proof that it is the sure cure for Indigestion. Some of these letters come from old folks who have known the virtues of Mother Seigel's Syrup for forty years; but all are from people who have experienced for nomselves the restorative qualities of the Syrup. Their experience is proof that this herbal tonic possesses some curative property which other medicines lack, and their testimony is proof—which is absolutely beyond doubt—of the success of Mother Seigel's Syrup in curing stomach and liver troubles.

When the minutes of the Electricity and Tramways Committee were submitted, Aldermsn Sm STHURST alluded to a recent fatality caused through one of their employes falling off a laider whilst attending to ma are lamp. He said the jury recommended them to use a four-wheeled truck. The committee were adopting • hoist., and one min and a boy would be able to do the work instead of three or four men. MANUFACTURERS AND ELECTRICITY.

Alderman SAIRTHURST read a letter from Messrs. Richmond and Co., congratulating the oommittee upon the exceedingly capable and expeditious way in which Mr. Mathias and his subordinates had rigged them up temporarily with motors, owing to a breakdown to their main engine. The whole of their machines were running satisfactorily in whet they considered an exceedingly short time.
Alderman SMETHURST thought this was a most important matter which should be brought to the notice of manufacturers. If manufacturers need electricity there would be no complaints as to black smoke.
Alderman BURTON remarked that If Alderman Smethurst could tell them how to puddle by means of electricity he would be glad.

Councillor Brtommurisr movol :—(3) T'oat In the future the price of admission for the first-class plunge baths on Wednesday nights from 6 o'clock be reduced from 6d. to 3d, (4) That the price of admission to the first-class plunge bath on &Inds), mornings shall be reduced from 6d. to 3d. until such times as new cheap baths for working men are erected._

Councillor VXII-NON seeonded, and expressed the hope that the question wonld be considerei not only from the monetary standpoint but from health considerations Councillor BUITLES suggested that the resolution should be withdrawn and referred to the new committee. Extensions of the Baths were contemplated, and they would then be in a better position to grant cheaper facilities.

Alderman SMETHURST pointed out that the baths had now been closed for the season, so there would be nothing lost by deferring the matter. Councillor DICKENSON said the Committee had plans already before them for enlarging the baths, and they would do all they could to meet Councillor Broad- hurst's wishes.

Councillor ROBERTS said that if the proposed reduc- tion could include slipper baths it would be more important in the interests of workingmen than the plunge bath. The resolution was withdrawn with a view to con- sideration of the whole question by the new committee. Councillor TOOLE : 1. suggest that Conncillor Broad- hurst be put on the new committee to 10-A after the interests of the working classes.

AMERICAN BLIGHT ON APPLE-TRESS.—A friend of ours, after trying various mixtures recommended ag certain cures, but which proved only temporary, used neat's-foot-oil, painting the affected parts with this, which smothered up the pest at once. This was done when the trees were dormant. The oil being thick, it should be slightly warmed, when it can be easily worked into all the crevices with a thick brush. There have been no traces of the pest since this remedy bag been tried.—" Gardening Illustrated."

div.head: THANKING THE MAYOR.
div.p: THANKING THE MAYOR.
COUNCIL GIVES A UNANIMOUS VOTE.
Unusual Speechmaking.

As Tuesday's meeting of the Warrington Town 'Council was the last for the. municipal year, Alderman SMET II URST moved :--`• That the lest thanks of this Council be presented to William John Forshaw, Esq., J.P., for the satisfactory manner in which he has dis- charged the , responsible duties devolving upon 'him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate of the Borough during the past year, and for the unvarying Courtesy end impartiality displayed by him when Vesiding over the deliberations of the Council, and in his intercourse with its membtra." He said any gentlemen who bad filled the office of Mayor otsuch an important borough as WarringtGn and had endeavoured to do his best was deserving, of the thank of the Council. It was an impossibility to Please everybody • they all had their little failings. The Mayor had en:deavoured, so far as in him lay, to do his duty to the town. There .had perhaps been some little dissatisfaction about certain matters, but it was bard for those who Lad not experienced it to realise the feelings that filled one's breast on having to appear before their gracious Majesties the King and Queen. Ile (the speaker) bad some little experience of it when be was presented to the King and he could scarcely tell them how he felt,althongh be had a very little duty to Perform. The impression would never fade from his memory. If he had had to take such a prominent part aS the Mayor on the occasion of the Royal visit, Perhaps he would have made a blunder in allowing the _Present to Princess Victoria to be taken away instead of keeping it until a more suitable case had been Obtained. He hoped they would accord the vote of thanks with unanimity. Let the past be passed and let them try to finish his Worship's term of office in peace 'lnd co ufort and contentment, with the approval of . *very member of the Council. Alderman BURTON seconded. He said the Mayor's duties bad been most arduous and difficult, but the way he had discharged them had earned for him the best 'thanks of the Council/-Persdnally he was well pleased 'With the way the Mayor bad performed his duties. Alderman B.N'Err said he hid the pleasure of pro- ' Posing the election of Alderman Forshaw to the -Mayoralty, and he could only say that his Worship had justified his appointment and had done justice to him- self and to the high office he held. As Alderman 'Smethurst had said, it was impossible for any man to give absolute satisfaction to everybody, and the man Who never made mistakes was more than human. Alderman Forshaw had from first to last heen anin.ated one idea and that was to uphold the dignity of the °Moe and to do his duty to his native town. He (Alderman Bennett) thought he had succeeded. In the hard work he had had to do be had been ably assisted °Y his good wife. The Mayor and Mayoress had been at the disposal of every sect, party and good cause, and . for that alone they were entitled to their best thanks. Alderman Forshaw bad acted with impartiality and dignity and had proved a worthy successor of many eminent men who had filled the position. , Councillor WILKINSON in supporting- said it was Ththevitable tl at they should have their little differences. ,lbey must always remember that "to err is human, to, lorgive divine." Alderman JAMES EVANS paid a high tribute to the services rendered by the Mayoress upon whom the eties of the position must entail considerable anxiety:` Was sorry that any reference had keen made to mis- takes. All he would say was that whilst the Mayor Luight have made mistakes, he was quite sure the `-'ouncil had made some. (Hear, bear). Councillor 71ROADHURST recalled the fact that the raYor taught him as a boy at St. Barnabas' Sunday He felt under a moral obligation to support the vote of thanks,especially as the Mayor had extended et:lth kind courtesy to him as a young member of the Council. Aldermen Forshaw had proved himself equal tO any previous occupant of the office. Councillor BIRTLES fa7d the Mayor had been in lroubled waters. Ile had sailed through them and now .1'43 came out on the clear stream. They hoped his DlNne would be safely carried forward during the whole of the time he occupied the position. °Councillor ROBERTS, as "the youngest member but 'l.e "of the Council, associated himself very cordially s'',lth the resolution. It was so long since he was th it he had forgotten whether he made any Mistakes or not. (Laughter.) He did not think he did ---(laughter)--but there might be one or two sensitive Illembers of the Council who thought differently, and rf;o doubt they were in error in doing so. (Laughter.) People would have their opinions and he welcomed .?I'Y cordially the expression given utterance to by ouncillor Wilkinson. That was an ocCasion when ltnhatters of difference which, after all, compared with I 8 matters of agreement were extremely small--(hear, taar)—oonld to allowed to be forgotten and obliterated. ythatever difference there might have been, there was \)oly one opinion with regard to the Mayor and *jfiYoress,and that was that so far as the members of the ouncil could wish them well, physically and in every „either way,they did so with all their heart. They trusted c• at both might long be spared to take a prominent Position in carrying out the administration of affairs 'o the town. I, Councillor CRAIK, as an independent, said the Mayor done very well indeed during his year of cfli:e. one could pass through the chair without making ' Mistake two so, and the way in which the Mayor had P.rried out his duties merited the approval of the .Councillor STEEL said the legal profession of War- felt'P they had been honoured in having Alderman orshaw elected as Mayor of his native town. When !,tesiding over the Bench of magistrates he had filled 11,!B position with dignity and he had always been oo "„ aide of leniency. the resolution was then put to the meeting and tried unanimously. 'rho MAYOR, in returning thanks. said Mrs. Fotshaw rd certainly be-n a considerable help to him in per- tr'lline his responsible duties. He could assure them 'it he had d.)ne his best for his native town, and if he ilLad made mistakes he was sorry. He was not infallible; de Was only human. He had endeavoured to fulfill the to the best of his ability, and be hoped with eltrtesy to the Council. (Hear, hear.)
The Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS SIX CONTESTS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS SIX CONTESTS.
THE MEN TO VOTE FOR ON MONDAY.
[Birtles
MR. C. JACKSON HOLMES (L). FAIRFIELD WARD.

A man who will be welcomed back to public life. Rendered long and valuable service as Treasurer to the Warrington Liberal Association, and will be an acquisition to the Council. Has the will and the time to give a lot of service on behalf of Fairfield Ward and the town generally. The street-paving in Fairfield is a by-word. Mr. Holmes has promised to do his best to remedy a 'state of things which he rightly terms " a perfect disgrace" to a town like Warrington. You want the best man for Fairfield. He's Holmes !
COUNCILLOR LORD (IND.). TOWN HALL WARD.

One of the" Watch-dogs" of the Council. Has represented Town Hall Ward for nearly seven years and rendered valuable service as an economist. The great work which he, together with Councillor Pemberton,.. did in saving the town from excessive expenditure on the Lawson Water contract should, alone, ensure for him the confidence of the rate- payers. Councillor Lord has made one of the highest totals of attendances at Council and Com- mittee meetings. Is a man who w.on't be dragooned. For this reason does'nt suit the Tories,who want him out. You put him in! •
[Parkinson. COUNCILLOR CUNNINGTON (L). ORFORD WARD.

One of the stalwarts of the economical.party in the Town Couneil. A man of few words but firm con- victions. Has paid particular attention to the interests of his own Ward, and attended loyally to every Council and Committee meeting unless pre- vented by illness. A member of the Old Age Pensions Committee, where he has always done his best for the aged and deserving poor. Don't let the mantle of Elijah fall upon a publican!
Photo] .. MR. T. HEWITT (L). LATCHFORD WARD.

Electors of Latchford can easily make a change for the better. Hewitt is a native and knows Latchford from the Bridge to the boundary. His opponent is a man who is trained to toe the line when the party whip cracks. You want a man who can act independently as his judgment dictates. Hewitt favours half-penny tram fares, which are an absolute necessity on the long Latchford route. Give him a trial. Hewitt is a worker of and for the workers!
MR. JAMES SHAW (L). ST. JOHN'S WARD.

Essentially a worker for the workers. St. John's people have known and respected Mr. Shaw for over half a century. Should have been in the Council before, and then the living conditions in this crowded ward might have beeebdtered. Has a record of Temperance and religious work which should ensure the confidence of his neighbours and electors. Shaw's word is his bond. Give him your vote on Monday!
[A. and G. Taylor. MR. J. T. BARTON (L). WHITECROSS WARD.

Son of the retiring member for the Ward, where he has resided for over 20 years and earned the good- will of a large constituency. Was Secretary of the Liberal Ward Committee for ten years, and has always been to the fore in those repeated Liberal triumphs which have made Whitecross famous. Favours the important scheme for schools and recreation ground in Lovely-lane, and is in every way suited to represent the Ward in the Council. Vote for the man who lives in your midst.

div.head: " PERFEGTION:'
div.p: " PERFEGTION:'
The Soap Trade-Mark Case.
MESSRS. CROSFIELDS APPEAL.

The Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Moulton and Farwell began the hearing in the Court of Appeal on Wednesday of the appeal of Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, of Warrington, from a refusal of Mr. Justice Swinfen Eady to direct the Registrar of Trade- maiks to proceed whir the registration of the word 'Perfection" as applied to Crosfield's common soaps notwithstanding the opposition of Messrs. Lever Brothsrs, Limited, Port I.:unlight. Mr. Justice Eady declined to direct the Registrar to proceed with the registration on the ground that the word " Perfection " was not a distinctive mark notwith- standing the user by the appticants in the past, and was not adapted to distinguish the goods of the applicants from the goods of other persons. Mr. WALTER opened the appeal on behalf of Crosfield and Sons at some lengi.h. He said that for twenty- four years continually 5h3 word "Perfection" had meant to.the trade and to the public household common soap of the manufacture of Messrs. Crosfield and Sans and no other household soap during the same period. The hearing was adjourned. Hearing was resumed on Timm:day when MT. Walter continued his argument in support of tie appellants, case. He said the quest' on was as in all trademark WKS, disoreticn. rhere me os r:11v no absolute right. to the registration of any mark. the point for con- sideration was the particular word before the court; and whether it was adapted to be distinctive. He sub- mitted that the word; was distinctive. The evidence shomed that every person who heard or saw the name "Perfection " tnow at once aat Crcsfield's soap was moult. Out of all the declarations on bchalf of the opponents'—over 500—only twenty-seven persons said that they did not know it. Every witness for the appellants, some 500 or COO, said that "Perfection" ruer.nt the goods of Crosfields, and no other. Lo:c1 Justice Fa.ewell : I thin% it is pretty clear that it is not very well knawn in London? Counsel did not ape.. Ile submitted that the judge in the cot rt below had drawn a wrong inference from the evidence with r( gard to that point. Mr. Astbury. K.C., said that he thought that " Perfection " instead of being printed in the short- hand notes with inverted commas and with a capital " P " should be printed as an ordinary English word. Lord Justice Farwell : If you ask for perfection snap, I agree you.want the hest soap; if you ask for "Perfection " with a capital "P" you mean brand. Mr. Walter: I know of no evidence of persons who go into a shop and ask for "Perfection" with a capital " P." Mr. Astbur7 said he did not wish ta raise the point; he enly mentioned it by way of a joke Mr. Jestice Moniton : No one doubts that if one goes into a shop end says," I want a bar of 'Perfection "be knows it is a brand. Mr. Astbnry : Ida not agree. Lord JuAice Moulton pointed out that the respon- dents, Messrs. Lever, had a brand named "Powerful." He thought that was the very worst name that could be used.

Mr. Astbury : It is a distinctive word. It mly be "Powerful " to bring the skin oft (laughter). Later counsel explained that the witness only give the first name of the brand. It's first name was "Powerful Cle- nser."
Mr. Walter, continuing. mentioned the words" if I am entitled to express my opinion." _ . .

Lord Justice Farwell : Yin are not entitled to express an opinion—you advanoe your arguments (laughter). Mr. Walter: That is so. (Laughter). Counsel did not differ with Mr. Justice Swinfen Eady that Messrs. Crosfield's largest trade was in Lancashire, Yorkshire and the Midlands. They had trade in other places of course; for imtance, one witness said they had five hundred customers in London. Counsel read to the court a list of names of other of Messrs. Crostleld's brHods, including" Good Julge." Tim Master of tie Rolls : I have heard of "Old Juige." (Laughter). Tho court tlun dealt with brands of different makers.
Lord Justice Moulton sai I he thought Vie names of soaps, with the exception of "Sunlizht " end " Lifebuoy," were the very worst ones that could be chosen.

Mr. Kedy followed on the same side. H€ said that Messrs. Crosfields did not seek to get a monopoly of the mord "perfection," or to interfere with traders who chose to say their sap was perfect provided that they did not use it as a particular mark for soap. The evidence proved tkst over the greater part of England Cro:field's soap was known as " Perfection " soap; that "Perfection soap " was recognised as a brald, and that -practically %%ithout exception, by the whole trade and a great part of the public; that everyone who knew that it was a particular soip which always ctme from the same source; and that there was no other nse of the word "Perfection" as a name for soap. Tne helring had not concluded when the court rose for the day.

div.head: INDIGESTION IS HEREDITARY
div.p: INDIGESTION IS HEREDITARY
AND IS OFTEN HANDED DOWN THROUGH F 0 U R GENERATIONS. CAUSING MANY COMPLICATIONS.

Mr. Stephen Walsh Speaks Out. Speakiiig at a meeting of his constituents at Pamber ton on Monday night, Mr. S. Walsh, M.P. for the Ince Division, atid it was not the cry of the rich man they bad to attend to to-day. The plea of the rich man had had a great deal of attention in the counsels of the nation in the past ; but the time ba come when the tragedy of the poor man's life would have attention. The opponents of the Budget professed concern about the poor man's beer and " bacce," and he thought the pine irds which were being displayed at the present time were an absolute disgrace to the in'elligence of their people. To say that with less beer and tobacco they were going to create less employment was the most bide )us travesty that he had ever come across, ani any party which descendad to such a depth of grossness deserved a defeat which, he felt sure, it would sustain at the hands of an outraged people. In the tl;ht which was being waged, there was nothing they had t) fear more than the dirty and reptile PCOSS which was trying to befoul the nation.

Mr. BALFOUR sets a AN INEXCUS- bad example where no ABLE SPEECH. bad e amplex was

needed. Some of his 'followers, as we pointed out in these columns last week, are much too ready to set aside all he proprieties of public life, to ignore all the Obligations of veracity, to free themselves orn all that is recognised as good manners. 4.`ivas not necessary to give them further Illoouragement in that direction at least. "Ir. BALFOUR said that he wished to say (3111 e things that need not be said behind .losed doors, and that ke would take full esPonsibility before the general public for what he said. This seems brave, but we I.l,c.lubt whether Mr. BALFOUR will say in the 41.°11se of Commons, where he can be at once c'lltradicted and confuted, what he said at

the Junior Constitutional Club in London, All defiance of public opinion and public judgment seems to be an expression of courage. It may, nevertheless, be only an example of cowardice. To say in one place what could not be said on that account, is not courageous, and we are sorry to be driven by Mr. BALFOUR'S own style and language to say that he has, to serve party ends, not in the House of Commons, but in the country, said with violence and in a style of indefensible abuse, what he has not said in Parliament.

The LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION, whose position as a Statesman should keep him under a continual sense of responsibility, whether he is in office or out of office, brings charges against the Lord Advocate which it is quite impossible to sustain, and in terms which reduce political controversy to the level of the gutter. We quite understand why he should do this. But we deeply regret, for the sake of public life, that he should be the man to do it. Such a task should be left to men like Mr. F. E. SMITH. The Conservative party is bent on returning to power, and perceives quite clearly that its only chance of doing so is by deceiving the people. Well, this should be left to the Party hacks. The Party leader ought not to lead where he can only do so by losing character and by throw- ing sincerity to the winds. There are other men for the job. One gentleman of the Opposition, while accusing the LORD ADVO- CATE in coarse and insulting language of persistent falsehood, went on to tell his audience that a great building project had been abandoned in Liverpool on account of the Budget. It was known long before, and a Liverpool member can hardly have been unacquainted with the fact that it had• been abandoned for quite other reasons. What was he doing when he accused the LORD ADVOCATE of contemplated falsehood? We leave the reply to this question to our readers. But is it not shameful beyond belief that the LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION, should follow in the rut made by Mr, F. E. SMITH? Mr. BALFOUR accuses the Lord. Advocate of "a frigid and calculated lie." That is unusual language for a Statesman. What is the justification for it? There is no justification. There is not even a shadow of justification. What has Mr. URE said? He has said that under a Tariff Reform system it must be difficult, if not impossible to procure money for Old Age Pensions, and he has said that a Tory Chancellor of the Exchequor (now Lord St. Aldwyn) had shouldered the Old Age Pensions idea aside because he could not discover by what financial means the pensions could be provided. And this it is that makes Mr. BALFOUR SO furious and so insulting. Let

us saytat once that the fury is stimulated, and that the insults arise out of genuine anger, because the simple truth is being told to the people, and because the LORD ADVOCATE draws quite natural inferemes from indisputable facts. No man living can be excused for saying about another what Mr. BALFOUR said about the LORD ADVOCATE. We do not retort upon him the slanderous charges which he made against a a man of unusual earnestness and sincerity, but we do say there is no point of view from which his violent and, as we believe, calculatedly insulting speech can be palliated or• excused.
"I come back to my
WHERE native town ashamed ENGLAND LAGS. and half-disheartened."

Thus writes Alderman BENNETT in an admirable report which he has presented to the Town Council on his recent Continental Town Planning Tour. In a series of special articles to the " Examiner " the alderman is giving a graphic and most interesting description of his journey as one of the party of thirty-four who, under the auspices of the National Housing Reform Council, , visited several contin- ental cities with a view, to studying their municipal institutions and especially their thethods of dealing with the hous- ing and town-planning problems. His official report summarises in his usual outspoken style the conclusions inspired by
his experiences and, as may be judged from the striking sentence we have already quoted, he has returned with the full conviction that

in matters municipal we in England have much leeway to make up—that, in fact, our 'foreign friends are miles ahead of us." The tour embraced Rheims, Nancy, Stuttgart, Ulm, Munich and Vienna and in not one of these places did Alderman BENNETT see a "real slum," like many we have in Warring- ton, although in one particular city the deputation was taken specially to what was called the slum district. None of the towns were ugly, and some of them were more beautiful than he can well describe. Dealing with the social habits of the people, Alderman BENNETT has some interesting things to say about the" mingled soberness and gaiety which are in such amazing contrast to the squalid drinking customs of this country" and he appears to attribute them to the lightness of the native beer and to the provision of large open gardens where excellent music is discoursed and food may be obtained as well as beer. A highly important feature of German municipal enterprise upon which the alder- man lays stress, is that most of the cities spend enormous sums upon public slaughter- houses. "One cannot but feel,"he says,"that in a matter which so vitally affects the health of the whole population, the expense is amply justified." How is it that our Continental neighbours have made such remarkable progress in their municipal affairs? Alder- man BENNETT touches the spot when he points out that "Private greed,- with them, must always give way to public convenience. They simply will not tolerate the wretched and unseemly areas of filth and poverty which make a plague spot of South Lancashire, and, when they build, they build for the future." That is the key to the position. We in England are hampered by the legacies of former indifference and incompetence, and by the opposition of self-interest. Much was hoped from the Town Planning Bill but the reckless mutilation of that promising measure by the House of Lords is calculated to make municipal reformers despair. A timely pro- test against the Lords' characteristic action has been forthcoming from some of the lead- ing experts on the housing question,who have addressed a memorial to the Prime Minister. The fate of the Town Planning Bill is another instance of that abuse of power by the second Chamber, which will not be lost upon tlip people who stand to lose by it.

Bermondsey was a BERMONDSEY. botch. The Conserva- tive candidate has been returned by a minority of the electors on a split vote. He polled 4,278 votes, against 3,291 for Mr. S. L. Hughes, Liberal, and 1,435 for Dr. Salter, Socialist, so that the combined Progressive pro-Budget poll exceeded that of the Tariff Reformer,Mr. J. Dumphreys by 448. The mistake was made in the first place by the Socialists, who hurried their candidate into the field, and then by the Liberals in causing a three-cornered contest. Mr. Hughes wasted his time and talents in an election where it was obvious that the Pro- gressive vote would have to be divided between himself and a Socialist. Of course, the result is hailed by the othe'r side as a blow to the Budget and a victory for Tariff Reform. They are welcome to conso- lation derived from such conclusions. The 'Budget will not be any weaker, nor Tariff Reform any stronger for all that Mr. IDumphreys has done or can do. We are told too, that the fate of the Budget in the House of Lords is now settled, The die has been cast—in Bermondsey. We can only hope that this at least is true. Once the Lords take the irrevocable step and there will e such a national reckoning as in their isolated grandeur they cannot have contemplated. Mr. Hughes himself fittingly reminds us that "As in Southwark in 1880, a snatched Tory victory in Bermondsey may be one more forerunner of a general Tory disaster."

The business and dis- " A CHILD AND A cussions at the meeting HALF TO THE of the Town Council On GOOD." (?) Tuesday were neither romantic nor exciting. Alderman James Evans, chairman of the Health Committee, presented a belated report on the health conditions of the slum areas, following upon a drastic criticism by the Medical Officer so long ago as 1907. One of the worst things about the Health Com- mittee is that it moves so slowly its duties to perform. The death-rate in the slum area—which comprises 425 houses—stands at the appalling figure of 531, which is neither better nor worse than it was two years ago. The Alderman extracted a crumb of comfort from the fact that the birth-rate in the. same districts is 547, giving the town a credit balance of "about a child. and a half." div.p: on the head any idea that there was reason for congratulation in this fact. The proper conclusion to arrive at was that this invaluable asset of a high birth-rate was being wasted and thrown away by the almost equally high death rate. Judging from the Chairman's statement the Com- mittee • has discovered the causes of the heavy life-wastage but is somewhat barren of remedies. It seems to us that a more determined policy is required if the slum areas are to be removed ; and inseparable from the remedial measures is the problem of the obsolete and overworked sewage sys- tem. The Council will—and the sooner the better—have to face the task of re-sewering the old part of the town. Until this is done the insanitary conditions obtaining in con- gested districts are almost beyond remedy. Opportunity awaits the man bold enough to tackle the problem.

It is obvious that the TARIFF REFORM Opposition cannot go to METHODS. the country with the cry; "Protect the ground landlord and let everything else go to ruin." But they think that they can rally the country to the defence of the landowners not by a bribe—it is nothing so substantial as that—but by a vague and kaleidoscopic promise of enriching everybody at the expense of everybody else—except the ground-landlord. The Budget, they declare, is an incitement to the working man to loot the capital of the country. Well, Tariff Reform is an incitement to a wild scramble in which every industry will be engaged in trying to maintain itself by robbing every other industry and the community at large. The Tariff Reformer approaches every industry in turn and says: We will enable you to put up your prices." And they think that the working man cannot see that, if the raw material of his industry is tax4l, there will not only be no margin of profit to pay him larger wages, but he will loae employment, since more expensive production means loss of markets. And at the same time food will be dearer, and the effective demand even of the protected home market will be lessened, because the victimised home consumer will have no money to spare for luxuries when necessaries are so much dearer.
The last Australian A COMIC SIDE- Tariff is developing LIGHT ON in a curious but after
PROTECTION. all natural way. The

manufacturers - under protection of the Tariff have raised their prices to the top notch and probably above it. An Australian Royal Commission has been sitting and has had the question of the advanced prices under consideration. The recommendation of this Commission_is that a Board of Trade should be appointed, with far reaching judicial powers, to investigate whether the Australian manufacturers are charging their customers more than they ought. It is claimed that these manufacturers are abusing the privileged position which the Tariff gave them and asking the consumer to pay more than a "fair price." This Board of Trade is to investigate the question of what is a fair price. _ There is something very comic about the whole proceeding. First the Commonwealth builds a wall to keep out the competition which would automatically control the manufacturer's price; then when this control is removed the inevitable happens, and the customer begins to whine to the Government, and a com- mission is appointed to prevent manufac- turers doing what the legislature plainly gave them the chance to do. Yet our own Tariff Reformers advocate the same get-rich- quiek methods as the salvation of effete old England. _ Obviously it is not the poor consumer who is likely to get-rich-quick under Protection. Australia's experience is merely another striking demonstration of the fact.
