We are glad that the Mayor received a unanimous vote of thanks on Tuesday from the Council. He deserved it if only for his assiduous attention to the duties of the office. But the vote might have been more welcome if the proposer and subsequent speakers had not been quite so apologetic for his Worship. "To err is human" was the general text, and the spirit one of forgiveness and good- will combined.

Lord Milner and the- "Saturday Review" have lately admitted that Tariff Reform will increase the cost of living, and now the " Times " of Thursday in stating the issue at Bermondsey, says (the italics are our own):. - in is whether this country will sanction the Budget, with all the germs of Socialism which it manifestly contains, or whether they will prefer Tariff Reform, even though for a time Tariff Reform may increase the price bf many commodities.
We suppose it is just as certain that we should all have higher wages to purchase these dearer commodities?

* * It is perhaps not* everybody who knows that Warrington possesses an island. For centuries Warrington has not taken any pride in the fact, but the corporation has suddenly begun to prize the possession and decided to spend £2O on the beautification of it by planting trees and shrubs. The island is in the river—and not on one of the recrea- tion grounds—and it can be seen from either Knutsford-road or Victoria Park. The old sheds and dead trees are to be removed, and the place made good to look upon. The Council might go a little further and create a sort of jungle or Zoo on the spot. Even Manchester has its jungle, and why not Warrington? f * * *

The Dukes and the Lords and other large landowners have been tumbling over one another to shake the humble hand of Mr. Dumphreys, the new M.P. for Bermondsey. The Duke of Abercorn waxed quite hilarious at the news and wired: "I believe you have saved the country. - Splendid!" Isn't it? We notice that his Grace of Abercorn possesses, according to the latest available return, some 78,662 acres. Can it be that these many acres constitute the" country" he so fervently thanks Mr. Dumpheys for saving?

* * The Member for the Borough Look a back seat for once, on Saturday. Women were naturally to the fore at the Women's Circle, and Mr. Crosfield seemed to find in the novel role of auditor a pleasant relaxation. Mrs. Crosfield spoke at both afternoon and evening gatherings, and surprised everybody by the advance she has made as a public speaker. Her two addresses were most apt, and very fluently and gracefully delivered. Mrs. Crosfield has not been a public woman" long, but she has soon proved her qualifica- tions for a somewhat exacting part. In fact, it was a subject for general comment among the critical males who happened to be present at the Circle gatherings, that the ladies could give points to many of the men in the
art of oratory. Another blow to the pride of the so-called stronger sex! * * *

An interesting point as regards seniority is likely to engage the attention of the Manchester City Council in the near future. As the ares are somewhat similar to those which arose here in July, when Mr. H. Roberts was returned to the Council our readers will no doubt be interested. There if an'aldermanic vacancy in Manchester, and thei senior councillor is Mr. Fletcher Moss; But if at Monday's municipal election Mr. W. B. Pritchard is returned, this gentleman will rank first in seniority and take preced- ence of Mr. Moss. He was defeated 12 months ago and the Standing Orders of the Man- chester Corporation state that "any interval of absence not exceeding thirteen months shall not be considered an interruption," so that all Mr. Fletcher's past service will count and he entered the Council a year before Mr. Moss. In Warrington the term of absence permitted is fifteen months, so that the same opportunity is given to a defeated Councillor to regain his seat and his seniority over younger members. * * *

The " sandpapering " of the Budget is now practically finished, and the only stage that remains before it goes up to the House of Lords is the third-reading debate. Since it is not permissible to make any change in bills before the House of Commons after the Report stage, ,we may now regard the Budget as being in its final shape. The third- reading stage will take place next week, and in the following week, two or three days after Guy Fawkes' day, the Budget will go up to the House of Lords. Let us hope that when they approach it they will remember the fate of Guy Fawkes. It is true that he tried to blow up the House of Commons, but he did not succeed, and he came to a very bad end. * *

Except for a few elegant remarks on Mr. Winston Churchill by the Duke of Montrose, the Dukes have been rather silent of late. The Dukes cannot forgive or forget Mr. Winston Churchill. Perhaps that is because he is one of their own order, and they cannot understand how one of their own order can be a friend of the people. In the days when the Dukes really represented something it was because they were friends of the people. The noblemen of to-day forget that it was the Barons of England who extorted Magna Charta from King John. If they would see the matter rightly, they would realise that Mr. Winston Churchill is• really on a far safer historic road thhn any of the noblemen who spend their time in threatening to take their taxes out of their wage bills.

No compromise. For the Budget Bill must be passed exactly as it stands. During the last few days there has been a revival of the rumour that the Lords intend to amend it. But let us be clear on that point also. The Lords can neither amend, postpone, nor reiect the Finance Bill. They have only one duty- towards it: they have to pass it.
* * The matter was put most clearly and con- cisely by Lord Rosebery in his speech in the House of Lords on the Finance Bill Of 1894.

I do not think that it is necessary, for the purpose of passing the bill, that they should make them- selves masters of it, because I deprecate altogether the idea that the House of Lords has any thing to do with money bills. Any discussion of it must obviously be academic, and, therefore, I should have thought "the least said, soonest mended" with regard to this measure.
Mr. Balfour, at Dumfries as recently as October .6th, 1908 said:
• It is the House or Commons, and not the House of Lords, which settles uncontrolled our financial system.

A Call for the Rev. J S. Hughes.

We learn that the Rev. J. S. Hughes who was for fourteen years pastor of the Hill Cliffe Baptist Church has received a unanimous call to a new and promising Baptist Church in the suburbs of Coventry. Mr. Hughes, who now feels in much better health, has not given his final reply to the invitation bat is, we understand, likely to accept. Parish Church Sale of Work.

The annual sale of work in connection with the Warrington Parish Church will be held in the Fairfield schools on Thursday, Friday and Saturday next. It will be opened on Thursday by the Hon. Colonel and Mrs. Lumley (grand-daughter of the late Lord Win- mai leigh) ; on Friday by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Mrs. Crosfield ; and on Saturday by the Mayor and Mayoress.

N.S.P.C,C. Work. The Warrington Branch of the National Society for the Prevention of Crtielty to Children has during the quarter ended 30th September 1909 inquired into 56 complaints of neglect, ill-treatment and other wrongs of childhood, of which all were found to be true, affecting 159 children and 86 offenders. Action was taken as follows :-53 cases were warned, 3 were prosecuted and convicted. The Society's Inspectors made 395 visits of supervision. The marriage was solemnized. at the Primitive Methodist Church, Morecambe, on Saturday, of Mr_ Joseph Howes, jun., Liberal registration agent for Warrington, son of Mr. Joseph Howes, the well- known political lecturer, Morecambe, and Miss Bertha Waywell, daughter of Mr. George Waywell, Ciambrook Farm, Orford. div.head: Warrington Soldier's Sad Death.
div.p: Warrington Soldier's Sad Death.

While-a detachment of the Ist Battalion Cheshire Regiment, which only went to Belfast a month ago, were at pontoon building exercise on Tharsday on the upper tidal waters of the river Lagan, near Belfast, a raft bridge, which had been thrown across the river, and was composed of planks strapped on barrels, suddenly turned turtle, and about thirty men of the detachment, under the command of Captain Rich, were thrown into the water close to the first locks. Unfortunately two soldiers —Lance-Sergeant Fitzpatrick, of G Company, and • Private Whelan of D Company— lost their lives. - Lance-Sergeant Fitzpatrick came from Warrington and only a fortnight ago he was here on leave from Belfagt, staying with his sister, Mrs. Tracey, 36, Naylor-street, He was thirty-two years of age and had been in the army twelve years. Both the drowned men were excellent swimmers and and it is stated that when last seen Sergeant Fitz- patrick was assisting his half-drowned comrade towards the bank, which is fairly steep at the place.

Warrington Citizens' League of Help. The above-mentioned League is now being organized in order that cases may be investigated and helped immediately affer the beginning of the New Year. At the present moment the work is being carried on by a a Provisional Executive Committee.—Mr. _Wilfrid Rowland, whose appointment as secretary has already been noticed, has now taken up his residence in the town, and the offices at Winmarleigh Chambers opposite the new Post Office will be ready for occupa- tion in the course of a few days.-.--It has been decided to make threo divisions in the town corresponding with the relieving offices's area recently approved by the Local Government Board. Each of the divisions will comprise three of the municipal wards —On Tuesday afternoon the Provisional Executive met at the Church House in Bridge-street, to consider the appointment of the Divisional Chairman and the District Heads. The District Heads will preside over the District Committees into which the divisions are sub-divided. When these appointments have been made the next work will be to form the District Com- mittees themselves, and it is hoped that a number of helpers will be forthcoming willing to represent the community in showing friendship to those who are in need of help. There will be no paid ivestigators, all the helpers being voluntary workers, TABLE AND HANGING LAMPS, new designs now showing.—J. S. GARL AND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Penny Concerts. •

The-penny popular concerts at Bold-street school continue to attract large audiences, and the schoolroom uus again well filled on Saturday evening. A most interesting programme. had been arranged and the artistes were all well received. A quartette by the Misses Annie Foster and Ethel Parr, Messrs. J. Gleave and R. Tranter, "A very bad cold," proved very amusing and the party received a hearty encore. "The Drum Major," sung by Mr. Tranter, went with a splendid swing. Mr. W. Milne was the humorist, and he created roars of laughter with his items, particularly the song. "Jimmy Law." The Rev. Thomas Miller was the chair- man, and during the interval addressed the audience, Mr. E. Wilkes was the accompanist. A series of penny concerts has been inaugurated by the Sacred Heart Young Men's Society and the open- ing venture of the kind took place last evening week. The Rev. Father Rocidiff and the committe are to be complimented on their praiseworthy endeavours to provide healthy recreation for the young and adult members of the congregation. The programme con- sisted of songs, gramophone selections, cornet solos, &c. There was a large attendance Two of the most pleasing items in the programme were the singing of Mary Marchant in "The banks of Allan Water" and of Mary Marchant and Willie Weston in the duet "Golden slumbers." The Rev. Father Rocliff presided and Miss Daisy Dolan was the accompanist. Master Willie Farrington and Mr. Joseph MeHale were the humorists.

div.head: International _ Correspondence_ Schools.
div.p: International _ Correspondence_ Schools.

The International CorrespOndence Schools who are engaged in giving technical training by means of the Penny Post to wage-earners engaged in all branches of commerce and industry, have just concluded through the medium of their 'Employment Department, an investigation into the state of employment amongst their many thousands of Students throughout the United Kingdom. The result may fairly be described as startling, as, so far as it has been possible to ascertain by careful enquiry, the percentage of their students out of employment is '037. When this figure is contrasted with the latest adv ices from the Trades Unions, making returns to the Board of Trads Labour Department, which shows that the percentage of Trades Unionigts out of employment Is 7.9 it is obvious that employers are loathe to part with men who are striving io improve themselves by means of study. The average age of the International Correspondence Schools students is between 26 and 27 years. The LC.S. have local headquarters in Springfield-street Mr. G. Hickman being the Divisional Superintendent.

At a largely attended meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope, Earlestown, held last Wednesday, in the Lecture MB the following resolu- tion was passed : " That the Earlestown Wesleyan Band of Hope at a meeting held in the Lecture Hall Cross-lane on Wednesday \ evening October 27th sincerely thanks Mrs. Simpson as a Guardian for the noble stand she made for the Band of Hope teaching and also for the welfare of the children attending Padgate School, and trusts she will be long permitted to defend the child against the awful havoc which alcoholic drinking causes, and further hopes she w;11 take the first opportunity of again bringing the matter before the board." MOSELEYS FOOD.—" Ardth in a minute." Strongly recommended by the Medical Press and Medical men. Ask your doctor.—Advt.

The Scottish Concert. As will be seen from our advertising columns a grand Scottish concert will be held in the Parr Hall on Monday, Bth November. A first class list of artistes has been engaged, and the high level of the previous concerts, held under the auspices of the Warrington Caledonian Associaiion is sure to be maintained. Mrs. Margaret Booth is a soprano of more than local fame, and her reputation is now firmly established as a finished artiste, having fulfilled important engagements in Manchester and London and other centres of musical culture. Miss Jennie Armstrong, by her conection with the recent perform- ances of" The Pirates of Penzance" established her- self as a prime favourite by her finished performances. Mr. J, Kerr Campbell,tenorAnd Mr. George Platt,bass, are two vocalists of tried excellence, and may be trusted to do full justice to their respective items. Mr. Theo Crozier (pupil of the late Professor Wilhelmj) is agairethe Solo violinist, and those whose privilege it was to hear him on the occasion of the last Scottish Concert will have pleasant anticipations which are certain to be realised. The humorous element is in the capable hands of Mr. Alec Chrystal, assisted by Miss Scotland, and a merry time will be the result. The accompanist is Mr, W. Payton. Sergeant Donald Murray, the Association's piper, will be in attendance and will give selecti9fns on the national instrument. The proceeds of the concert are in aid of the Society's benevolent fund and the Warrington Infirmary.

div.p: A SOLDIER'S ESCAPADE. RODE TO LONDON ON STOLEN BICYCLE. At the Borough Police Court on. Wednesday George Roberts, a private stationed at Orford Barracks/ was charged with stealing a bicycle from Orford Barracks, the property of Robert Forshaw.—The Chief Constable said that prisoner had given the police all the informa- t" on he could in the matter, but they had been unable to recover the bicycle. It seemed that prisoner took the bicycle which belonged to another soldier and rode to London to his mother's house, and handed the hicyle to another man. He had been in the army for some time and had borne a previons good character. He thought that if the Bench would bind prisoner under the First Offenders Act it would be advisable.—Defendant was bound over in the sum of £lO to come up for judgment if called upon. UNHAPPY MARRIED LIFE. "I would rather put myself at the bottom of. the ' Cut ' than live with him again," was the statement of a young married woman named Margaret Hoyles, who charged her husband, Joseph Hoyles Haadock-street, with assaulting and beating her on the 27th of October, as hereby she asked for a separation."—Mr. T. S. Steel, who appeared for complainant, said it was always his desire, whenever possible, to bring about a reconcilia- tion between the two parties. The parties in that case had only been married three months, and he suggested (and be believed be would be supported by the Chief Constable) that the case be adjourned, for a month, to let .Mr.rirth do what good he could in the meantime.— Complainant was determined that she would not go bock to her husband and said he was always ill:treating her.—Mr. Firth who bad bud the case in hand, said he could do nothing as the mothers on each side were always pulling the strings. The defendant however was a cracked-brained customer and did things that he had little need to do.—On complainant again saying she would tot go back to her husband Mr. Firth said that S 5 per cent. of those who were panted separations Trent to live together again.—After some deliberation the magistrates decided to adjourn the case for a month to see if the parties could be brought together.— Complainant left the witness box protesting. FARMERS' SON'S STRANGE CONDUCT. A remarkable story of a young man's strange conduct was heard at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, when Robert Dakin, of Orford, was charged with obstructing the tramway in Manchester-road, also with furiously driving a pony and trap.—Mr. A. Browne represented defendant who did not put man appearance. —The Chief Constable said that he expected that the defendant would not appear and that was a case where a warrant for his apprehension should be g,anted, if his friends did not give an undertaking that the man would be medically examined. He thought from his behaviour that he was of weak intellect He had been in treo habit of obstructing tramcars with his trap and the drivers had done all they could to avoid obstruction The Tramways Committre bad complained and an officer had been specially detailed to keep observations on the man. He saw the defendant obstruct a car, and on going up to him, he drove away at a furioui pace, anything like 15 to 18 miles an hour. Sergeant Stewart went to see him at his residence and on going in the yard saw ft man (who turned out to be defendant) and on asking him his name, he rushed into the house and locked the door and would not give the Sergeant anything at all. It was certainly a case where defendant should be put under some restraint. He had been in clarge of a milk cart. and had been a source of considerable danger to those riding in the cars, for when he saw cars approach- in the opposite direction, be rushed his trap across the track 50 that the emergency brakes had to be put on Mr. Browne said be was sure the friends of Mr. Dakin who lived at Orford would be extremely-. obliged for the Chief Constable's statements. For some time past owing to an unfortunate affair that occurred in town, Dakin had seemed strange and suffered from neuras- thenia. When it was discovered that be had been doing these silly tricks of going between trams, his father insisted that he should not go out with the cart again and he would give an undertaking not to let defend- ant go out again with vehides. Defendant however was considerably better than he was and they did not think his condition was such as he should be sent away. The parents,both father and mother were terribly upset. He asked the magistrates under the circumstances, to allow the summons to be dismissed on Payment of costs. The Chief Constable said he could not withdraw the Case before eefendant was medically examined. With a view to this being done the case was adjourned for a week.

Warrington Borough Court. MOD AV.—Befote the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Smethurst, Nessrs. %V. Rol erts, Firm ss, H. Thornton, T. Locker and G. Pilling. - THEFT OF CLOTHING.—Margaret Cole, Bank-street, was charged with stealing a shirt value Is. from the backyard of the Feather's Hotel, Bridge-street, the previous Saturday.—The Chief Constable sta'el that the prosecutor was a single woman who was emplo3ed by Mr. Reeers at the Feather's Hotel, Bridge-street. On Saturday she placed the shirt in the lavatory early in the morning. About dinner time it was seen safe and at one o'clock Mr. Rogers, who was sitting by the kitchen window overlooking the yard, saw the prisoner go int) the back yard and look in the ash tub. Subse- (Featly she went to the lavatory and after:vards left with something under her shawl. Mr. Rogers followed her and took her back to the hotel and sent for the police. P.C. Hayes came on the scene and took her to the Police Station.—Prisoner was sentenced to seven days imprisonment. SCENE IN LIVERPOOL-ROAD.—Emily SepIIOUT, Of Evelyn-street, was summoned at the instigation of Annie Clarke, out-door licensee, Liverpool-road, for using obscene language in Liverpool-rc ad.—Mr. Browne who prosecuted said that defendant went into the shop and used most. disgusting language. A gentleman who was standing by asked Mr. Clarke not to take any notice of the woman and he in turn was abused by the any who also smashed a number of jars which were on the counter. Defendant who kept interrupting was tined gland costs (305.) in all. _ .

- Tl:EsDAY.—Before Messrs. H. Roberts (chairman), C. .Jackson Holmes, J. Rymer Young and NV. Richardson. WHOLESALE THEFTS BY MARRIED WomsN.—Mary Jane Houghton, a married woman, of Wright-street, was charged with stealing from a pawnshop in Mersey- street, seven ladies skirts, two pairs of boots and a table cloth the property of Jane Houghton, pawnbroker. The Chief Constable said that the woman was before court the previous week charged with stealing a table cloth. It bad leen ascertained that she had stolen a number of skirrs and the case was accordingly adjourned. Inquiries had been made and it was ascertained that prisoner had stolen during the last four months, seven ladie3 skirts, two pairs of boots and a table cloth. Sh 3 had beea in the habit of pledging at this shop and on going out bad taken the property referred to from a rack. Mr. Houghton 11,.(1 been suspicious and erected a contrivance whereby if anything was taken from the rack a bell would ring. The prisoner went into the shop last week and as she was leaving the bell rang. An assistant went out but failed to discover that an thing bad been taken. Prisoner's husband said he did not think his wife was responsible for what she did. She had no apcessity for doing this. The Chair- man said prisoner would he fined .C 2 10s., but if she came before them again they would have no option but to send her to prison. DID NOT KNOW HER NAME.—" Mrs. " Lewis, of Oxford-street, who said she did not know her cbristian name as her husband called her so many. waa charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Oxford-street. —Sh.s was fined 10s. DISORDERLY BERAvtoun.—Ellen Ridgway,llaydook- street, was fined 3s. 6d. for disorderly behaviour in Ilaydock-street on October 18th.—Detective Redding- ton said the street was in an uproar all the morning. SLOT METER RIFLED. —James Diamond, a native of Ramsbottora was charged with stealing 14s. led. from a slot gas meter, in the house 109, Orford-lane, the moneys of the Corporation.—The Chief Constable said inquiries had been made at Wigan where prisoner had been working as a collier for three years in the Standish district. The case was adjourned from last Saturday with a view to finding out it prisoner had previous good character so that he might be dealt with leniently. Prisoner did not belong to Warrington. It appears that Susan Lee who with her husband- carried on a chip potato business 109, Orford-lane occasionally employed prisoner. On Wednesday the HU of this month she found the slot meter smashed open and only a few coppers in it whereas there should have been 15s. or ]6s.—She suspected the prisoner • and gave information to the police. P.C. Metcalfe made inquiries and eventually arrested prisoner who on being charged said "Yes, I took it." Prisoner who bad previously served in the Militia but had to leave owing to bad health, was bonni over for 12 months to come up for judgment if called upon.

TITURSDAY.—Before Messrs. C. White (chairman), NV. Roberts, J. Rymer Young, NV. T. Williams and Dr. Naden. A NOTORIOUS THlEF.—Samuel Warburton, 14 Ship- yard, was charged on remand with loitering in the neightourhood of Lovely-lane, with intent to commit a felony, and also with stealing a cap the property of Joseph Titchard of Ship-yard. He pleaded not guilty. With reference to the theft of the cap' Titobard identi- fied the article as his property. He did not tell prisoner that he could have it. P.O Berry said that at 6.30 a,m. on the 20th of this month he was on duty in 13ostack- street and on going in Selby-street he saw prisoner g..ing in the direction of Lovely-lane, carrying a sack with something in it. He went towards him and prisoner ran up an entry in Selby-street. Witness gave °bate and prisoner dropped the bag. Witness picked it up and found it to contain seven dead foals. He gave chase, but did not succeed in catching prisoner. He afterwards made inquiries with Detective Reding- ton and arrested prisoner later in tha day in Barbauld- street. They had been unable to find the owner of the birds. P.C.'s Clarke and Sankey spoke to seeing prisoner the same morning. Detective Reddington said that he in company with P.C. Berry made inquiries and searched all the lodginghouses in the district. On going into Buttermarket-street they saw prisoner whom Berry pointed out. On piisoner seing them he walked at a fast rate across Market-gate into Cheapside, through Castle-street and into Barbauld-street. They followed him there and arrested him. They questioned him as to h's movements that morning and he could not give a satisfactory abswer so they took him to the Police Station and charged him with stealing the cap. He replied th it the cap had been given to him by Titcbard. He knew nothing about the fowls. Prisoner said that the police had arrested the wrong man. He had been four time previously before the court, three time for fowl stealing.—The Chief Constable described him as" a notorious fowl thief." He was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.

div.head: Juvenile Court
div.p: Juvenile Court

THCRSDAY.—Meesrs. C. White (chsirman), W. Roberts, J. Ryn.er Young, W. T. Williams and Dr. Naden. SENT TO A REFORMATORY.—Iiatry Forste'r (t 4 8, School Brow, who was remanded on the charge of steal- ing a purse containing money arida amber of Canadian postal orders the property of Dinah Muir' with a view to sending him to a reformatory school, was again before the court. The Chief Constable said he had been is communication with the authorities of the reformatory school at Market Drayton and they were willing to take the boy over. He suggested that the boy be left there until he was 19 years of age. It would considerably benefit the boy who was only 14 years of aze.—The defendant was accordingly sent to school for five years.

Methodist Free Church Buckley-street. The Anniversary Services were preached on Sunday last by Mr. W. Taylor of Chester, morning and evening. In the- afternoon a Musical Service was presided dyer by Mr. Bate when an excellent address was delivered by Mr. W. Taylor. Mr. Shaw read the lesson, the soloists being Mr. Joe Hannan and Miss Ilipkiss. Mr Haley and Miss Plinston acted as accompanists.

Wycliffe P.S.A.- Society. There was a good meeting on Sunday, when Mr. W. Beswick presided and spoke upon "A purpose in life," Mr. E. W. Evans gave the address, his subject being "We would see Jesus." The two Greeks reftrred to in the text bad beard of the work of Jesus, His sympathy and influence. The times were bad, the people wicked. Sin's werk.vvvs at its greatest. It was the fulness of time for the appearing of Jesus. Jesus a worker with His hands, gave dignity to labour. Jesus had great feelings of sympathy, a Divine gift to min. The influence of Jcsus was great then, and was the same to-day. The whole world UM influenced by His love and power. Mr. G. Colley and Mr. Carter aiso took part in the meeting. Mr. PB3 ton presided at the organ. The Secretary said the Society had secured the services of the Williams' Jubilee Singers from America, who will give a number of their sacred pieces at the open meeting on Sunday next. The service would commence at 2.45 prompt. Mr. Yong° would give a shott address, and he asked the brethren to come arty as he expected a crowded Church.

Bewsey-road Wesley Guild. A concert arranged and submitted by gentlemen only was held in connection with the Besysey-road Wesley Guild on Monday evening last in the Lecture Hall The Bev. E. B. keeling presided. Allhough the pro- ceedings were entirely in the hands of the male members, the programme was so well varied and admiraMy given, that everything passed off in a very pleasant and interesting mariner and the gathering was simply delighted with the entertainment. The "Burton " Glee S;ngers contribute:l " 0' peaceful night " and "in absence," and Mr. G. Gough gave a splendid rendering of "The Lowland Sea." "Good Company" by Mr. J. Sefton earned well-merited applause. Mr. W. Pearce played two short pianoforte solos with characteristic brilliance, while his brother Arthur well sang " Anchored." Mr. J. Mathcr rendered "The Sailor's Grave " ; Mr. J. E. Hannan, "My Queen " ; Mr. J. Tynan," Great Uncle Jan Trippit and Mes4rs. Sefton and Dutton "Battle Eve." The " Burton " Qu rrtette contributed "Shamrock and Mr. L. Woods played on the violin " The Pirates of Penzance "and `La Traviata." Rev. Thomas . Miller on Germany.

The Rev. Thomas Miller addressed the reetnbeis of the Bold-street Rib's Class on Sunday afternoon on his impressions of his recent visit to the Continent. He said he was very much impressed by the fact that be saw very few anxious faces. He never saw any poverty. It might have been that he did not go deeply into the life—one could not go far in three weeks. At Cologne he did not see any poverty, but there were sotr.o very poor people. He was not struck as in England with the people lazying about all over the neighbourhood with nothing to do. There seemed to be a great contentedness among the people. He referred to the fact that the Government provided homes for comsumptives. The Government found it cheaper to send their smitten as far as practical to the sanatorium, old age was provided for and sickness and invelidity. Ile thought that removed a worry from life. Whatever it was that would remove the poverty and the great cause of anxisey which was over the labouring classes in England—whether it was Socialism or anythiug else—be hoped it would soon he removed. Aeother thought that impressed him was the military element. Ile was a peace man and he believed in dis.ramment but he must say that very rarely did be see a man that was round-shouldered. He was very much impressed by the size of the people. He thought they s,nt their worst specimens over here as bandmast,rs. (Lteighter) In a convers.,tion with an influential gentleman in Germany he said that if war came it, would not be the feeling of the Enellsh people or the German people but because of those who worked scares in newspapers to get a good circulation. On every hand the rev, gentle- man had received courtesy and he had never seen any drunkenness except on the part of some students on a boat who had become a little too patriotic. There were no Lars except at Cologne. As a rule the German when he went for a drink sat down and listened to the music. If a country were judged by its churches it wail 4 be said that Germany was very religious. Each way they looked they found Churches. They appealed in Germany rather to the sensual side of religion for it was warty all ritual, and the appeal to the eye did not leave sufficient room for the culture of the soul and simplicity of means in the presence of God. The churches were very gorgeous. There was a grant sacrifice for learning and the government were willing to pay for it. The training of a child, as far ache could gather, in an elementary school was more practical and more inclined for languages than ours. He saw two battlefi •Ida —Waterloo and Worms. The former was a very brave battle, but the latter meant more for them and that was the battle of Martin Luther and the great Roman Catholic Church. Thut battle was, as Carlyle said, where civilisation was born. Warrington Church Society. The anniversary service in connection with this Society was held at St. James' Church, Latchford, on Tuesday evening, when the preacher was the Rev. Canon J. Davenport Kelly, of Manchester Cathedral. He said that those who watched the sips of the times were never tired of telling us that in their judgment we hid arrived at a very critical period. If we replied that we had heard that before, and that there never seemed to have been a period in the history of the Church when there was not a crisis impending or arrived, they askea us to lok at the words uttered not by one class of people alone, not by the clergy or those who naturally might he supposed to take a view dependent upon the position of the Church, but at what was said by men of all classes. The politician, for example, could mesa the present time that the questions brought before lam were net concerned with this or that party, but with the great principles of Government. Again, those who cared for education were distressed to see what a set was made in many places against denominational instruction in religious knowledge and, further, those who cared for the Church as a whole were naturally in a state of anxiety to see %%hat an attack was being made against one portion of the Church in the Province of Canterbury, in the matter of the four dioceses that were to he found in Wales. Continuing, the preacbrr said it had occurred to him that it might therefore be useful to consider some portion of Scripture that might have a tendency to brace them up for new efforts, to strengthen thAir resolution and to infuse into their hearts a truer faith that; strong in the name of the Lord, would be able to meet any antagonists from without or from within, without fear as to the future. The Canon proceeded to speak on the words "Be of good cheer. It is T, be not afraid" and emphasised the lesson that when the Church seemed to be in imminent peril Christ eame near to help them. He urged his hearers to live pure, unstained lives, and to assist in driving back the forces of evil, such as intemperance, ungodliness, indifference and impurity.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" The Hypocrites:"

The management of thi-s-popular theatre are show- ing commendable enterprise in treating their patrons t., such, an interesting variety of first-class productions. This week we have a return visit from '''The Hypocrites," one of the most powerful of modern dramas in which Mr. Henry Arthur Jcnes tuthlesly exposes some of the shams of society, and shows what courage is required of the moral reformer when the "powers that be" are arrayed against him.- The Rev. Edgar Linnell, the young curate of Weybury, soon comes into collision with the . squire when hp ' tries to put his advanced ideals into practice in a sleepy parish where things have long been allowed to go their own sweet way. His • scheme for a model publichouse is tabooed because it Will give offence to the wealthy brewer and he is commanded to apologise for his temerity. But his crowning " indiscretion " is committed when he points out the plain course of . duty to the squire's son and attempts to dissuade him from a great wrong Threats and cajolery are employed in vain. The curate sticks to his guns and after some scenes of tense excitement and suspense, he triumphs in the end. Mr. Benson North carries off the honours of the evening as the Rev. Edward Linnell. He impers-mates the militant parson to the life and declaims . his many telling lines with great force and eirnestness, his portrayal throughout being so realistic as to call forth loud cheering. Mr. Basil Dyne achieves a conspicuous success as the Rev. Edward Datibeney, the- self-C(412 placent vicar of Weybury, and Mr. W. 'P. Sterling-is also well placed us the brusque Mr. Willniore, the Lord of the Manor. Another clever study is that of the family lawyer and estate agent by Mr. George 'rraill, and Mr. Douglas Jefferies does justice to the part of Lennard Willmore. Miss V. St. Lawrencelas a difficult role as Mrs Willmore, who is always trying to shield her wayward son, but she acquits herself, with credit. Miss yenta Vivien iS a charming Helen Plugenet, Miss Celestine Bertram gives a touching representation of Rachel Neve, and Miss Grace Baring causes great merriment as the fussy and inquisitive Mrs. Blaney. The orchestra, under Mr. Norman Latham's conductor Ship, plays some capital selections between the acts. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMIE. - " TIIE FLAG LIEUTENANT." .
AIR. EDGAR KENT AS "THE FLAG LIEUTENANT."

For next week an attraction of a very differen' ttype is announced, in-a play which has established. a most successful record in London, having -had a continuous run for over a year, and is now meeting NVith an equal success in the provinces. "The Flag _Lieutenant "is, as its name implies, a naval play, and is noticeable for its remarkable realism, every detail, from the after- cabin of the admiral's ship to the whistle of tbe steam launch as it rushes through the waters of Malta Harbour (a chsrming setting of which is given), being faithfully rendered. One of the most striking features of the play is its curiously modern tone, which brings forth the naturalness which is the characteristic feature of the present-day actor, and the depicting of life in the British Navy as it actually exists to-day. The play is brimful of interest, without any undue sensationalism, from start to ,finish, and replete with sparkling dialogue and fine touches of humour, and is calculated to rivet the attention of every class of playgoer by the gradual. development of plot and incident, culminating in the final scene representing the celebration of the King's birthday on board " H.M.S. Royal Edward." The company has neen carefully selected by Messrs. Lyn Harding and Sidney Cooper, and everything _points'to a most successful visit.

Wycliffe Young People's Society. This Society held its weekly meetipg on Monday evening in the Memorial Buildings, Mr. Eccles presid- ing. Mr. G. A. Dunlop, assistant 'curator at. the Museum, read a highly interesting piper entitled "Sidelights on Shakespeare." A short discussion followed. • Afterwards Mr. A. Millar the (hon. secre- tary) proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the 'essayist. This was seconded by Mr. Charles Hawthorn and was carried unanimously.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
AN INTERESTING HISTORY.
[By Mr. John P. Reynolds].

• An interesting history of the seventy-six years' work of the Warrington Musical Society . has been compiled from the Society's records by Mr. John P. Reyjaolds, the hon. treasurer, and .it is hoped that its publication here and in the-pamphlet form in which the society is issuing it, will .result in an increased public interest in this praiseworthy organiza- tion and consequently in a largely augmented sub- scription list. There were last season 84 subscribers out of a population in Warrington alone of 72,000, or equal to .about 116 persons per 1,000. Surely, as :Mr. Reynolds says in his preface, this is not a very creditable record for a town standing as high in the ,musical world as Warrington undoubtedly does. .The Society has almost all through Its existence, been much hampered through. lack of funds, and con- sidering the excellent work it has done, and is still doing, it is very desirable that it should be put on such a footing as would secure it against loss on its working, ,and enable its Committee to still further extend iti usefulness (1) by granting free musical education in cases of unusual talent without means of development; (2) by the establishment of scholar- ships at the Royal College of Music, Manchester, or elsewhere, and (3) by raising the. standard of its performances still higher. An effort is being made to establish a reserve fund or endowment of £l,OOO. A start has been made,.and £4OO is already invested out of money handed over to the Society's treasurer by the committee of the opera section of the Society. It is hoped, that further sums may be raised in this way, but ' the last two operas 'having proved sanewhat unprofitable, other help is urgently needed. Mr. Reynolds expresses his indebtedness to the late Mr. John White, who very kindly revised the history before it went to press, and added some very interest- ing facts and particulars.

that the above concert reflects great credit on all vi ho took part in it. The music was well selected, &c., &c." Mr. Kerfoot, the Society's conductor, appointed at the first meeting, occupied that position till October, 1837, when a difficulty arose, owing to his declining to assist in choosing the music for the concert due that rhonth, "in consequence of the inefficient state of the choir." A special general meeting was thereupon called, and the conductor was asked if be had any objection to officiate according to the present estab- lishedrules. Mr. Kerfoot declined to answer this and at a subsequent meeting, called on October 3rd, it was resolved "That certain difficulties having pre- sented themselves, this meeting be and is hereby adjourned until further notice and that the meet- ings of the Committee be also suspended during 'the same period or until the annual meeting. This was held on January 2nd, 1838, when certain alterations were made to the rules, and it was decided to look out for a professor as conductor, Mr. Eaude, a local musician and organist of the Parish Church, being eventually appointed organist and accompanist. At the same meeting it was decided to solicit the support and patronage of Mr. Blackburne. To this he kindly acceded and he was for many years intimately conm cted with the Society. On February lith, 1838, Mr. Eyton, of Liverpool, was appointed conductor of the Society at a minimum salary of ,:tl5 per annum, and it having been decided "to engage six females as a class of choral singers," he was further appointed to teach them at a salary of £lO per annum. Jr.A • Eyton's period of office was short and not very success!ul ; he had been obliged to bring over singers from Liverpool to help the chorus, which was inefficient owing to resignations and bad attendance, and as he had not received the encourage- ment or obtained the pupils he expected, he resigned on November 19th, 1839, and his letter of resignation was laid before the general meeting on January 9th, 1840, when it Iras moved and seconded "that the. 'Society be dissolved." This was not carried, but on an amendment the meeting was adjourned to allow of further cousideration. At the adjourned meeting, it was unanimously resolved to continue, and the cordial thanks of the meeting were tendered to Mr. J. Wilson Patten (afterwards Lord Winmarleigh) for his valuable I support, and expressed good wishes for the welfare of the Society.

Followi-ng on this meeting, a Mr. Gillings was engaged as leader at £25 per annum, and rehearsals were resumed on Tuesday night in teach week. In, May, 1840, it was proposed to make the " Lecture Hall " the headquarters of the Society, but lack of funds, and difficulty attending the removal of the organ caused this proposal to be abandoned. In November of the same year, however, "Mr. Blackburne having acceded to a proposition for accommodating the Society in the Town Hall, Market Place, at a rental of z£lo per annum, it was resolved to remove forthwith and to raise a fund to remove the organ and to pay off the Society's debt,which amounted to .£112.". In all, about £l2O was raised, including :.4:10 from J. W. Patten, Esq. Mr. Blackburne was Lord of the Manor at Warring- ton at this time, and as such owned the market tolls. The Town Hall, so called (afterwards for 30 years called. the Music Hall) was a good sized plain room over store rooms and warehouses, used in connection with the Market, and close to the Blackburne Arms, then called the Cock and Ti umpet. There was a small plat'orm or orchestra in. the Hall bitt there were no retiring rooms, so when the interval came in a performance, the principal artistes had to descend the narrow staircase and cross over "in the open" to the Cock and Trumpet, there to be regaled in an upper room with cake and wine. Between this time and Beptember, 1812, there is nothing of special interest in the records: but on the 25th of that month, financial reasons rendered it necessary to dispense with the services of Mr. Gillings, and on February 7th, 1843, Mr. Eaude was aprointed in. his place. Mr. Gillings was, however, specially engaged for concerts on May 23rd, 1813, and on October 15th, 1844.

In August, 1813; the Society again 'found itself in debt, to the extent of £B6, exclusive of a debt of £6O on the organ, ar,d it was decided to again open a gubscription list; it was also decided to give a Ball in aid of the Society. This was given on February 15th, 1844. and realized £l5 Bs. A Farther sum was raised by subscription. For some years after, the ball was given annually, and a supper was also given annually to performers out of funds specially provided, to which subscribers and their friends were admitted at a charge of 2s. or 2s. 6d. per head.. These suppers generally took place at the Waggon and. Horses Inn. .and were presided over by William Beamont, Esq., and other influential gentlemen. In January, 1844, the first move was made towards obtaining a 'Public Hall for Warrington, hut nothing came °tit then. The rules of the Society were again altered iind amended on Feb-tit-my- 10th;- 1847: the preamke once more setting out clearly the objects of the 'Society, viz. :--" The . Warrington Musical Society is established for the encouragement •of local talent in the performance of vocal and instrumental music, and for improving and extending musical taste in the town and neighbourhood by means of concerts, or such other proceedings as the committee may consider best adapted to effect those objects, and the Society, in the election of officers and in the conduct of its proceedings,- disclaims and forbids the introduction of any party feeling, either religious or political, at any of its meetings:"

On August 22nd, 1848, a proposal made by Mr; . Peter Pylands (then Mayor) was considered. He suggested that the Society should give a concert oa- tbe first Monday in each month, to which the members. of the Mechanics!. Institute and the Natural History Society should he admitted free, they in turn provid- ing lectures or -entertainments on the other Mondays to which the Musical Society's members should be admitted free. To this proposal the committee agreed, but it being impossible to get up concerts at such short notice, the number of concerts was limited to five. At the annual meeting this year, the Society was again in financial difficulties (attbuted. to corri7 mercial depression), and it Was necessary to raise funds by special means to enable the dress concert due to subscribers, to lig given. A. hall or soiree was suggested and also an exhibition of works of art, but this .latter suggestion was opposed by Mr. J. F. Marsh on the ground that the society was not of sufficient importance and because he feared that such an exhibi- tion would eclipse the first establishment of the new' Museum. A soiree and bail was therefore decided on. I In 1851, there was a difficulty as to the orchestra I owing to a deficiency of violinists, and in January, ,1852, the committee decided to re-commence the vocal and instrumental classes, the • members - of .the , Mechanics' Institute being invited to co-operate. Oa ' March 30th, 1852, the Oratorio "Judas Maccabeus,7 was given with such success that it was repeated .popular prices "for, the benefit of the lower classes, prices of admission being Is., 6d. and 3d. ThiS how, I ever, was not appreciated, and. led to a serions loss, and another deficiency of £24 was anLounced 'at the following annual Meeting. . Another arrangement was now made with Mr. Blackburne, and the ball was taken exclusively' by the Society, at a ,rental of £2O per annum, and was let out by .the Committee when not required by the • Society. - In September, 1853, a resolution was passed limiting the issue of tickets and programmes solely-to subscribers ; this was again confirmed on March 9th, 1857, and remained in force .for some years. Oa October 17th, the following minute appears : " That the next concert take. place on November 7th, and that in consequence of the treble- singers not having attended the practices, there will be no chorus on this occasion." At the annual Meeting, Februai-y. 12th, 1853, the accounts showed a balance in hand of £23, £42 having been - raised by two balls to wipe off ibp debt and provide for the painting of the hall. In 1856 there appears to have been another society formed, called the Choral Society, and application was made to the Musical Society for the use of their hall. This was granted on. the understanding that the members of the Choral society rendered assistance at any Musical Society's concerts when required. There . was another society (unless it was the Choral under, another name) in existence in 1857, of which a Mr' Rimmer was the conductor, and Mr. John White. I organist. This society announced its object as being I (1) " To effect a combination of all the musicianS ia I the town and neighbourhood.. (2) To diffuse a' -more Igeneral'appreciation of good music among the inhabi- tants of Warrington." It had a membership (chorus and band) of about 50 performers, and gave public concerts

'1 here is no doubt that the Musical Society was at this time greatly hampered in its operations by the want of a good hall (as was again the case later, prior to the building of the Parr Hall), and at the annual meeting on January 13th, 1858, it was resolved " That in the opinion of this meeting a Public Hall la much wanted, and the officers of the society are requested to take steps to bring the matter before the town." This, combined probably with other influence, resulted in the building of the Public Hall in the year 1861, and .in 1864 as above mentioned) the Society's organ was greatly enlarged and erected la this new hall, under an arrangement with the Public •Hall Co., which gave the Society free use of the hall for a certain number cf nights in each year. " The organ was opened by Mr. Best on May 23rd, 1805. (To be eontinucd).

div.head: HISTORY.
div.p: THE HISTORY.

It appears that prior to the yea? , 1831, there existed. in Warrington three separate Musical Societies, work- ing at least to some extent antagonistically, as in the minutes of the first general meeting of the Society (the lion. and Rev. Horace Powys, M.A., in the chair), the following " appears :--" That thanks be given to the 11 n. and Rev. Chairman for his able and impartial conduct in the chair, and throughout the proceedings and deliberation to effect a conciliatory union of the three Societies, and thereby to accomplish the extinc- tion of all animosity amongst the lovers and sup- porters of music." The preliminary meeting was held on December, 1833, and it was then decided to call a general meet- ing on January 2nd, 1834, when the rules and byelaws of the new Society were settled and officers elected. To name all the officers elected during the 76 years -would take up too much space and be of comparatively little interest. 1, however, append a separate list of the presidents, secretaries, treasurers and conductors. As pioneers of the Society, the following even now well-known names may be cited :—Messrs. Jas. Marson, ;John RylandS'. Wm. Hall, Edelsten, Guest, Pickmere, Ridgeway, -Henry and John White, J. W. Patten (afterwards Lord Winniarleigh), R. A. Cross (after- wards Lord Cross), Wm and Jas. Stubbs, G. Greenall, Beamont and J. Ireland Blackburne. •

At .the outset, the Society was divided into two separate departments, choral and barmonia—the choral for the performance of sacred, and the harmonic for miscellaneous and secular music. Each were to give two concerts in each year ; the choral in February and August (afterwards altered to March and October), and the harmonic in May and November (the latter altered later to December). Separate Com- mittees consisting of a President, two Vice-presidents, Treasurer, Secretary and Assistant Secretary, and nine members, were elected for each department. The rules and bye-laws adopted at the first general meeting are interesting reading, but are too lengthy to give in detail. I, however, quote the following as giving the key-note .of the Society, which has been adhered to all these years, and as •(to some extent) indicating the different state of society then existing. Rule I.—Defines the Society and Departments., Rule 2 reads :7--" In the election of members and. in conducting the proceedings, this Society disclaims and absolutely forbids the introduction of any party feel- ing, religious oe political. Should any member be .gaty of infringing this rule, he shall be reprimanded by the President-in the first instance, and should the offence I)e rt.peated, he shall be subject 46 expulsion at the discretion of the Committee."

Bye-La' 0 reads :---" Every ordinary member who shall be absent at a quarter past eight, shall be fined two-pence, and if absent at nine o'clock, four-pence, unless same arise from -sickness or absence on business."

Bye-Law 11 reads :—" Members selling their tickets of admission shall be expelled." "Members appear- ing in a state of intoxication or otherwise misbehaving themselves durirg a public performance or general rehearsal shall be immediately expelled." This rule was enforced in several instances.

One of the first acts of the Committee in 1834 appears to have been the taking of the "Music Hall," a room in Bewsey-street, at a yearly rental of £l3, to be used for rehearsals and concerts. When not required by the Society, it was let out far other purposes. On February sth, a contract was entered into with Samuel lien'', of Manchester, to build an organ cost- ing £155. .This was an F organ with six stops on the great and four on the swell-It was vested in Trustees; the trust deed being dated April 30th, 1835. (In 1810, this organ was removed to another and better Iroom—the ToWti hail - (afterwards called the Music L.Hall) in. the Market Place, which was rented frOm Mr. Sohn Ireland Blackburne, and it remained there till 1865, when it was rebuilt and greatly enlargedAamost entirely at the cot of Joseph Lytton, ESq., Who" paid about £5OO for the work done. The enlarged organ was.then erected in the new Public Hall, nylands- street, and was again vested in Trustees). The first practice of the Choral Department took place on Tuesday, January ith, 1834, and that of the Harmonic on Tuesday, January .14th, with Mr. Kerfoot as conductor. Another class was also started in accordance with Byelaw 5, which reads "that twelve members t)f . the Society of good moral character, who shall possess good voices and natural taste for music, shall receive initructibn for not exceeding two years free of all cost?' This byelaw was rescinded in 1836.

The first concert of the choral department was given on March 25th, with a programme selected entirely (with the exception of one chorus by Beethoven) from Haydn's and Handel's music, and that of the harmonic department on June 10th, 1831, with a miscellaneous programme. The second concerts were similar in character, and were given in September and December Of the, same year. These were repeated each year till 1836 when at a general meeting held on June 21st a resolution was passed uniting the two departments. At all these concerti the Society's orchestra took part. and rendered symphonies, overtures, quartettes, &c., by Haydn, Handel, Romberg, Viotti, &c., &c. In 1835, ,the band mustered sixteen members, e.g., 4 violins, 2 tenors, 2 'cellos, 1 double bass, 2 flutes, 2 horns, 1 trumpet, 1 trombone and drum, played by some of the gentlemen named in a preceding paragraph, and others. Some of the instruments, e.g., 2 horns, 1 trumpet, 1 trombone, were purchased by the Society and loaned to members. A piano and a quantity of music were also purchased.. ' The following paragraph from the 'Manchester Guardian" of June 14th, 1834, is somewhat interest- ing reading and amusing :
WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

"Under the patronage of the Hon. and Rev. Horace: Powys and J. W. Patten, Esq., M.P, the first concert of. the Harmonic Department of the Society took place at the Music Hall, Bewsey-street, on the 10th inst. What cannot skill and perseverance ~effect ? If we had been told even twelve months ago that Warring 7 ton would ever have boasted of a Musical Society like the present .one, so well-organised, so Munerous its members,- so much unanimity among them and so superior its public 'performances we should no doubt have replied, "this is too , good news to be true.' Warrington is too party spirited; its inhabitants know comparatively nothing of music, and will, we are con- fident, never attain to much-eminence. _

"Several very respectable individuals have been actively engaged in the foundation and promotion of this Society, but as Mr. Kerfoot is the only professor c:nnected with it, and on whom the most important part muss necessartly devolve, we -think unqualified praise is due to him for so generously and gratuitously exercising his knowledge and superior musical talent. in bringing about and oontinuing to support what had so long bee-i a , desideratum, but apparently impracticable. div.head: KING IN EAST ANGLIA.
div.p: THE KING IN EAST ANGLIA.

His Majesty had a loyal and enthusiastic reception in Norwich on Monday. This was the first occasion for two hundred years that a British Sovereign had set foot in the capital of East Anglia, and the inhabitatants made the most of the historic event. The King lunched with the Mayor and Corporation, inspected the Territorials, witnessed a parade of veterans, was cheered by ten thousand children, and laid the foundation of the extension to the Norfolk and Norwich Hospital. His Majesty was greeted everywhere with the utmost enthusiasm, the Royal precession oeing rapturously cheered as it made its way through miles of gaily decorated streets. Our illustrat.on shows the King presenting colours to one of the Territorial units.

div.head: PRINCE ITO.
div.p: PRINCE ITO.

Prince Ito, "the Bismarck of Japan," who Was assassinated by a Korean, was the great man to whom Japan largely owes her western civilisation. He went to Korea after the war With Russia, and ruled the people with a rod of iron. Be was highly unpopular with the Koreans, and was cursed by the children in the streets.

WHERE THE KING SPENT HIS WEEK-END. QUIDENHAM HALL. On the occasion of his visit to East Anglia, His Majesty spent the week-end with the Earl and Countess of Albemarle at cuidenham Hall, which is a picturesque Georgian residence of red brick with stone dressing, and a handsome front. The Earl of Albemarle has many interesting portraits and he can also boast of a fine collection of war trophies. A unique feature of Quidenhath Hall is that the principal bedrooms bear the names of the various naval and military battles iu whicb members of the Keppel family have distinguished themselves.

MORE ABOUT THE CHESHIRE PROPHET.

Our pilgrimage 'ln search of Nixon the Cheshire prophet"has given grave dissatisfac- tion to many of our readers, and if we are to maintain our reputation we must of necessity return to the subject. Our article contained a half-admission that the subject had carried us into the realm of the grotesque and that we felt unable to give a serious ending to our enquiry. Indeed we only explored his birth place,and our statement upon this point have since been challenged on the ground that the neighbouring village of Whitegate con- tains and still shows the cottage in which this wonderful man was born.

In dealing with a character whose birth cannot be fixed within a couple of centuries, the modern antiquarian is at serious dis- advantage and his statements are liable to become very nebulous: there seems nothing for it therefore, but to go back to the earliest written records and allow the readers to form his own judgment. We have found an ancient print dating from the early days of Queen Anne which professes to give with accuracy the prophecies of Nixon, but before we transcribe it, let us tell of a small pilgrimage upon a recent autumn day in search of Nixon relics, and let us also give the reader an introduction to the famous Robert himself.

div.head: NIXON OF TRADITION.
div.p: THE NIXON OF TRADITION.

Every chronicler agrees that he was regarded as a fool in everything except his. prophesying. "A short squab fellow with a great head and goggle eyes "he lived a sulky life, hating children and beating them if they came within reach, and occasionally going into trances in which he spoke as an inspired oracle. His fame spread and the King sent for him to reside at Court for purposes of Royal amusement. Nixon was distressed and wept,declaring that if he went to London he would be starved. When he made his appearance at Court the King, having hidden a ring, tested his powers by asking him to find it. The Cheshire yokel replied "He who hideth can find." This tickled the King and he decided to keep Nixon as part of his retinue, and lest the prediction of his starva- tion should come true ordered that he should to be kept in the kitchen. Nixon had a true Cheshire appetite—he could manage a leg of mutton at a sitting—and made himself a nuisance by his habit of licking and stealing meat. In a moment of anger the cook locked him in a small chamber. Here he was forgotten ; the Court was moved from London and he was left to starve.
So runs the story as universally accepted, and it is too ancient to be meddled with.
THE HEADLESS CROSS.

On a recent autumn day when the weather and the fates were propitious we were minded to go and do a little exploration in the country of Nixon. All the versions of his sayings include the blood-chilling chant A raven shall sit on the top of Headless Cross In the forest so grey, And drink of the nobles' blood so free.

The linterpretation !is said to be that great battles wouldbe fought in the forest and that blood would run so freely that a raven sitting on the top of the Cross would be able to drink the blood that flowed past. It would have hadto be several feet deep to permit the bird to reach it, and this consideration doubtless added to the awsomeness of the prophecy. But Cheshire people tell us that the Head- less Cross has now sunk into the ground so low that a bird of average length of neck could reach the ground while perched upon its summit and it only needs that a battle should come and that a few of the Daven- ports, Cholmondeleys, and Chetwoods should go and obligingly get killed there and the prophecy might come as true as all the rest. We decided to go in search of the Cross to see for ourselves. The circuitous forest paths by which we reached it won't be described here except in the observation that we found an appetite long before we found a Cross._ We are going to tell thu reader a simple and easy way of reaching it. On the Tarporley Road is an old Inn which rejoices in the title " Cabbage Hall." Several hundred yards from it on the War- rington side a small road branches into the forest and half a mile or so along it in front of a cottage stands the so-called Cross.

But the Cheshire orade;;;e-w-r-ong: This is not a Cross and it hasn't sunk into the ground. It is an upright stone firmly socketed in other stones but broken down by the accidents of centuries. A large piece of the shaft was shown to me by the cottager, lying behind his gate post. It is undoubtedly the ancient boundary mark of the forest of Mara and takes us back many centuries. The adjoining forest land is called Abbots Moss. In this name and in the stone there linger interesting reminders of the days when the Abbots of Vale Royal were the rulers here and hunted the stag in the wild glades of the forest. But if the boundary stone be not the Cross the pilgrim.has not far to go to find one. Tumbled into the shallow ditch not far from the highway is the socketed base of an undoubted Cross and this may be the remnant ofthe memorial familiar to Nixon. We are inspecting the stone when the cottager assures us that he can show another if we like to traverse his field. We are sceptical, but agree to go. And our guide is right. Planted in a hedgerow remote from all the ways or by-ways, we are able to inspect and measure a fine relic, of which we imagine Cheshire antiquarians know nothing, the base of a fine medieval Cross.

div.head: TRUE PROPHESY OF NIXON.
div.p: THE TRUE PROPHESY OF NIXON.

And now for the "True prophesy of Nixon" as assuredly believed and written two centuries ago. "There lived in former ancient times a fool whose name was Nick's Son. He was kept in the family of the Cholmondeleys of Vale Royal. One day he came from ploughing in the field and laying down the things he had in his hand, he remayned a little while in the dumps, and then with a hoarse voice said "Now I'll prophesy." 'When a raven shall build in a Lyon's Mouth, then a King of England shall be driven out of his Kingdom and never return, and an Heir shall be born to Cholmondeley's Family: An eagle shall then sit on the Top of the House, and this Heir shall live to see England invaded by Foreigners, who shall come as far as Delamere Forest; but a Miller, named Peter, shall be born with two heels on one foot, and shall at that time be living in a mill, and shall be Instrumental in delivering the Nation: a boy shall be born with three Thumbs, and shall hold the King's Horses, while England shall three times be Won and Lost in one Day. The Invader shall be killed, and laid across a Horse's back like a Calf, the Miller shall be Knighted by the Victorious Prince, and after that England shall see Happy days and men of valour and merit shall prosper again.
Oulton Mill shall be driven with blood
VINO
an

instead of water, and there shall be so great slaughter of Men that Horses Saddled shall run about till their girths rot away. As a token of the truth of these things the wall of Esquire Cholmondeley's House towards the Pond shall fall; if it fall down- wards the chuich shall be oppressed, but if upwards, against the rising hill on the side of it, it shall flourish again; the Pond shall run red three days, and on the Stone Cross pillar in the forest a crow shall sit and drink the best blood in England."

div.head: FULFILMENT.
div.p: THE FULFILMENT.

Such is the oldest and perhaps least- adulterated version. And everything seems to have come true except the bloodshed. The raven built its nest in the mouth of a stone lion, and King James thereupon abdicated: The eagle sat on the house top and the heir was born; the miller with the heels and the boy with the correct number of thumbs duly appeared, but were dead before the invaders arrived; Oulton Mill clicks on waiting for the battle, but the Pond at Vale Royal ran clay-red for three days to every- body's mystification; the wall fell and as it fell up-hill the Establishment was saved and the day of disestablishment indefinitely postponed. For the rest we are waiting—but not hoping. 'We cordially advise the reader to go in search of Nixon and his relics. He may not find either ravens or crosses or the brook that ran red, but he will find forest pines and bracing air and an appetite worthy of the prophet himself. And we can tell him where he may sit under the pines and get a tea to match the appetite, and all for sixpence, but the secret is too good to give away. A.M.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday,the Rev. T. R. Matthews presiding. There were also present :—Miss Broadbent. Mrs. Simpson, Mrs.Colling- wood, Messrs. G. Mather, A. J. Jolley, W. Gill, J. Bi'tinge, W. Houghton, W. C. Brooks, W. Furness, R. Lee, J. A. Rushworth, R. Bolton, W. Flannagan, M. W. Seton, T. Ritchie, A. Brooks, A. Bottomley (clerk),R.W. Peacock (aissistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master) and A. Wright (superintendent of Cottage Homes).

div.head: FARM COLONY.
div.p: A FARM COLONY.

At a meeting of the House Committee a letter was read from the Christian Social Service Union with respect to the farm which they had opened at Marple for the purpose of training and reclaiming unemploy- able men. The charge per week per man for mainten- ance is 12s. It was recommended that no action be taken in the matter.
This was agreed to. TIIB NEW BUILDING.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee twelve tenders were received for the loan of £6,657 required for the provision of the new aged and infirm block. It was recommended that the offer of the Hull Savings Bank to lend the sum of £6,657 for a period of thirty years at 3fl per cent, plus loan charges at the rate of 10s. per cent, on the amount proposed to be borrowed. the loan to be repaid by equal half-yearly payments of principal with interest on the balance remaining unpaid, be accepted and that the Clerk be directed to make the necessary arrangements for the money to be received by the Treasurer of the Union. Mr. JOLLEY in moving the adoption of the minutes said the accepted tender was the most favourable one. The minutes were approved. VALUER' SALARY. _ _ _ _

Mr. J. BILLINGE moved, 'on the recommendation of the Assessment Committee, that Mr. R. It. Meacock. the valuer, be granted an honorarium of £lOO for special services rendered during the current year. Mr. JOLLEY seconded. Mr. W. C. BROOKS said the amount seemed a large ono and he would like some information as to the extraordinary services rendered by the valuer. Once officials had tasted the sweets of these handsome grants they would not like parting with them. He feared the grant would be a permancy. The CHAIRMAN said he supposed each case would be dealt with on its owe merits.
Mr. W. C. BROOKS: We have had no tangible evidence as to the extra work of the valuer. -

Mr. BILLINGE said he took it for granted that twentieth century business men in Warrington who had read of the enormous work the Assessment Committee had gone through during the part year and of the many revaluations which had been made, would be cognisant of the facts of the case. The valuer had bad an extra- ordinary year, large works Ecc. having been revalued,and the committee were unanimous in recommending the £lOO grant. -

The CLERK said that during the past year the valua- tion of the Union had gone up tremendously. Much new work, in addition to the usual duties, had been placed on the shoulders of the valuer. The honorarium was unanimously sanctioned. STOUT FOR, HOSPITAL INMATES.
The Board then O-oiiside-reWiWiid;;;Tosr-the supply of Guinness's stout.

Mr. FLANNAGAN : Are there any sampler, Mr. Clerk? (Laughter). Mrs. SIMPSON: Who uses the stout? The CLERK: It is used in the hospital on the recom- mendation of the medical officer. Mr. MATHER : As medicine. The Board accepted the tender of Messy s. William Owen and Son, Warrington.

INCREASH IN RELIEF. The CLERK submitted an official return abowing that there had been an increase in the amount of r chief granted in the Union during the half-year ended Lady Day of £620 as compared with the corresponding half-year.

div.head: WOMAN'S BATTLE WITH, ULCERS.
div.p: WOMAN'S BATTLE WITH, ULCERS.
Painful Trouble Ended by Zam-Buk.

When the skin-tissue breaks dow n and sloughs away into ulcers a common expezience amongst women—Zam-Buk is the one remedy that will stop the festering and build up mew healthy tissue. Mrs. Emma Marshall, of 7, The Grave, Reading, told a local reporter a personal experi once that proves this.

"My left ankle beran to ache, and felt very weak and tired," said Mrs. Marshall. In a week or two it had swelled alarmingly, and the akin all round got discoloured. For th ree months tiro doctor attended attended me, and. a trained nurse came regularly to dress the ankle. Beside a using various ointments the nurse appliel hot-water bandages to the swollen ankle. The skirt burst, leaving three big sores, "These sore; festered, and the burning pain was awful. I felt as though the flesh was being drawn from the leg 'bone. If I touched the ulcers it was as if pins and reedles were being stuck into my flesh. For months I never could sleep longer than an hour each night. I became so run-down that I was sent into the country near Woking. My ankle remained in ' a bad state, And I suffered so severely all the. time I was away that I thought I should never see- home again. The ulcers spread up my leg, eating away both skin and flesh. Ordinary ointments and E %mixes proved quite useless; they did not even relieve the pain. "Whilst staying in the country I was persuaded: te I let Zam-Buk have a ch9nce of healing my ankle. At this time the ulcers were so angry-looking that I as afraid of something more serious developing. B. Zam-Buk soon brought improvement, and caused m e to hope for a cure at last. Thanks to this rare balm's' soothing influence, I began to get good sleep at night, and during the day I felt very little pain. The inflammation and swelling disappeared, and the ulcers round the ankle dried up. When the holes caused by the ulcers had filled up with flesh. Zam-Buk grew a new, clear skin over the old sore places. "When I returned to Reading it was to surprise my friends by the ease with which I walked about after being crippled so long. This splendid Zam-Buk had made a complete cure."

COMMERCIAL FAlLURES.—According to "Kerop's Mercantile Gazette" the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, Oct 22nd, was 163, viz., :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 91 ; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 72. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 91 ; Deeds of Arrangement, 86—Total 177; being a decrease of 14. The total num- ber of Commercial Failures recorded during the 43 weeks of the present year is 6,355 ; the total number recorded in the corresponding 43 weeks of last year was 6,799, showing a decrease of 441.

ASSOCIATION OF LANCASTRIANS IN LONDON At the Annual General Meeting held on Friday, Sir William Henry Holland, Bart., M.P., was unanimously elected President for the ensuing year in succession to Mr. Justice Walton.
