div.head: By Philip Snowden, M.P.
div.p: By Philip Snowden, M.P.
ONE EFFECT OF THE BUDGET.

The Budget is having an effect upon the Municipal Elections. It is difficult for the public to be interested in two things at the same time. There has been so much talk about an early General Election that the people have got into the humour for it, and they are not disposed to put that interest aside for the minor matter of a town council election.

This frame of mind is very unfortunate, for I have no hesitation in saying that the municipal elections are far more important than the Budget. The character of the government of our town during the next year will affect the health and welfare of the people far more than anything the Budget can do if it passes into law. The wise old watchword " Eternal Vigilance is the price of liberty" should be remembered just now. The indifference of the people is the oppor- tunity of the reactionary and self-seeker. There is a serious danger of the municipal elections resulting in the victory of the anti-municipal party owing to the indiffer- ence on this occasion of the progressive forces.

div.head: STIMULATING INTEREST.
div.p: STIMULATING INTEREST.

So far as I ,can learn the Labour and Socialist party will run this year about an average number of candidates. They will have a considerable number of seats to defend owing to their members having to seek re-election. Every year the fight for the Labour Party becomes harder owing to the combination of forces against them. Every- body will agree that the Labour and Socialist party has greatly stimulated interest in municipal government. They have in many towns compelled the other parties to fight, and the increased interest has brought a much larger percentage of voters to the poll. This increased poll has told against the chances of the Labour candidates, with the result that in recent years a smaller per- centage of successes has been won although the number of votes recorded for Labour and Socialist candidates has considerably increased. aTHE LABOUR PROGRAMME.

The labour candidates are standing as usual on a programme of municipal Socialism. They favour the public ownership of all public services and they are for thorough efficiency in the schools. In many towns a strong point is being made of the adoption of the Feeding of School Children Act. Many towns have not yet adopted this measure, though the need for it has been incontestably proved. The Labour candidates stand for the municipality being a model employer, and on the other hand for the municipal employees being model workmen. The Labour Party has no sympathy with the workman who looks upon a situation under the Cor- poration as a "soft job." A workman who will not give as good, or a better day's work to a municipality than he would to a private employer is a disgrace to the working class and he ought to be dismissed instantly as a danger to the existence and success of municipal enterprise.

div.head: SORTS OF WORKMEN.
div.p: SORTS OF WORKMEN.

I have no disillusions about the working- man. I know that he is not exactly a stained glass angel. I know that he has all the faults and all the virtues of our common humanity. Among the workingmen there are the good, the indifferent, and the bad. The good can be trusted to do the fair thing; the indifferent and the bad need stern discip- line. It is generally a bad workman who resents control and authority. No business can be carried on without organization and discipline. Obedience to men in authority is as necessary in municipal as in private service; but some Workmen have got an idea that in the municipal service every man should be allowed to do just as he likes. This is a notion which will have to be dispelled, or municipal enterprise will be beaten every time by the competition of highly disciplined private businesses. The Labour Party in municipal affairs cannot countenance such absurd ideas as those; they are determined that municipal workmen shall have the best wages, the shortest hours, the best 'conditions, but they are equally determined that the workmen in return shall give the best of their services. The success of municipal enterprise proves that the municipal servants are on the whole a very fine body of workmen—indeed among the very finest of our artisan population. A GOOD RECORD.

The record of our Labour town councillors is a very creditable one. Wherever they have participated in local government they have added to its efficiency. They have brought a rare enthusiasm to the work and a close attention to duty which is unusual. In many towns they have been pioneers in reform, and many a well-established municipal service of which the ratepayers are proud would have been in the hands of a private company to-day but for the agitation and efforts of the Labour councillors. The Labour councillors are in close touch with the people, and they know the needs of the people, and if the working people themselves will not manage their own business, it is certain nobody else will do it for them.

div.head: MINERS' M.P.
div.p: THE MINERS' M.P.

The recent Conference of the Miners' Federation ratified the decision of the ballot to join the Labour Party, and I understand that the affiliation is now completed. The accession of the miners to the Labour Party brings the membership up to about 1,700,000, which is more than the membership repre- sented at the Trade Union Congress. It is nine years since the Labour Party was formed. For two or three years it seemed 'as though the scheme was not going to succeed very well; but eventually the textile unions with their enormous membership [joined the party and then things went ahead finely.

div.head: LOYAL BODY.
div.p: A LOYAL BODY.

Mge miners have been the last to come, ttt they are all the better for being late, be cause they have had time to watch the Lc anntre Party and to understand thoroughly tattiit is they are joining before taking the dec Wive:step. I have no doubt whatever that the miiners, will prove to be as loyal to the prin &riles of the Labour Party as any other of th r ztiffiliated bodies.

div.head: WISE PRESIDENT.
div.p: A WISE PRESIDENT.

The çà iniiners' candidates will run on the Labol a .rarty ticket at the next election, inclue ling the sitting members. There is some i 'trouble in Northumberland, but it will no doubt be satisfactorily settled before the ele +dim comes. When one remembers that ne %aly all the miners' M.P.'s have run in the past as Liberal-Labour candidates one ca 'net withhold admiration of their loyalty na falling into line with the decision of the Ic lagit .of their members. The Miners'

Federation is fortunate in possessing in Mr. Enoch Edwards, M.P., a President whose tact, penetration, and sound common sense mark him out as a leader of whom any organisation might be proud. GERMAN TAXATION.

In the distussions upon the Fiscal Ques- tion we are apt to regard Germany, Australia, and other protected countries as being altogether favourable to the fiscal policy which happens to be their present one. But in these protected countries there is a very strong Free Trade party, and in Germany it is a rapidly growing one. The enormous vote polled by the Social Democrats at :the last General Election—a vote about double that of any other party— was a Free Trade 'vote. The elections in Saxony and Baden, which have just been held, have resulted in a phenomenarvictory for the Socialists who fought the election mainly on the question of indirect taxation. Ithe German new taxation is very much resented by the working classes, because it puts too large a part on themselves, and leaves the rich relatively lightly taxed. It is interesting to note that these new indirect taxes are mainly excise taxes, which, as I pointed out last week, seem to indicate that the German Chancellor has not much faith that taxes put upon the foreigner will be paid by the foreigner. The revolt against indirect tax is becoming powerful in Germany and the probability is that the next elections for the Reichstag will see the Social Demo- crats make a poll of over 4,000,000 votes and more than double their representation.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Wilsons of Tranby Croft.—Mrs. Wilson, who hag been left a widow by the death of Mr. Arthur Wilson of Trimby Croft, is well-known in London Society, as is also her unmarried daughter, Miss Muriel Wilson, noted for her dramatic talents. Miss Wilson plays in French as successfully as she does in English, and has often figured as a star performer in amateur theatricals at Chatsworth, and other famous country houses. Mrs. Wilson, snd Miss Wilson are to proceed shortly to the Riviera for the winter. It was in 1890 that the famous baccarat scandal occurred at Tranby Croft, one of the house party for the Doncaster Races being accused of cheating at cards. The King, then Prince of Wales, was a guest at Tranlay Croft,at the time, and afterwards appeared in Court to give evidence in the case in which Sir William Gordon-Cummins was unsuccessful in bringing against certain members of the Wilson family. The Sailors Friend.—Lord Brassey and those who are associated with him in the matter, have appealed for help on behalf of three institutions for sailors, namely, the naval reading room at Dover, the Rest at Milford Haven, and the similar institution at Wey- mouth. It is enough to know that the first scheme— and doubtless the others—has the hearty support of Miss Agnes Weston, whose noble work for our blue- jackets is worthy of an equal place in our admiration with the crusade against pain and suffering, which Miss Florence Nightingale so heroically led in the Crimea. Lord Brassey and his friends cffer to name beds according to the desire of donors of £5, and rooms after the subscribers of very moderate sums. Unlovely Bermondsey.—Bermondsey, the scene of the Budget by-election, this week, is one of the most unlovely spots in London's province of houses. It is not noted for slums, but is one vast unbroken area of small houses of a habitable description' and a Bermondsey vicar has remarked that, apart from the public-houses, there was not a family among them who could afford to keep a servant. There was, however, a time when Bermondsey was a fashionable watering place and an aristocratic residential locality. It was renowned for its medicinal waters, commemorated in the name of Spa-road, but its glory departed early in the last century, and the district became famous for its tanneries. It is now chiefly a manufacturing centre for jam making, confectionery, hat making, and trades, employing cheap female labour, and it has been notice- able during the election that the factory hands are almost invariably hostile to the militant suffragists. The Women of Spain.—The political unrest in Spain which every now and then results in scenes of violence and agitations against the ruling classes, is said to be largely a revolt of women. Those of the wage-earning class hold strong political convictions, and the vast majority of theta are on the side of the reformers in social and political affairs. As is the case with all the Latin races their emotions are quickly aroused, and in many of the industrial conflicts and political agitations it is the women workers who are the instigators, and sometimes the leaders of acts of violence. Mostly they possess a fine physique, and display more vigour and energy than the men. The better-to-do classes naturally live a life of greater seclusion, but that does not deter the middle class Spanish woman from interesting her- self in political activities. Pen Names.—Whether or not it was the example of "George Eliot," women writers seem fond of adopting the masculine pseudonym of" George "and thus some- times leads to their books being reviewed as having been written by a man. This has lately happened to "George Pesten," the pen-name of Miss E.M.Symonds. It is said that she elected to be a" George" because she thought the name was lucky, and it was perhaps only some such trifling sentiment that evolved "George Sand," George Fleming," "George Egerton," " George Colmore, and " George Omar "—all of them women. " Lucas Malet " was the selection of two sur- names in the family, by the well-known writer—a daughter of Charles Kingsley—and it was mainly the fear that she might fail to write up to the reputation of that distinguished name in literature that induced her to conceal her identity. There are very few, if any striking instances of men having reached literary fame under the signature of a woman.

The Popularity of Cottage Homespuns.—The demand for hand-made homespuns increases year by year, a state of affairs in no small measure due to the King and Queen, and members of the Royal Family, who have long teen staunch patrons of these homespun iNclustries. Golf and shooting suits for men, coats and skirts, _wraps, and headgear for women and children.

travel-ling rugs, etc. etc-., are, at the present time, all built of homespun, dyed the most artistic shades, and woven with patterns designed by the best artists. Practkally such articles wear "for ever," the roughest treatment has little effect upon them. Moreover the sometime considerable difficulty of procuring the genuine material is past and over; for, failing shopland, there are now depots of the large national associations all over Scotland, Ireland and Wales, with big central branches in London, where the products of cottage workers are received direct and sold to the public. Necklets and Muffs.—To the girl or woman to whom good furs are an impossibility, and common ones appear undesirable, this season is presenting many advantages. Strips of narrow fur of good quality are often "picked up "—especially at sale times—very cheaply, and just now comes the opportunity to put them to excellent use. For example, the little necklet (built upon a slightly stiffened and padded shape) of rucked chiffon, and finished with the bands of fur, forms a very modish little wrap, and when a very wide, , flat mnff can be provided to match, the effect is excel- lent. By the way, muffs seem to grow wider and fl Ater every day. Still the renovator deed not despair. Much may be done towards bringing a last year's model up-to-date, by taking out the elastic at the sides, and adding either broad bands of far, or wide flatly-falling frills, as may prove most desirable. The Scarf Bodice.—For evening wear, the scarf- bodice is considerably to the fore. The robe—if the notion is to be a success, should be Princess in form, the upper portion being absolutely plain and tighly fitting, with narrow shoulder straps. Then the scarf arrives ! This should be very long and supple, and heavily fringed at the ends. First of all it is passed across the bust, and drawn to the back, where it is crossed, the ends being thrown over the shoulders the soft stuff and heavy fringe forming a most becoming veil for the bare arms.
Millinery for Sportswomen.—Many fascinating models are to he found at the milliners for the out.of-

door girl, including the thick Zibeline felt hats in half- sailor, half-cloche shape with band and bow of soft feathers in iridescent 'lades. Then there are the new " scout " hats of blue, dull green, and golden brown leather adorned with a clump of shaded game feathers, which will come cheerfully through the very worst our climate can do for us. For the girl who golfs, or who loves the rod and basket, these hats are quite the most desirable ever placed on the market. Food Adulteration.—From statements made at the International Food Conference in Paris, it would appear that everything we eat and drink is more or less adulterated, and without doubt that is the primary cause of the prevalence of appendicitis in these modern times. In the old days, legislation interfered less in such matters mcve uian it does now, but,if traders were not more honest, they were at least less skilled in the arts of adulteration, in face of which the Food , ani Drilgs Acts are to a great extent a dead letter. All the various chemicals added to food as preservatives are harmful to the digestive system, and yet there is hardly one of us who does not swallow these compounds in greater or lesser quantities every day. Not only do they cause indigestion but skin irritation, from which numbers of people suffer without knowing the reason is often caused by boric acid, so much used as a' preservative in bacon, butter, milk, fish, and other foods. _ _
Discoloured Decanters.—lo clean decanters that

have become hopelessly discoloured with wine that leaves a deposit,fill them with water, and a goodly supply of finely chopped potato skins. Leave the decanters closely stoppered, for some days, for the skins to ferment. Then shake, empty, rinse well with several waters and reverse until dry.

div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVZIL]
HIS FATHER'S SON.
BY TOM GALLON
'Author of " Tatterley," "Dicky Monteith," "Kiddy," "A Rogue in Love," "Fate's Beg- gar Maid," "The Charity Ghost," Ito.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: The guests have separated after the dinner which celebrates John Ba:cendale's inheritance of his fortune, and he has told Evelyn Kaylor, te beautiful girl he is to marry, that he has not a care in the world. Yet there is a strange foreboding of coming ill. He feels practically certain that someone is prowling about the grounds. When the last guest has retired, Felix Goode, the family lawyer, begins the unfolding of the sinister secret which is to alter the whole tenour of John Baxendale's life. In revenge for a wrong which his father did to a woman named Johanna Cridge she had stolen sway one of twin sons, leaving tho awful message that, just as her life had passed into darkness and evil, so should his. He should be educated, and yet trained to a life of infamy. That brother of John Baxen- dale may now at any time confront him. This story is told him at his father's request, under his dying injunction that it shall be preserved a secret. Baxendale, when on the way to his room, hears a sound in tho drawing-room. Entering, and go- ing to One of the windows, he confronts and seizes a burglar, to find himself face to face with a man in his own likeness. Then John Baxendale does a dramatic thing. Inquiry convincing him that this man is his own brother, he astonishes him with the assurance that he purposes to divide eqUally the inherit- ance between them on the sole condition that the new-comer leaves the country and keeps the secret. He is taken with Rufus's suggestion that he should go and see the life he has lived, and so one evening makes his way to Middle- ton's Rents, on the south side of the river. On entering the houss he is felled from behind. With mischief in his eye, Rufus Cridge puts on the clothes of his wealthy brother. He goes to Baxendale Hall, and there meets Dick Munby, the barrister, who—astonished at "Baxendale's" gruffness -- leaves him with Evelyn Kaylor, with whom Cridge makes good his opportunity to plead for an early wedding. That night the family lawyer, passing the village inn, is drawn in by the landlord. "John Baxen- dale" is within, intoxicated, but Felix Goode's sharp ears and eyes tell him that here before him stands "the other man." Where is John Baxendale?

div.head: CHAPTER IV.
div.p: CHAPTER IV.

John Baxendale awoke to consciousness with but a dim remembrance of what had happened. That strange dual personality puzzled him now while he thought of it. He found himself, as in a horrible nightmare, going patiently over the points in the story, in a vain endeavour to discover whether he was John Baxendale, or whether, by some ex- traordinary chance, he was that other man called Rufus Cridge, who had forced his way into Baxendale Hall at night. Now, as in a waking dream, he saw the grinning face of Rufus Cridge over the back of the chair, and yet heard john Baxendale's voice challenging the old lawyer; now he came face to face with his brother in a dingy room, and thcn lost everything in a moment. He came to himself in what. seemed to be a sort of cellar, it was dry and fairly clean, and was lighted from above by a grating, covered with glass at the other side, and seemingly part of a pavement. A heavy door resisted all his efforts to open it; his erica were beaten back upon himself, muffled and futile. He eat down to think about all that had happened, and to work out, if pessible, this puzzle in which he was so suddenly in- volved. There had been a John Baxendale, of Baxendale Hall, only, son of a John Baxen- dale that was dead. So much he remembered clearly.. Stop! Not the only son, for 'some- where in the world was another man, born in the same hour, and having almost equal rights with himself. That man they called Rufus Cridge. John Baxendale had meant to do a great act of justice, of reparation—he was to share with the outcast the estates he had •xpected to enjoy alone. He remembered setting out to do that; knew that he had meant to see first that darker side of life Rufus Cridge had known, the better to understand how much the poor wretch had lost. And. then, in some fashion, he had lost consciousness, and had found himself locked in this place. _ He remembered what that man Rufus Cridge had looked like—his shabby clothes. and broken boots, and deplorable look—he re- membered all that perfectly. And then sud- denly John Baxendale looked down at him- self and cried out in horror. For he war Rufus Cridge—worn and shabby clothing, and broken boots, and everything. How had the change been effected. It took a long time for him to understand what had happened, or how this man he had meant to benefit had tricked him, and Changed places with him. It took him longer still to come to the understanding of the fact that that wastrel--ex-sol-bird and ruffian— was at large upon the world, clad as John Baxendale, and walking in his actual like- ness. What would he do first? •

The thoughts of the prisoner flew to Baxen- dale Hall. In a flash. he remembered that nc one there knew of the coming of this Rufus Cridge but himself. As by an instinct he seemed to understand that Cridge would make for that place straight; would take up his life there as the John Baxendale every- one knew, and would take it up with perfect safety and impunity, From that thought it was but a step to the thought of Evelyn—with another man, in the image of John Baxen- dale, enjoying John Baxendale's privileges, talking with her, laughing with her, holding her hands—embracing her. That • way mad- ness lay, and John Baxendale flung himself against the barred door, and shrieked for help and liberty. But no one came, and hie cries were apparently unheard, although above him more than once he saw the shadow of passing feet over the glass beyond the bars.

Meanwhile, in the room above—that room in which he had been struck down—a confer- ence was being held, for these who had this desperate matter in hand had axes to grnd on their own account. A night had passed since John Baxendale had so strangely changed places with Rufus Cridge, and in that night, while all the house slept, the stunned man had been carried down into the depths, and hidden away beneath the house. In Middle- ton's Rents no one was likely to pay much at- tention to any noise or any shouting, such things were of much too frequent occurrence. The old woman of the dark eyes had changed her position from the fireplace to the table. There she sat now, With her elbows planted upon it, and her long thin fingers plunged into the heavy masses of grey hair that crowned her head. It was a craving, anxious, eager face—the face of one who had waited long for an hour that was coming, and had come to the hour at last, and was ready for it. On either side of her was a man—the two who had been in the room when first John Baxendale entered it, and one of whom had struck the blow that brought him down. It was the man of the grey head and the -venerable beard who was speaking. "Ven- geance is all very well, Mother Cridge, but it's empty stuff to feed on," he said. We've had a lean time lately, a deuce of a lean time, and suddenly Rails taps fatness. It's always been share-an'-share alike. Why couldn't me an'_ Tuttle go. down with 'im, eh?"

" Ah !" gas- id the man referred to, at the other side of the table—a lean, thin, mean- looking creature, with shifty eyes too near to- gether, and with a voice as thin and mean as himself—" why not? Mark my words, when it comes to Rufus 'aving 'is chance of playin' the gentleman, we shan't get so much as a look-in." " Silence !" exclaimed the old n-omsn, bringing a, strong hand heavily down on the table. I tell you we inust have patience. Have I waited all these years to have my chances thrown away now by others? Rufus I can trust; you shall share the spoils after- wards. sack and burn; and destroy, and ilrag down: ,vou'ro the wolves that shall rued)

n When 1 let 'you loose. "It seems to me," pursued the grey-haire( man, "it really seems to me that you've for gotten, Mother Cridge, exactly how we'r placed. Look at the position. Before thi John Baxendale came 'ere there was a Joh Baxendale out in the world, and a Rufus Cridge 'ere. Now the position's the same. There's a John Baxendale out in the world :or what looks ..like one) and there-'. a Rufus ridge, down below in this very 'ouse." He (::(inted to the floor, and nodded meaningly is he spoke. "I tell you again that I trust Rufus," said tho woman. "Do you think I have lived the life I have for all these years—in poverty and wretchedness, hunted, and despairing, and forlorn—net to know by this time what I mean to do? Rufus precipitated matters in coming face to face with the 'man when he did. I had prepared another plan. But he acted as I might have expected—he lured John Baxendale here, and made the most of his opportunity. There's one danger, and one oaly—and that's the girl." The man with the grey beard—Amos Voles —pursed up his lips, and nodded a.croes. at the thin man at the further side of the table. "I'd bin thinkin' of the girl, Tuttle," he said, with a glance at the door. "The girl's a fool, and the girl's in love, and she may play the deuce with us all." "Leave Bella to me, I know what I'm about," broke in the woman Cridge, sharply. "I tell you I trust everything to Rufus. He hasn't been trained in the ways of the devil for nothing. I know exactly what he'll do. I've dreamt of it night after night. when I've sat in this place and in other places, and have seen him growing up, and known how he was growing up. The straight-living, gentle, kindly John Baxendale will change his habits from this day. If he doesn't set that Sleepy _Hollow by the ears in less than a week my name isn't Johanna Cridge." "And the one that's. left behind?" Amos Voles pointed again to the floor. "Takes up the burden of his life as Rufus Cridge," said the woman. "Rufus is wanted. I believe, rather badly for one or two mat- ters. He was always reckless. When those things are brought home to him—well, he'll be here to answer for them. It's a pretty scheme, with only one weak place in it—and that's the girl. If the worst comes to the worst, she must be persuaded that the man here is Rufus. Perhaps she'll be able to per- suade him herself." _
"Look out!" exclaimed Voles, springing to his feet and girusting back his chair, "here she is!"

The door had opened and a young woman had come in. She must at some time have been rather pretty, but the life she had, led, and the people with whom she had mixed, had not conduced to good looks or to dainti- ness. She was somewhat showily dressed, and had about her an air half of defiance, half of fear, as she entered the room, and looked from one to the other. _ _ _ _

_ "10, Bella!" said Mr. Saul Tuttle, with what was intended for smile upon his face. "You're looking blooming:" She. looked him over with silent contempt, then turned to the woman, who was standing beside the fireplace. "Where's ttufus?" she demanded. "How should I know?" retorted Mother Cridge. "You ought to know, if anyone does." " I suppose I ought, but I don't," said the girl, a little sadly. "He thinks he's going to play fast and loose with me, and he isn't. I know the game he's playing. I know I'm not good enough for him these days, and so he thinks he'll cast me off like an old shoe."
"Don't get 'eated, Bella," said Mr. Voles, soothingly. "It's all the fun of the fair, ray dear. We 'ave cur ups an' our downs, you know:'

"I've done the dirty work of you all this long time," went on the girl, passionately, "just because of him. heaven help me, there- wasn't anyone could say a word against me when I first came to know him. I was straight, and I was clean, and you know • it. And now he thinks he'll be done. with me. But he shan't—he shan't. There are a few things I can say to the police, if necessary. I can give him away for things people don't suspect. And I'll do it, too, if he tries to keep out of my way. I'm strong enough and loyal enough, if I'm treated well, but I—" "There, that'll do, Bella. You're exciting yourself for nothing," broke in the worn:tit, sternly. "Rufus knows who his friends are, and he's not likely to go back on you. Only it happens that just now he has other work on hand—work that takes him awax from us. He's not here, and I don't quite know when he'll be back. Will that satisfy rm.?" "No, it won't," retorted the girl. "I want to see him, and I mean to see him. I've lied for him, and stolen for him, there's nothing I haven't done for him, and he's roused a demon in me that won't be easily put down. And he's promised— Well, you know what a man promises a woman," she added, in a lower tone.

"Well, that's something to be settled with him, and with him alone," said the elder woman, coldly. "I tell you that Rufus is away in the country • a job that couldn't 'wait. Will that satisfy you?" Della glanced from one to the other of them. Evidently she saw that no further news could be gleaned there. Presently she went out again, slamming the door of the room behind her, and was lost in the maze of streets outside. She was raging with fury at the thought ,that this man was deserting her, and that these people were helping him. Through her mind raced a thousand schemes for getting hold of him and outwitting them. At last, like a restless spirit, she came back again to the house as night was falling, wait- ing about in the shadows of the houses in the faint hope that he might be found there, and that she might have speech with him. She stood in an alley beside the house, star- ing gloomily at the opposite wall, and going over in her mind the scenes of her girlhood before ever London had swallowed her up and gone far to destroy her. Passionately she wished herself back again in those scenes; and yet, with equal passion, wished that the man she loved might come and take her in his arms again, as he had done before, and soothe her with promises, even though she knew them to be lying ones. And so, stand- ing restlessly there, debating what was best to be done, tahe glanced down at the pavement on which she stood, and began half mechani- cally to dig away at a thick glass pavement. light let into the stone, probably for the lighting of some underground cellar. Her thoughts were far away, but the toe of her shoe was busy with one cracked piece of thick glass that seemed loose, and as in her pas- sionate energy she worked savagely at it, part of one of the little squares broke away and fell through into some depths below. She heard the tinkle of the glass beneath her. And on the falling of that glass there floated up to her in the dark alley where she stood, a cry—the cry of someone in distress. She looked quickly all about her, and saw that the alley was untenanted save for her- self. She dropped to her knees swiftly and bent over the tiny hole and called; `.-What is it? What's wrong?" The cry came from below, clearly, and yet with the faintness of exhaustion. " Help ! They've abut me in this place, and left me to die! Help !"
She glm.lced round quickly again, and saw that no one woo near, then put her lipo to. the apexture and called down:
"I'll get you out; trust me, 'l'll get you out. It's Bella, you know you can trust Bella!"

She got to her feet and started for the how... door. She knew now that the man she loved was shut away down there, and that they had lied when they said that he was in the country. She would face them with her knowledge. She would rescue. him, if she had to boat down the door with her small, bare hands. She started to run up the stairs at breakneck speed. But wiser counsels prevailed. Here was mystery that must be matched by cunning: There was some strong reason why this man should have been imprisoned in this place, and yet declared to be far away in the coun- try. That he was not' a voluntary prisoner, biding from lor. was certain from the fact

teat he had cried for help, and Chat he Isad said he had been left there to die. Here was her chance at last. She would save him, and so earn his everlasting gratitude. She lvent into the room to find the old woman alone. And now there was about Bella an air of apology that should mask her anxiety and her eagerness. She began with a note of pleading. "Well, I've walked about and I've shaken the demon out of me," she said, with a little laugh. "After all, a man must please him- self. I SUDDQ3C. and we poor women must out ap with their whims and their fancies. Don't take any notice of me, Mother Cadge. I al- , ways say twice as much as I mean. May. I sit here awhile? There's no one much to talk to puw he's gone." "Stay .as long as you like," replied the old Noman, grudgingly enough. "As for Rufus, se'll come back one of these days, I've no loubt. And you wer,g always a favourite of There was a key that fastened in the man the loved.—that key she must have. Bella sept her sharp eyes at work, even while she :alked to the old woman. She raged within serself at her helplessness, and at the know- edge that, for some reason she had not yet !athomed, Rufus Cridge was a prisoner below ;hat house: She must wait with what patience the might until the opportunity came for her o secure the key, or to find out where it was. Presently the old woman nodded in her hair, strove to rouse herself, and frowned ttalf sleepily, as a protest against her own Irowsiness, then dozed again, with her head falling forward on her breast. This time she dept soundly. But as a precautionary .neasure Bella waited for a minute dr two, nail the deep breathing of the elder woman Issured her that she might safely move. Then :he slid to her knees, and in that fashion 'rcpt across the floor, and. with her eyes on he face of the sleeper, softly lifted Mother 'ridge's. outer skirt. A deep pocket in the )etticoat had something hard in it like metal. ,i3exterously the girl pulled it open and dived ter hand in. There was not so much as a ittgle as she drew out a bunch of keys. Then :he crept away on her knees, still watching ;he sleeping woman, and so gained the door, tnd was gone like a flash down into the lepths of the house. Someone was beating feebly at the door of he cellar as she clumsily fitted key after key nto the lock, all the while whispering en- tearing words, and promising haste, and de- ;hiring that she—his own Bella—had come :ct save him! So at last, with the door open, ;he went in and held the astonifihed man in ter arms, declaring again and again this ;rcat thing she had done, at risk to herself, 'or him and for him alone. And John Baxen- tale strove to stare into her face in the dark- ices, wondering who she was. "Rufus dear, you know me, you know " she pleaded, holding him close and :hispering. I don't know why they locked on away here, but I'm going to save you. Yell trick them all, you and I, dear—just -ou and I alone. Don't you hear me? After- Jar& you shall say: It was Bella did thits, t was Bella helped me, when all others were

gaiiist me!' And that, dear, shall plead for ic as nothi-ig else can do. That will bring •rick your love for me, that shall make us one gain. Don't look so scared. All is well now, ,d I'm going to help you and take you away -om this place. No one shall harm you. My 116 are kissing yours, my heart is beating Tainst yours. All is well!"

'John 'Baxendale saw beyond her the open 'nor, knew that in 60111 C strange fashion this fioman loved Rufus Cridge, and believed 'iat she was rescuing that man. Through her illy lay safety, for it was Rufus Cridge she • leant to • Lefriend, end it was obvious that ;he knew nothing of any John Baxendale. )nly let him get out into the world again, and lc) would set this tangle right? He would de. hire who he was and what wrong had been lone him • he would go back to Evelyn and ;et himself right with her. But the first thing o be done was to get away from this dread- house, into which he had been hired. The irk thing to do, to enable him to .accomplish -hat, was to play the part of Rufus Cridge. He was as much in the dark as that real aufus. Cridge was down at Baxendale ffe knew nothing of this • woman, and could )nly surmise, from her Wild talk, that she was :n love With Rufus Cridge, and was willing to .)efriend him—or the man who stood now in us likeness. .

"Yes, I know. I trust you, Bella," he said, taking his lesson quickly. "Take me )ut of this place; take me away with you. iliet us leave these people behind. Come, you ihall he my guide. We'll cheat them yet!" Happy in the mere thought of going away with the man in that fashion, Bella, with a 'augh, crept out of the place, and listened for .1 moment or two at the foot of the stairs lead- ing up into the hone; satisfied at last, came 4ack, took John Baxendale's hand, and drew him out of the place. In less than a minute they were in the street, and walking rapidly away together. John Baxendale, in the shabby 3uise of Rufus Cridge, was free. But this woman had to be accounted for and dealt with.
Where are you taking me, Bella?" he asked, after they had traversed many streets in silence.

"I'm taking you to my place, dear," she replied, drawing his hand under her arm and holding it there in the warm clasp of her own. You ought to know the way. You've been there timee enough." He said nothing in reply, and in a little time they came to a shabby side street, in a poor neighbourhood he did not remember to have seen before. In front of one a the houses she stopped, and putting a key in the lock of the door opened it, and beckoned to him with a smile to follow her. After they had closed the door she answered a querulous inquiry in a woman's voice from somewhere in the darkness, and .then drew the man up the stairs, and into a room near the top. In a pathetic, humble fashion, she set to work to get some food upon the table. Pressing John Baxendale into a chair, she begsed him with many endearments to eat, assuring him again, and again that he was safe now, and that she would, if necessary, give her life for him.

He had eaten nothing since midday the day before. He fell upon the food ravenously. When he had finished he looked across at the woman, where she was seated on the other side of the table, and strove to carry into his look something of what he must tell her.
"What is 'our name?" he asked, surpris- ingly. "Bella I know, because you have told me. Your other name I don't know."
The tears began to gather in her eyes. She stretched out her hands to him across the table.

"Rufus dear," she pleaded, "you're not going to throw me' over, after all? You're only joking with me—me that has done such a lot for you. They meant to murder you, Rufus, I'm sure they did—and I—" "Saved me from them," broke in John Baxendale, steadily. "But, before Heaven, I have never seen your face before this day. 1 am not Rufus Cridge, I am another man alto- gether."

- She came round the table very slowly, never taking her eyes from him for a mo- ment, touched his dress and his face, examin- ing him minutely with the light of this neu knowledge in her eyes. Then suddenly she started back from him with a cry, staring at .him wildly.
"It's true; I see now that it's true," she exclaimed. "Another man—in his clothes, and in his place, and with his voice. What does it mean? What have you done with him?"

"Be patient, and listen to me. I will tel! you everything,'" he replied. . So he told her all, from the very beginning. Of the story he had heard from the lawyer: of that old matter of vengeance, as worked out through long years by the woman Johanna Cridge ; of the coming of his brother to Baxendale Hall secretly at night; of Baxendale's promise to go to him in London. Then he told her of Rufus Cridge's treachery, and how he knew that at the pre- sent time Cridge must be standing in hie place at Baxendale Hall, with no, one to suspect the truth.
"-Don't you see," he exclaimed at last, passionately, "don't. you understand that all the world will think that he is Baxendale, and that I am Rufus Cridge? Even you thought that at first."
The likeness is marvellous," she said slowly, looking at him; and then she began t. iftugh, "& Rvins a centleman—dressed

in goon clotnes, anti with money in big poc- ket ! That's fine; and why shouldn't he re- main so? He's had his twenty-five years in the gutter; now it's your turn. I'm not go- _ . • ing to interfere." There was but one way, he saw, in which he could break. down that resolution; •he would play upon her jealousy. "About that you must please yotirself,',' he said, quietly. "AS a matter -of fact, rye no doubt Rufus will find thin2s pleasant eneenh • ..tere's a lady there to whom I am engaged to be married. and who, knowing nothing of the story, must inevitably believe that Rufus is John Baxendale. She is a very beautiful woman; this new John Baxendale will have avery right to claim her for himself, unless I mu prevent it." "He belongs to me—he's mine!" ex- claimed the girl, fiercely. "He's mise by every right !" "He is scarcely likely to remember that in this new turn of affairs," said John Baxen- dale, watching the effect of his words upon the girl. "He has stepped at once into my place—my house and my fortune; everything will be his, if he succeeds in the imposture. Is it likely that he will acknowledge you, when by doing so he declares himself to be Rufus Cridge?" "I'd forgotten that," said Bella; "I'd clean forgotten that. No, he must come back to me; but he must come back as Rufus Cridge. I'll help you; I'll tell the truth whenever you call upon me to do so. Ho be- longs to me; I can't let him go." He understood more from her words and her expression than she actually told him; he pitied her from the depths of his heart that she should be in the power of such a man as Cridge; falteringly he told her so. But she interrupted him fiercely. "Oh, you needn't say anything against him, be- cause I won't listen to it,', she cried. "Ile's a good sort, and he's goe a heart, if you know how to find it. He'll do the right thing by me—that I'm sure of. And if I thought you were going to harm him, I'd be ready to curse myself for ever having helped you out of that place." ".I don't mean to harm him, if he will only ,be reasonable," said John I3axendale. "I mean to share my fortune with him—on a condition I have already named. He shall have plenty of money, Bella, and if I can manage it, I'll see that he does the right thing by you, and takes you with him when he goes out of the country. But he must come out of his disguise, and must become Rufus Cridge again.' "You won't do him any harm?" the girl pleaded again. "Not if he is reasonable," said John I3ax- endale. " Now that I am feeling stronger," he went on, gratefully, "I am going to seek out my friends, and set to work to unmask this man. That will be for your good as well as mine—because I am convinced he will have nothing to do with you while he sees a chance of doing so much better under the name he has stolen. Good-bye," he added, holding out his hand to her, " and believe that I am more grateful to you than I can —.Tress."• ' "What is the name of the place to which he has gone?" asked Bella. mean, the place at which you live?"' "Baxendale Hall, Deepington, Sussex," he told her; and then left her, and went out in his shabby clothing into the streets of London. At first he did not know where to turn •, moreover, he was afraid that at any moment a hand might be laid upon his shoulder, and a stern voice speak in his ear; for was he not in appearance that Rufus Cridge • who had been a criminal all his days? However, he crept safely through London under cover of the darkness, and prbiently found himself outside that old pile of buildings in Holborn known as Saxon Inn: There he knew that his friend, Dick Munby, had chambers; to him at least he could appeal, and tell his story. But he discovered that it was one thing for the well-dressed John Baxendale to demand admittance at the gate of Saxon Inn late at night, and quite another thing for the shabby Rufus Cridge. The porter barred his way, and laughed derisively at any suggestion that such a man could be a friend of Mr. Richard Blunhy, or could want to see him. He threatened him with the police if he did not take himself off at once.
, Hopeless. and penniless and afraid, John Baxendale faced the world of London with the knowledge that he must spend the night in its street.

Meanwhile, in that poor lodging in which Bella had regaled him with food, under the impression that he really had been Rufus Cridge, the woman sat, blaming herself bit- terly for what she had done. Her experience had taught her to trust no man, and she knew that it might happen that this John flaxen- dale, with everything to gain, might bring ruin upon the man she loved.- She had been wrong to listen to him; she should have be- trayed him again to those who originally held him prisoner. If only she could undo what she had done; if only she could earn - the gratitude of Rufus Cridge by helping him in this new business he had undertaken!

_ "I'll do it; I'll warn him of what is going to happen; I'll put him on his guard. As for this other woman "—she snapped her fingers and laughed—" I can manage her, if it conies to that. But I must warn him of what they mean to do; I niust help him." She at through the night, planning and thinking what was best to be done. And in the early morning she started for Baxendali Hall and Rufus Cridge.

ECZEMA DEFIED SIX HOSPITALS.

"I contracted my disease at school in London, England, when I was fourteen years old—l am now thirty-three. Our family physician diagnosed my disease as itch. But after several months treatment without receiving any benefit, I was advised to go to a hospital. I attended the Hospital, London. Then and on two other occasions, without my getting alb, benefit, they treated me for eczema. Then I tried ointments from doctors and druggists, and patent medicines, including -. The disease was confined to face, arms and legs, my face being actually raw at times. ' I came to America thirteen years ago, but my face became worse, if possible. When in New York City I was advised to go to Hospital, whence I was sent to the— Hospital in Brooklyn. I was put under the care of Professor but this also added to the number of unsuccessful attempts. I returned home to England and tried the Hospital, Liverpool, the -- Hospital, London, also the world-famed Hospital, but without getting cured. I came back to America five years ago. Three months ago I decided to give the Cuticura Remedies a tridl and I can, safely say I am cured of one of the most torturing skim diseases a man ever had. Richard Curley, New Canaan, Conn., U.S.A.:, Jan. 10, 1909." "I am familiar with Mr. Curley's case and his cure and believe his statement to be true. John F. Burke, New Canaan."

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
MR. WEBSTER APPOINTED ENGINEER.

Another important step in the Warrington Bridge scheme was taken at the meeting of the Town Council .on Tuesday evening, when Mr. J. J. Webster was appointed engineer. Alderman SMETHURST had given notice of the following motions : —( 1) To consider the appointment of an engineer to act as adjudicator -upon the plans, specifications, and tenders received for Warrington Bridge and to pass resolutions thereon. (2) To con- sider a communication from the Local Government Board as to the procedure to be followed in obtaining or exercising powers for the construction of Warring- ton Bridge and to pass resolutions thereon. Alderman SMETHURST emphasised the necessity bf taking immediate action as they, would have to apnly for Parliamentary powers by December. The tenders were coming in rapidly. • Alderman BENNErr said that after long consideration the Council came to the conclusion that the best method to adopt was to let all ferro-concrete builders send in their own plans and designs and then appoint an entirely independent engineer to adjudicate upon them. He did not think they could do better than appoint Mr. J. J. Webster. Councillor ROBERTS said the Council had not yet decided whether they would consider the appointment of an engineer. The TOWN CLERK submitted that Alderman Bennett was quite in order. The very fact of their discussing the name amounted to considering the appointment of an engineer.

Alderman Thterrtuasr moved and Councillor Wilkinson seconded the first resolution. Councillor ROBERTS said the matter was one which should not be discussed in ,public. Opinions that were not particularly- complimentary or which were very complimentary might be expressed. Councillor Fuvrolc-Smint suggested that the question should be referred to the Bridges Sub-committee. The TOWN CLERK : It ceased to exist to-night. Councillor FULTON-SMITH : Why should we tie the hands of our successors? Alderman SMETHURST : We cannot wait until next Council meeting. We must proceed with it or it will be too late,to go to Parliament. It was ultimately decided to discuss the two questions in committee, after which it was resolved,on the recommendation of the Boamott SURVEYOR, that Mr. J. J. Webster be appointed engineer to act as engineer to superintend the carrying out of the build- ing and completion of the works, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to apply to Parliament for a Bill to obtain the necessary powers. The committee again formed themselves into the Council and confirmed their decision.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.
The Proposal to Abolish Them.
ANOTHER ADJOURNMENT.

There was a little surprise in store for thon members of the general public who attended the special meeting of the Warrington Education Com- mittee on Monday evening in the expectation of hearing a full dress debate on the proposed abolition of school fees. Instead of a long discussion there was simply a formal proposition to adjourn the con- sideration of the subject until the next monthly meet- ing, and this was carried by a majority of seven The meeting was called in response to the following requisition --!` October 20th, 1909. To the Chair- man of the Education Committee. Sir,—ln accord- ance with the standing orders, we request you to con- vene a special meeting of the Education Commtttee on Monday, October 25th, at six p.m., for the purpose of considering the question of the abolition of school fees and Passing resolutions thereon.—Edwin Plinston, Thomas Barton, Thomas B. Bradshaw, George Walker, Thomas Birtles."

Councillor FULTON SMITH presided and there were also present :—Mr. H. Roberts (deputy chairman) Aldermen Bennett, James Evans, and Smethurst; Councillors Barton, Birtles, G. N. Vernon, and Wilkinson; Revs. James Davies, N. Wilson and J. Yonge ; Messrs. T. P. Bradshaw, R. T. Fairclough, L. Greening, A. J. Jolley, C. E. Parker, E. Plinston, C. H. Unsworth, and J. Upson, Mrs. C. Jackson Elolmes. Mr. J. Moore Murray, (director) and Mr. R. B. Roberts (assistant director). Mr. UNSWORTH moved that the meeting be adjourned until the next- monthly meeting, to be held on November 22nd. They all knew, he said, that the business proposed to be discussed that evening was the same 'business as that which was gone into at the last meeting, when it was unanimously decided to adjourn until November 22nd. FAIRCLOUOII: I consider that this is hitting below the belt. I--
The CHAIRMAN You can only move and second the resolution and not give us an oration. Mr. FAIRCLOUGII : Then I second it. _

The CHAIRMAN itit the resolution to the meeting and there voted for it: Alderman Smethurst, Mrs. Holmes, the Rev. J. Yonge, the Rev. Father Wilson; Councillor Wilkinson, the Rev, J. Davies, Alderman James Evans, Mr. R. T. Fairclaugh, Mr. Greening,Mr. Unsworth, Mr. Upson, and Councillor Vernon-12; and against it: Mr. Jolley°, Councillor Barton, Mrc. Plinston, Alderman Bennett and Councillor Birtles— five.

The CHAIRMAN : The resolution is carried and the meeting stands adjourned until the 22nd November. One or two members did not vote, and another arrived after the meeting, which only lasted two or three minutes, was over.

div.head: SALVATiOti ARMY.
div.p: SALVATiOti ARMY.
Musical Festival.

The Salvation Army Band held a musical festival in Cairo-street Schoolroom on Monday evening last and the selections played reflected great credit upon the band and its leader, Mr. J. Lee. The band has made great progress of late years and the local corps has eason to be proud of possessing such a hard-working ind competent body of instrumentalists. ' The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK presided over a good attendance and was supported by Colonel George Eiolrnes and Adjutant Christman. The CHAIRMAN said that his first words might be common but many common things were true. kle was very happy to be with them; happy beciusb he could will them spiritual brethren. He might call them Hallelujah lassies and laddies. (Applause). He was ;lad to be with them, because it brought back to him memories of 25 years ago, when be used to wear a certain little steel shield and across which were the .vords " Salvition Army." (Applause). He wore it out sheer chivalry. They were not so respectable then, -ind he wished they were not so respectable now. (Applause). He meant the respectability that lacked enthusiasm and would not go down to the gutter and ouch the lowest man and woman with tender hands. He alluded to the departure of Adjutant Christman mod hoped that he would do well in his new sphere. (Applause). Colonel HOLMES said that the Chairman would agree with him when he said that the Army in regard to music had improved. He thought they might claim for the Army that there were some matters in which redly old truly progress bad been made and music was not east of them. Perhaps people in Warrington were iardly aware what an excellent band they bad iu the ialvation Army. When they went to Liverpool the )ther night and played along with seven or eight if the best bands of the Salvation Army he thought they vere well ahead of all. Music was not the only thing hat they were making advance in, for lately they had argent calls for officers from the Argentine, Korea and Japan. They were signs that God was with them and igns that the organisatian was progressing. God was irospering tbe work for the salvation of thousamis. (Applause). The programme submitted was a varied and interest- ing one. The bruid gave splendid renderings of" Songs if Gladness," "The Great Master's," "Before Jehovah's Throne," "Swiss melodies" and "The Gospel ship has long been sailing." An instrumental luartette, composed of Messrs. J. Bate, E. Lee, J. Ayres, and .1. McElroy played "The soldier's song," %lite Messrs. G. and C. Rowe, fattier and son respec- tively, rendered a vocal duet entitled "Ahoy." Bands- man Siddle gave the recitation "His mother's song," md the bawl sang the chorus. Sister Ayres sang very iweetly "I cannot sing the old songs," and Masters A Potter and C. Rowe played an overture on the violin. Bandmaster J. Lee gave a spirited interpretation of 'We haven't done our best thing yet," and his son, Fred contributed a pianoforte solo entitled "Minorca march," which received well merited applause. Bandmaster J. Lee and Messrs. J. Bate and J. Stevens sang well "The King's highway."

div.head: Makes a Woman Wretched: The Common Evils of Bloodlessness.
div.p: Makes a Woman Wretched: The Common Evils of Bloodlessness.
All its painful Ailments Cured by
Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

Every woman will sympathise with Miss Alice May Butler, whose life*was made. so wretched by Anemia (the common scourge of her,sex) that she became a melancholy invalid. In this imhappY, state she remained until she took Dr. Williams Pink Pills, and received from them New Good Blood that gave her health.

" I am delighted with my unexpected cure," she said, when interviewed at 21, Kings' Road, Luton. near Chatham. " I was bloodless and frail until I began taking Dr. Williams' Pills, but no girl could wish for better health than I have now. _

"I gradually became vry- bloodless when in Ty teens,' and at seventeen was quite unable to enjoy life. It seemed as though I was going to my grave. I was colourless and starved looking, always very cold and trembling, and my lips and ears wire waxen white. Every day I found it more and more difficult to do work or take an inter- est in anything. Different treat- ment rec om- mended seemed useles ; though I consulted a doctor aa d persevered _
with the-medicines

prescribed, I only felt worse. The doctor at last told me that my case was almost hopeless. "Any exertion made me tired. It was impossible to walk upstairs without a rest at every few steps. I had a constant backache that made me feel sick and disinclined to move. If startled by sudden noises I would remain trembling for a long time, and some- times my heart would thump terribly. Friends and doctors said that I wanted more fresh air and exer- cise ; yet when I tried to walk I reeled with dizziness. DISTRICT NEWS.
Thelwall.

MOTOR SIGNAL.—At the Runcorn Rural Council meeting on Tuesday, Mr. T. Baxter in answer to a query Put by Admiral Jones-Parry said it had been decided by tho County Council, that a motor danger signal be placed near the Thelwall schools.

div.head: Walton.
div.p: Walton.

ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S RESIGNATION.—the Walton Inferior Parish Council wrote notifying the Rural District of Runcorn on Tuesday, that Mr. Joseph Whitfield, assist Ant overseer for the Perish, had resigned on acconnt of advanced age. The Council had appointed Mr. Harry Lawrence as his Euccessor and also as cletk to the Council.

div.head: Daresbury•
div.p: Daresbury•

TILE POST OFFICE.-oWin to the small amount of business transacted at the Daresbury Post Office on Sunday, the Liverpool Postmaster wrote to the Runcorn Rural District Council suggesting that the office should be open frons 9 to 10 a.m.only on SandAy instead of from 8.30 a.m. to 10 a.m., and asking if the Council had any Objection to this.—There was no objection at Tuesday's meeting, and the Clerk was instru3ted to write to the Postal authorities accordingly.

div.head: Grappenhall.
div.p: Grappenhall.

VICTOTUA RoAD.—At the meeting of the Rtincorn naral Di:trict Council on Tuesday, a letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the borrowing of £1,258 in respect of the making of Victoria-rod. Grappenhall, under the Private Street Works Act, 1832. The sum of £59 was deducted from the estimated cost in regari to the sewerage, which must be charged as special expenses to the contributory place.

div.head: Risley.
div.p: Risley.

RISLEY PRESBYTER TIN SCHOOL—A cinematograph entertainment was given by Mr. W. Parkinson, of Warrington on Saturday evening. The principal feature was a trip to the Coinish Rivera by the Great,Western Railway, which was greatly enjoyed. Other items evoked much laughter 4 There was a good attendance in spite of the inclement weather and all enjoyed themselves. Rev. J. J. Glover proposed and Mr. `Jos. Clara seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Parkimon for his amusing awl entertaining display, Which raceivel hearty support.

LE'rl7EE.—.l lecture, illustrated by limelight views n in the kriends' Schools, on Monday evening. Mr. W. E. Brown presided over a good attendance of ccholars and friends. The lecturer was Mr. C. Coates, Who gave an interesting lecture on "A visit to a paper mill," The lecturer, who wes well up in the snisject cenamenced with the wood pulp and led up to the finished ;'srticle paper. He explained that it requited great skill la colouring din pulp to produce the various shades of raper. He else illustrated his ltcture by showing saw pies. Miss Francis Davenport proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Coates and expressed a wish that he woad s )on pay another visit to the school. Mr. W. E. brown rezoned the vote whlch was heartily cart led.
