S_A.NKEY CRICKET CLue.--The above club held a Most successful whist drive and dance on Friday night of last week in the Sankey Sunday school when about 130 were pre ent to commemorate the club winning the chnmpicnship of the Warrington and district Junior Cricket league for the second year in succession. The dancing was to the music of the Messrs. Ray, Bros. There were 12 tables of whist engaged and after an exciting contest the wieners were, ladies Mrs. Leigh PG, gentlemen Mr. %V. Armitage 125. During the interval the presentation of the medals took Place; these were silver with gold centre's. Mr. A. Bailey (chairman of the Junior League) presided and was supported on the platfoom by the Vicar, lessrs. Edwin Draper, and Fulton-Smith.—Mr. Draper la presenting the medals said he was glad to be in a Position to again present the medals to the Sankey Club and to hope they would still continue to be sno- cessful. The Chairman in a few well chosen remarks expressed his regret that the Sankey Clnb had not been a9cepted in the Ist division of the Warrington and district league. The Rev. J. R. Jones M.A., proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Draper for presenting the Medals. Mr. Fulton-Smith seconded and this was hearths? carried. Messrs. S. Hayes and A. Davies acted as M.C. for dancing. Mr. S. Bingham was in charge of the whist drive and Mrs. George Clarke pro- vided the refreshments. The following are members of the cricket club who received medals :—E. Foster (captain), S. Bingham (sub-coptain), H. Daintith, V. Millington, A. Corradine, S. Hughes, W. Williams, D. tlewitt, J. Plant, H. Payne. A. Webb.

div.head: SANKE Y Pi% RISH COUNCIL.
div.p: SANKE Y Pi% RISH COUNCIL.

A meeting of the above Council was held at the Sankey Schools on Monday night. Mr. W. Taylor Presided, the following also being present. :—Messrs. V. Furness, J. W. Walters, H. Fairclough, W. H. Ireland and J. Smith (clerk).

The first item on the agenda was the SPEED OF THE MOTOR CARS through the village. The Clerk said he had wraten to the Superintendent Of Police, Whase headquarters were at Widnes, asking aim to have special watch kept on the roads through the village, particularly near the schools. he had 'eceived a reply which ran as follows :—" Referring to Your letter of the 22nd inst., I beg to inform you that the matter has been carefully considered. Bearing in al:nd %hat you say regarding the bend in the road and the danger of children attending the Sankey Sunday and day schools, I can see no" reason why the speed limit of motor cars should not be reduced to 10 miles Rrt hour. However, lam having special watch kept by the police to detect motor cars, to prevent them going at a speed dangerous to the public. At present I have a dozen cases pending against motor car drivers. I hope we will be able to put a stop to the nuisance.—W. STRicKLAND (superintendent). •With reference to the placing of notice boards in the village warning motorists of the approach to the School, the Clerk said lie had written to Mr. Sutton, the Clerk of-the Rural District Council, and he in reply atated that the only way in which they could get the 'Teed limit fixed at 10 miles an hours vahile passing through-tee village was by making an application, to the Local Government Board. Mr. Furness said that motorists were genet ally quite Willing to dim diminish their speed if some intimation was airen. .
Leland said that in some districts they had °cards with the word "School" and a finger pointing in the direction. Continuing, he said it wanted some stringent role to stop motorists driving at such a
terrific rate. There were some motorists who had sense but there were a good many who had not. (Laughter). The subject then dropped. SANKEY POST OFFICE.

The Clerk read a letter from the Surveyor of the G.P.O. with reference,to the closing of the Post Office which said : Sir,—Owing to the small amount of busi- ness transacted it is proposed to open the Great Sankey Sub-Vast Office from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m. on Sundays in future, instead of from 8.30 a.m. to 10 a.m. as at present. Before !flaking the alteration, however, I shall be glad if you will t ring the matter before your Council and let me know at your earliest convenience. No objections to the proposal were offered and the Clerk was instructed to write saying that they complied with the proposal.
A TELEPHONE WANTED.

Mr. Furness skid it would be a great cpnvenience if a telephone was flxed up at the Post Office. It would be of great use to the farmers and residents also. Tie suggested that a letter be sent to the postal authorities asking them to fix up a telephone. Mr. Iraland seconded and the motion was carried unanimously. C LER K'S REMUNERATION.
The Clerk was thanked for his services as assistant overseer.
Mr. Smith briefly returned thanks.
Lynim

WEDDING ATTHE PRDITIVE METHODIST CHURCH— A very pretty wedding took place on Monday at the Primitive Methodist Church, between Mr. Mlliim Moss, son of Mr. W. T. Moss, Newfield Villas, Lymm, and Miss Alice Appleton, daughter of Mr. Henry Appleton, Statham, Lymm. The bride, who wore a prune costume, was given away-by her father. Miss Elizabeth Moss wds the bridesmaid. Mr. Frank Appleton acted as best man. Afterwards the bride and bridegroom drove away in a motor laudau for their honeymoon.

SOCIAL EVENING.—A social evening was held on Monday last; in the Wesleyan schoolroom, in connection .with the Guild. The Chairman of the evening was Mr. Watrworth. About 40 members enjoyed the following programme :—Miss A. Finch, pianoforte solos; recita- tion, Mr. H. Perrin ; solos by Miss A. Ogden, and Miss M. Winstanley •' duet by ‘t iss C.Elliott and Miss Mairs ; reading by Mr. H. S. Brown. Mr.- R. Simpscn rendered a solo entitled When I get back again to Bonnie Scotland " and was loudly encored. He also took part in a duet "Lerboard Watch," assisted by Mr.B.Pearson. Miss M. Winstanley acted as accompanist for the evening. In the interval the members partook of refreshments' and the committee are to be highly praised upon the success of the first meeting. LYAIAI CHORAL SOCIET7.—A most enjoyable social gathering was held in connection with this Society on Wednesday evening in the Drill Hall. Only one thing marred an otherwise exceptionally successful function, the frigid temperature of the room due to a break down of the heating apparatus. The physical atmosphere was in most conspicuous contrast to the warmth of friendliness shewn on every hand, in fact one may say that Wednesday's meeting was a Wily sociable social The first part of the pragramme consisted of musical items and opened with a pianoforte dust by Miss F. Champ and Mr. T.M. Eastham. Miss Bradbury sang "All for a green ribbon" ( Com Jones) and "Irish Lullaby," Mrs. Walker "The slave song," Mr. Ernest Jones "Two little Irish songs," bud Messrs. J. Gibbon and A. Saville gave a humorous duet "The twins." A special reference ought to be maee to the magnificent rendering by Mr. W. J Mitchell (of Manchester) of "The Trumpeter," "Beloved awake! arise ! " and "Son of mine." Th 9 members of the society gave a couple of part songs "The gallant troubador ' and "Hush thee my babie," in a manner highly creditabl.. A Whist Drive under the able leadership of Mr. E. Taylor and a dance at which Mr. F. Latham aated as M.C. followed. The catering which had been under- taken by a committee of lady members of the society WAS everything that could be desired and evoked words of praise and satisfaction on all sides. It is gratifying to note the increased interest .in the society that is being shown by the peop'e of the district, an interest due without donbt to the musical progress made by the members under tha cfdaient leadership of the conductor Mr. T. M. Eastham. LYMM COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was held on Thursday evening in the Towq Hall. There were present :—Mr. 0. G. Smith (who presided), the Rev. G. B. Thurston. and Messrs. W. G. Groves, It. H. Gutobed, S. Davies, T. H. Warburton, W. Ewart, F. O. Moston, W. Mullard (clerk), Dr. de Jong (medical officer of Heal( h), D. Mort (surveyor), and W. L. D:naldson (gas engineer).
FINANCE.

Mr. F. 0. Mostyn reported that the balance in the bank on the general acconnt was £9lO 3s. 3d., cheques drawn that night £291 Gs. 6d., leaving a balancs of £6lB 16s. 9d. The balance in the bank on the gas account was £690 12s. 31 cheques drawn that night £360 145.,8d., leaving a balance of £389 17s. 7d.

div.head: EXTRA MEN FOR SEWER WORK.
div.p: EXTRA MEN FOR SEWER WORK.

The minutes of the atnitary Committee showed that Mr. Gotobed had proposed, Mr. Davies seconded and sarried unanimously, that three extra labourers he employed for one week in connection with the addi- tional work on the new Sewer at Broom Edge.

div.head: WIDENING OF WHITBAIIROW-ROAD.
div.p: WIDENING OF WHITBAIIROW-ROAD.

The minutes of the Fire Engine Committee showed that a letter had been read from Mr. J. H. Holt with regard to the cost of the above. It was rroposed by Mr. Mcston, seconded by Mr. Ewart, and carried unanimously, that the letter be put back for further consideration.

div.head: GAS MAIN.
div.p: GAS MAIN.

The minntes of the Gas Committee showed that they had resolved that it be a recommendation to the Council to lay a 3 inch gas main (about 130 yards, cost .£2O) in Woodbine Avenue off Sandy-land subject to the owners of the road giving the usual authority to break up the road, the same being a private road. All the above minutes were adopted by the Council.

div.head: PROPERTY OWNERS AND BROOK LANE.
div.p: PROPERTY OWNERS AND BROOK LANE.

111 r. Ewart moved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the property owners of Brook-lane that unless sornethin,,,, were done immediately to put Brook-lane in repair the Council would take action. He said that if something were not done in a very short time the foot- path would be as bad as the road.He had already sem land conveyances pushed along the footpath instead of along the road and he had seen one wheel of a cart on the footpath and the other on the road. The property owners of Brook-lane had been informally asked about it and he understood they were willing to take their share in the work. He would propose that the Clerk write to the property owners and say that unlecs something were done the Council would take into consideration the road and use their powers although it would entail a great expenditure. He %as speaking now as much in the interests of the property owners as of the tenants, because if the Council took over the road it would have to be done thoroughly from one end to the other. It could now be done at a very reasonable cost and it would probably last for 15 or 20 years. The Rev. G. B. Thurston seconded. _ _
Mr. Ewart aided that some of the owners were pre- pared to pay more than their proper share. It was decided unanimously that the course proposed by Mr. Ewart be adopted.

div.head: LYM Al-LANE CROSSINGS.
div.p: LYM Al-LANE CROSSINGS.

Mr. Warburton referred to the Lymm-lane Crossings and said that there seemed to be nothing satisfactory about the lighting of the crossings. In that rough and dark weather it was rather strange that there had been no accidents. The man in the box could not see any- body on the other side of the road. He cited cases a here the signal man had closed the gates wible people were crossing the line because he was unaware that they were there. He thought it was time that they wrote to the company complaining of that state of things. They bad got the fixtures from the old lamps and yet they did not light up. He would also mention that since there had been a siding to the Salt Works people were being continually stopped while shunting operations were going on. He moved that the attention of the Railway Company be drawn as spon as possible to the complaints. Mr. Gotobed seconded.

The Rev. G. B. Thnrston said they should postpone the sending, of the resolution till they had bad a meet- ing down there. He mentioned that there was a wall which was very dangerous, and something ought to be done to remeiy it. He thought they shonld have a small sub-committee so that they could go aud view the place. Mr. Ewart proposed that a sub-committee be appointed to visit the place and report at-the next
meeting, the committee to consist of the Rev. G. B. 'Thurston, Messrs. Davies, Gotobed and Warburton. The Rev. G. B. Thurston seconded, and this was agreed to. THE AUDITOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Waller Robbs, assistant district auditor reported the completion of the audit of the accounts of the Council and offices for the ye ir ended March 31st. The following is ti summary of the receipts and expendi- ture and also, for thepurpose of comparison, the pre- ceding year's receipts and the expenditure. ReceTts, 1907-8 general account,£3,o9s 3s. SJ. • gas works account, £3,329 15s. 4d.; loan account nil ; 1908-9, general account, £3.531 4s. 5d.; gas works account, £3,312 17s. 7d.; lan account nil. Total receipts 1907-8, £6,425 18s. 9d.; 1908-9, £6.8.14 2s. expenditure 1907-8 general account, £3 410 9s. 3d. ; gas works account, £30190 19s. Bd. ; loan account nil. 1908-9 general account, £3,789 3s. 4d.; gas works account, £3,322 9s. Od. Loan account nil. Total expenditure 1907-8 £6,801 Bs. 11d, : 1908-9 £7,111 12s. 4d. The cash balance in the hands of the treasurer at the close of the year was as follows : General account, £3OB 15s. 7d ; gas vork s account, £589 05.2 d. ; loan account £6 17s. Bd. The outstanding loan indebtedness of the Council at the close of the year was £6,056 13s. 4d. There is no record in the General balance account of the amount owing at the end of,the ytar by the C )rumittee and sondry debtors nor in the gas works balance accw-nt of any repayment of debt. I asked your Clerk to consider the expediency of opening accounts under these heads in the ledger in future.

div.head: Stockton Heath.
div.p: Stockton Heath.

CHORAL UNION.—A highly successfal social in connection with the Stocktoa Heath Choral Union was held at the Hall Cafe cn Monday evening, atout eighty members and friends being present. Dancing and games were engaged in and solos were rendered by the choir.

DEATII OF MR. JOHN MOORE.-0111* rewlers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. John Moore, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, who passed away on Sunday, at the age of 53 years. Mr. Moore had been in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company as a signalman for 35 years, but about two years ago he retired owing to heart trouble. Mr. Moore was a great lover of gardening and floriculture and was a successful exhibitor at the shows of the Garden Society. He leaves a widow and two sons and a daughter.

div.head: Padgate.
div.p: Padgate.

JUNIOII G LTILD.—A meeting of the Junior Guild was held on Wednesday evening last, wh( n a very interest- ing address was given to the children by Mr. C. Wilcockson, of Stocktol llelth. There was a large number of juveniles present, and a very enjoyable time was spent.

PAIMATE WESLEY GUILD.—The usual weekly meet- ing Of the Wesley Guild was held on Mond iy evening last and proved to be one orunusual interest. Short personsl experiences of Salvation Army work were given by Adjutant Lawsan and Adjutant Camp membets of the Salvation Army. During the evening a duet entitled," Glad to remember what Jesus hath done" was very beautifully renzlered by Adjutant and Mies Lawson. The Rev. T. Gadding who occupied the chair spoke vt ry warmly of the work of the Salvation Army and exp:essed himself in deep sympathy with the move- ment. A vote of thanks t 3 the spe.tkers brought a very interesting evening to a cicse.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL

The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held on Tut.sdty at the Dutton Workhouse. Mr. T. NVright presided, and there were-also present :—Messrs. J. Spruce, C. E. Linalter, junr., 0. Egerton-Warburton, Admiral Jones-Parry, P. Booth, P. Collins, W. Mynekyme, J. Hallows, J. Balsbaw, G. Watson, E. Brach, E. Bretherton, H. Mawdsley, G. Pilling, J. H. Davies, A. Broome, W. Harrison, W. Turner, J. Whitlow, S. Horton, W. Winstanley. W. Weir, 0. F. Ashton _(cleck), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances), and Dr. Adams (medical ()Muer of health). Mr. E. Marshall, secretary to Runcorn Urban District Council, wrote at-king the Rural Council to appoint a sub-committee to meet some members of the Health Committee, to make an arrangement for the joint use of the small-pox hospital at Moore.—The proposal was agreed to. \ Mr. Rudford Shawcross, of Cromers Lake, Overton, drew attention to the disgraceful state of the Middle lane leading from Manley-road to Cromer s Lake. It was nothing but a quagmire and "enough to give us our deaths." The writer added : Just imagine what we have to put up with cut here and the best of it is paying 'you rates and getting no return, cot even a load of c 'nders, fro 4 one twelve months to another.— Tne Clerk said he had informed the Surveyor of the road and he in return had written that the road was not repairable by the Council. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above was held on Tuesday at Dutton Woikhouse, Mr. I'. Baxter presiding. There were alse present :—Messrs. J. Spruce, T. Wi ight, C. E. Linaker, jun., G. Egerton-Warburton, Admiral Jones Parry, S. Woodward, C. E. Linaker, jun., P. Booth, W. M. Morris, I'. Collins, H. Mynekyme, J. Hallows, 3. Balshaw, G. Watson, E. Brit* E. Bretherton, H. Mawdsley, G. Pilling, J. H. Davies, A. Broome, W. Harrison, W. Turner, J. Whitlow, S. Horton, W. Winstanley, W. Weir, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), T. Cooke, W. dePrez, and J. Pearton (relieving officers), A. J. Persons (master). The Cl. ik to the Chester County Asylum wrote stating at a meeting of the Visitors' Committee the c3st of maintenance for pauper lunatics in the asylum for the quarter ending 31st December 1909, was fixed at Bs. sd. per head per week. The much discussed topic) of boiler heating and stoking by the inmates was again brought forward by Mr. J. Spruce who said that it had been definitely decided to appoint one man to do this work, also the necessary plumbing, glazing, Scc. He moved that the proposition be accepted. Mr. Morris seconded and said that as a guardian be felt a certain amount of responsibility after the affair at Toxteth where a boiler explosion took place and a vote of censure was passed ou thetteardians for allowing the stoking of boilers to be done by inmates.—The motion was carried. RUNCORN TORIES PAY TRIBUTE TO SIR JOHN BRUNNER.

On Tuesday night a largely-attended Unionist and Tariff Reform meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall. Mr. John Littler, J.P., presided, and he was supported by Sir Richard and Lady Brooke, Mr. Charles Williams (the prospective Unionist candidate for the Norzhwich D;vision), and Mr. N. Gratton Doyle (prospective Unionist candidate for Gateshead) The Chairman, in his address, said on behalf of the Runcorn Conservative and Unionist Association be would like to extend his sympathy with Sir John Brunner on the cause of his intended retirement from the representaVon of the Northwich Division in Parlia- ment. Much as they differed from Sir John in political matters, they could not but recognise the many efforts he had made for the public good—(applause)—and their hope and desire was that after such a strenuous and .useful life as Sir John had led he, and Lady Brunner might have many Tears of happy and healthful life before them. (Applause.) Mr. C. Williams also made a graceful reference to Sir John, and, dealing with political affairs, contended that every country that had adopted Protection had become stronger, and he advocaten that England should make the foreigners pay to come into our markets, and bring about Free Trade within the Empire. He believed that if the Britisher was given a chance in his own rivulet he would knock the foreigner every time. _ _
Mr. Gratton Doyle said Free Tra(le was as dead as Judas Iscariot and as little lamented. (Laughter and applause,)

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND• NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND• NEWTON.
TEAPOT AS A WEAPON.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mary H. Redhead, a widow, of Legh-street, E .rlestown, was charged with unlawfully wounding her son, William Redhead (13), whose head was bandaged. The lad stated that while he was t iking his clogs off his mother struck him on the head with a teapot for not having the fire right. Ho was taken to the doctor. His mother had had some drink. The prigoner said she did it in a temper. The magistrate's clerk (Mr. Grecn said she might easily have been charged with something more serious than this. The prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, the Chairman describing the office as a most wicked one. • EARLESTOWN BETTING CASE.

Peter Singleton, a blacksmith's striker, of 35, Athol- street, Earlestown, appeared before the Willoas magistrates on Thursday.on a charge - of keep- ing a Letting-house, while Joseph Singleton, his brother, was charged with aiding and abetting. Mr. W. Madden, barrister, defended. - Sergeant 13;trrow stated that in 'consequence of com- plaints he and Inspector Carr watched the defendants' house for thirty-five minutes at noon on October 12th. I hree men, tmo women, a boy, and a girl entered by the back door, while Jeseph Singleton came to the yard gate, where he received seve:al slips of paper and money from a man. On the 20th, witness, the inspector, and Police- constable Lennie proceeded to the house with a search warrant. The door was fastened, and it wt.'s a few minutes before it was. opened. When they got inside and read the warrant over, Peter Singleton said, " You can look, but you sill find nothing. I have not done any betting this week; but had you come last week you might have found some. . I have been told by Dring's men you would be coming." There was some newly-charred paper in the firegrate, while they found a slip on which were eighty-eight betting transactions, books relating to betting, and £5 in money. In answer to Mr. Madden, witness said that when watching the house they were concealed in the Bruns- wick Chapel. They counted the money at the house, but on counting it at the police station there was ss.

less. With regard to the slip of raper, witness admitted that there were no names of horses on. There were initials and aliases of people. Mr. Madden.—You are not down there, are you? Witness.—l don't know, sir. Mr. Maddtn.—l see there is " W.M." here; those are my initials. I don't like that (laughter). In answer to a further question, witness said there was a man asleep in Led when they went ,aith the search warrant, hut they did not arrest him. Inspector Carr gave corroborative evidence, in the course of which Mr. Madden asked to see the officer's notebook. Witness objected, but afterwards handed it over with the remark : "it is courtesy to let you have it."
Mr. Madden : lEayit is my right. In-vector Cart: No it isn't. ,

Mr. Marken: I say it is. Addressing the Bench for the defence, Mr. Madden dealt with police methoes in betting casts. He said there was an immense amount of vindictiveness in that case. How the police touched the picture up bezause they found so little! ]hey threw out a sprat to catch a whale, and saw what effect it would produce. There was no more virtue in a policeman giving evidence than anyone else. He was not a bit mole truthful because he wore a blue uniform.

Peter Singleton, on oath, said they reared poultry, and people called at the house to buy eggs and other th'ngs. He had not done any betting for some time before. Several men called, but he had refusEd to take their bets.

In answer to Superintendent Ross, defendant said he gave over bettirg because he knew the'police were always watching, and it was misery to him. Joseph Singleton denied taking bets. He had come home for dinner when the police arrested him. He did not approve of betting, Witnesses were called to say that Peter Singleton refused to take bets from them during the week ending October 16th.
Peter Singleton was fined £lO ani costs in each of two cAses, hnt the charge against Joseph Singleton was disinissed.

div.head: TRADES EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.
div.p: TRADES EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.

The Parr Hall is at present the scene of an attractive exhibition promoted by a syndicate .of lead- ing firms with the object of btinging prominently. before the public Pimix,rtant food preparations and _methods of cooking them, domestic, sanitary, labour- saving and scientific appliances, and providing whole- some entertainment: Since the exhibition opened on Tuesday it has been visited by thous Ands of the towns- people who have found a great deal to interest,instruct and entertain them. The exhibits are tastefully arranged and there are numerous novel and ingenious contrivances—in fact everything which enterprise can suggest is done to make the displays Us pleasing as possible. The following firms comprise the syndicate and are the principal exhibitors : Alfred Bird and Sons, Ltd.. Devonshire Works, Birmingham, who show their famous Bird's Custard Powder and other home specialities. George Bray and Co., Ltd., Bagley Works, Leeds; gas burners, mantles, and gas lighting appliances. Cadbury Bros., Ltd., Bouroville ; cocoa and chocolate. Clavers and Sons, Ltd., Histon, Cambridge; jams, marrnalade and table delicacies.
Hovis, Manchester, London and Macclesfield; Hovis bread. -
J. Mackintosh, Ltd., The Toffee Mills, Halifax; Mackintosh'a extra cream toffee.

The "Matchless" Metal Polish Co., Ltd., Liverpool; metal polish, paste and liquid and " Komo" specialities, The Nugget Polish Co., Ltd., Vauxhall-street. London, S.E. ; boot polishes and leather preservatives. A. and F. Pears, Ltd., New Oxford-street, London, N.C., toilet soaps and perfumes. H. D. Pochin and Co. Ltd., Worsley-street, Salford, panshine kitchen magic. New Hydroleine Co., Castle Soap Works, Ashby-de- la-Zouch, Witch soap. In addition Alessrs. Wadsworth, Sankey-street, War- rington have a staud which has attracted \general attention. They show afire collection of pianos by such noted makers as BrOadwood, Chappell, and Collard and Collard whose great reputation is sufficient to guarantee the quality of their respective instruments. A popular feature of the exhibition is a series of cookery lectures by Miss Grace Ball, L.C.A. who gives some highly instructive demonstrations. The enjoymeLt of a visit to the hall is much enhanced by the choice musical nrogrammcs submitted by a ladies' orchestra under the direction of Madame Clarissa Matthews. There are also biograph entertainments at frequent intervals, the pictures being up-to-date and amusing. Each evening the illuminated fairy fountain throws up 'columns of prismatic splendour, presenting a unique and beautiful spectacle well worth seeing. The exhibition will continue until Friday evening next.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS CHARITY BAZAAR.

The proceeds of the five days' bazaar held at St. Helens Town Hall last week for the extensicns to the Providence Free Hospital amounted to £2,161. Of this £4ll uas taken on Saturday. The total, with subscrip- tions, is how about £5,600, and the committee an.) workers, and especially Lady Mbry Gerard, president of the ladies' committee, are to be most highly compli- mented on their prolonged and successful efforts.
ALLEGED BRUTAL ASSAULV. "BIT A PIECE OUT 'OF• HIM."

Martin Quinn, labourer, of 66, Pocket Nook-street, was remanded at St. Helens on Monday, ca a charge of wounding Peter Fulham, a fellow lodger, by biting a lump out of his side.—The Chief Ccnstable said that at half-past ten on Saturdaymight prisoner was using hal language in the house where he lodged.He was told to be quiet on account of the children 'being in the house, but be became disorderly and struck Fulham. They closed and fought, and while they were on the ground Quinn put his head under Fulham's armpit and bit him on the side. George Shipley, another lodger, pullqd Quinn off, when it was seen there was blood on his face. A piece of flesh had been bitten off the man's side, and he was taken to Dr. Davie and afterwards to the hospital. After his arrest a mnn took a chair to the police office,' and said that Fulham's injuries had been caused by falling on it. The doctor agreed that this was impossible, and the hair that was on the chair was a fake. Fulham gave evidence, and said there was no chair near where they fell.

div.head: HOCKH.
div.p: HOCKH.

littchford played Winnington Park at Winnington last week. During the first half of the game they quite held their own with their powerful opponents, exhibit- ing a sound defence, and were unlucky to be losing 1-0 at the interval. Shortly after the resumption Winning- ton scored again and then a true example of English weather brought the match to an abrupt termination, further play-being impossible. Swinton Park defeated Latchford "A "at Latchford 6-1. The visitors scored first and Unsworth equalized but after that Swinton gradually got the upper hand and were leading at half-time 3-1. The second half, owing to heavy rain, resembled a pole match, but the Swinton team adapted themselves to the prevailing donditions splendidly and considering the state of the ground plaled right good hockey, the forwards in particular combining very effectively, and thoroughly deserved to win by 6-1. div.head: Guardians and Temperance.
div.p: The Guardians and Temperance.

Sir,— I was very glad to see the letters of Mr. Dale and others in your issue of the 23rd commenting on the action of certain" gentleman" who represent the voters of Warrington. I fail to see and understand the advantages of alcohol when we can see quite the reverse any day in the borough. Doubtless their remarks will be remembered when the next election comes along. Then they will probably lie under the table !—Yours, etc.,
TEMPERANCE.

Sir,—llay we through your columns express the feel- ing of the Warrington Ideal Lodge Good Templars held on Thursday last, October 28th re the action taken by the Warrington Board of Guardians at their last monthly meeting. Not only do we look upon it as an insult to the Lancaehire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union, but to all those who are interested in the Temperance cause.. We hope that all those who have the Temperance cause at heart and who take an interest in the children will do their utmost to push this matter forward and try to get the decision altered. We are on behalf of the Good Templars, J. RICHARDSON, L.D. C. L. SAVAGE, C.T. F. M. GREGSON, Sec. Warrington. Oct. 28th, 1909.

div.head: Education Cominittes and School Sites.
div.p: The Education Cominittes and School Sites.

Sir,—lt strikes me that' the majority of the Educa- tion Committee are more eager for cheap bargains in school sites than paving regard to the health and convenience of the children committed to their charge.

Why Grace's pottery of all other sites in the town should be chosen to build a school 4on passes my comprehension. I quite agree with what Mr. Upson says, and can testify that all building operations north of the railway have practically ceased on account of the unsalubrious atmosphere of the neigh- bourhood caused by the fumes from the Longford Depot and the Gas Works. Certainly neither the health nor convenience of the children has been con- sidered in the matter. Allow me to remind Mr. Smethurst that the neighbourhood of the proposed school is very thinly populated and if the new school is required for Longford-street and Orford-lane area would not the Blue School playground be a better site, or, better still, come to terms with the managers of Silver-street school and build an additional school on the area lying between Silver- street and the "Rodney," purchasing the, old dilap dated property standing in the way. If a site is r equired for Bewsey why not •purchase the vacant and and propertrbounded by Bewsey-road, Tanners'- land and Marson-street ; or if that is too expensive purchase the field at the bottom of Hoyle street which might be had almost for the asking and throw a foot- bridge over the railway either into Folly-lane or Dallam-lane. If a site is required for the con- venience of Bewsey and Whitecross why not take one of the numerous plots in Lovely-lane, notably the one lying between the railway and Monks-street? Could not one or two of these sites I have enumerated be secured and earmarked for educational purposes? Surely it is worth while spending a few hundred pounds for the benefit of the children. It will be a better investment than wasting it in building palatial shops in Bridge-street and other parts of the town.— I remain, Sce.,
PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: Nation in Arms.
div.p: A Nation in Arms.

Sir,—Your correspondent " Anti-War " only vouch- safes me five lines of a reply, so much is he (or she) taken up with the Socialism which permeated the letters of other critics. In passing may I note with some amusement that " Anti-War " is as dogmatic on the question of Socialism as on the much less important one of National Service. I am summarily disposed of by the statement that "most of our admirals strongly advocate a home defence land force as well as that at sea." Well, I am quite at one with " most of our admirals." All I object to is a land force compulsorily recruited from embryo conscripts, and the fallacious argument that under any other system we are at the mercy of the foreigner. Why, "most of our admirals "have not yet demanded compulsory training for the Navy which, with the shortage of seamen, and the paramount necessily for naval superiority, would be a much more reasonable project. First let the urgency of the need be prored, and the nation may be got to consider seriously the revolutionary proposal of compulsory military training. But, after all, "a nation in arms is a sad and even depraved ideal !—Yours ecc., E. V. W.

Sir,—l read Anti-War's reply with disappointment, for its lack of constructive and instructive argument leads one to think that Anti-War's zeal for militarism, and ignorance of Socialism, exceeds the quantity of knowledge he or she possesses upon these vital ques- tions. Its evasion of all the points I raised against militarism is conspicuous, and instead of replying to my contenti9n that profit hunting was the cause of war, Anti-War coolly turns round and says that socialism is unchristian and will not benefit the -worker, but that the N S.L. will because it intends them to have a whole fortnight's holiday each year without cost. Because of this I suppose the inference is that militarism is Chtistian. Let me say here at once that whatever the workers get, whether it is a fortnight's holiday or an electioneering feed, it does not come to them free. Whatever the 'workers get they have dearly paid for directly or indirectly, the details of which I have not space enough to explain at present. Secondly, I cannot believe that it is compatible with Christian ethics to teach John Bull the easiest way of killing Franz Wilhelmstein when neither have cause or quarrel to learn to shoot each other. Dr. Sb.adwell's saying that " Socialism is ,the mortal enemy of Christianity " I think could be applied better to militarism, and the opinion of the Encyclopedia Brittanica that " the ethics of Socialism are identical with the ethics- of Christianity " couldbe better applied to Socialism. But whether Socialism is un-Christian or militarism is pervaded with the Christian spirit, I still believe that war is a lamentable concomitant to commercial buccaneering. I believe that Socialism will abolish buccaneering and its necessary appendage, militarism. I believe the worker would be no worse off if Kaiser Wilhelm sat in the place of Edward VII. The standard of livelihood in a capitalistic state is a pre- determined 'fixity and will remain so as long as the land and means of production are used for private profit and not for public good.—Yours truly, LABOR OAINIA VINCIT.

Sir,—l hope you will pardon-me trespassing upon your valuable space, but really I cannot think your correspondent Anti-war is serious, to say the least he is amusing. For him to state that Socialism is obviously antaganistic to the real interests of the working man without making some attempt to prove or justify his assertion, makes it quite unnecessary to argue the question. At any rate the Socialists have, the conrage to come forward and fight for better con- ditions for the worker. They are not satisfied that whilst he isfullfilling the necessary period of military training laid down by the N.S.L. he should receive fresh air only. •But the Socialists say he is added to fresh air all the year round. Your correspondent's asser- tion that the worker's place would be kept open for him is all very well (on paper.) There are thousands of working men for whom the only place that is kept open for them to-day is that modern Bastille commonly known as the Workhouse. In conclusion, Mr. Editor, regarding Dr. Shadwell's denunciation of Socialism as repiesented by Socialist organisation of to-day. He says that "Socialism is the mortal enemy. of Christianity." Not being a Churchgoer but still believing in the Pauline doctrine of" he that will not work neither shall he eat," and further believing inthe Lord's Prayer containing the following sentence : " Give us this day our daily bread " prompts one to ask if this is not Christianity I should very much like to know what the ethics of Christianity contain. I remain yours sincerely,— • A WHITE SLAVE.

div.head: ST JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST JOHN'S WARD.
Meeting in Support of Mr. Shaw's
Candidature.

An enthusiastic meeting in suop 3rt of Mr. Shaw's candidature was held in Mick-street, Mission last evening. Mr. George Walker presided, and was supported on the platform by Messrs. John Upson, R. Henshall, J. Griffiths, E. G. Hughes, and J. Howes, junr. —Soveral letters of apology for non-attendonce were read.

Mr. James Dolls, who had an engagement at Penketh wrote :—" As you know, I have always been, anti am opposed to municipal coutests being fought on party lines. War- rington requires honest and capable government by the best of her sons, and, in my opinion, in respect of the requisite qualifications, you are far and away the better man before the electors of St. John's Ward, and I wish you success." The Rev. John Yunge wrote: "I am growingly anxious that the liquor traia should be defettei in every legitimate way, and as Mr. Steel is on the side of that traffic and you are not, I hope with all my heart that you will defeat him . . . . The other side will put in all they anyhow can; hence the necessity exists for every stone to be turned by your helpers to sec-ire if possible the desired victory not only of Liberalism, but even more of morality and temperance." Mr. UPSON commended Mr. Shaw as a man of high character and gre-it common sense, who had lived and worked in the ward, not only for his own interest but for helping others in all ways, and promoting the best interests of his neighbours. (Applause.) Men wore puzzled by the literature and speeches of the other side to know whether it was a Parliamtntary or municipal election. Their talk of "preliminary canters" and "armour bright" was playing the game low. (Loud applause.) Municipal elect-or:is were not a means to an end but an end in themselves. (Loud applause.) If they were to have a town which would be an example to others they must see that those whom they sent to the Town Council had no interests of their eam to serve. They must see that they were men of upright character in every respect, men against whom the finger of reproach could not possibly be pointed, men who had earned respect by their lives amongst them, and men who would follow the right in spite of all con- sequences, even if unpopular. He maintained that the candidate who was before them that night was a man of that type. (Applause.) If they returned Mr. Shaw they would have a man who would seek to promote their best interests in every way, and if they did not return him the loss would not be his but theirs. (Applailse). Mr. Shaw, Who is a good speaker and illustrates his points by timely jokes, said that if he were not elected next Monday, he would feel it a great honour even to be selected as a candidate for St. John's Ward. (Applause.) Mr. Steel had made a complaint that his (the speaker's) had been an 11th. hour nomination. He thought Mr. Steel had nothing to complain about for he had at the -time of his (the speaker's) nomina- tion an address on the walls and therefore Mr. Steel had an advantage over him. (Applause.) He referred to questions which had been put to him by the Association of Foundation Managers of Church_ of England Schools, and by the Trades Council. As he stated in his address to the electors of the Ward he wished to promise nothing definitely. With re3ard to school fees being abolished he had not a perfect knowledge of the details and the effect upon the voluntary schools and also upon the rates. He could not in a concrete form give any pronouncement upon the question at the present time. Promises were easy to make and difficult to Mill. But he would say this: that whatever came up that would facilitate the improvement of the moral and social conditions of the people he would give it his best judgment and according to that judgment he would give his vote. (Applause). If that did not suit them he would go and sit at home and remain honest to his convictions. (Loud applause). He would do all in his power to enable the Corporation workmen to receive a fair rate of wages. Cancincling he said that as his name was at the top of the voting card he hoped it would be at the top of the poll. (Applause). Mr. HENSHALL moved and Mr. WRIGHT seconded • and Mr. GRIFFITHS supported a resolution in favour of Mr. Shaw's candidature.
The resolution was passed enthusiastically and no questions were asked.

div.head: Telephone Socletg.—Whlst Drive and Dance
div.p: Telephone Socletg.—Whlst Drive and Dance

Entering upon the second year's series of meetings in circumstances that gave every promise of a success- ful session, the South West Lancashire District Telephone Society held its first gathering in the Kings' Cafe, Warrington on Wednesday evening. The District Manager, Mr. H. Chambers, presided, and an inaugural address was delivered by the President of the Society, Mr. T. A. Proud (Liverpool), Assistant Superintendent of the Province. In doing so, he offered words- of encouragement to the staff, and emphasised the importance of the Society, which would help them to exercise intelligence in their work. The service they were engaged in was a very fascinating one, and every incentive was offered to them to improve their positions. He did not believe they would ever come across such a large concern in which there was less favouritism shown. Some of the best positions were now occupied by men who had entered the service without influence and who had held subordinate positions. There was a great field of usefulness for them all, and if they would take an interest in their work, they woutd get their reward. In conclusion he expressed the hope that the Society would be as successful this session as last. (Applause). A whist drive and dance had been arranged, and an exceptionally enjoyable programme was submitted. Many inttresting whist games were played, and the prizes were carried off by the following ;—Ladies: Misses Hamilton, Mather, Magrath, Mrs. Dean, Gentlemen: Messrs. H. Sherrington, J. W. Dean, Evans, Payne, Mr. F. W. Ashton acted as Steward and the awards were gracefully presented by Mrs. Lightbown. Excellent selections of dance music was supplied by Mr. A. Starkey, and the duties of M.C. were ably under- aken by Mr. T. Taylor.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 30, 1909
THE INFIRMARY.

Resignation of Dr. Joseph. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., presided at a special meeting of governors of the Warrington Infirmary, held at the Institution yesterday afternoon. There was a good attendance.
RESIGNATION OF DR. JOSEPH.

The SECRETARY (Mr. J. H. J. Hampson), read a letter from Dr. Joseph resigning the post of honorary surgeon, which he has held for nearly thirty-one years in addition to a house surgeoncy of five years. "It is with regret" he wrote "that I feel compelled to relinquish duties in which I have always taken the utmost pleasure, but which are now too great a tax upon my time and energies. I take this opportunity of thanking the governors, Board of Management, my colleagues of the medical staff, together with your- self and the others with whom' have been associated, for the kindness and courtesy invariably shown towards me during my long period of office. The CIIAIRIIAN said they were all sorry to receive that letter, and he suggested that they should ask Dr. Joseph to re-consider his resignation until March, when the annual meeting would be held. This course was unanimously agreed to. ADDITIONAL TRUSTEES.

The Rev. H. V. PIGOT moved that the following gentlemen be appointed additional trustees :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Co'onel J. D. Buckton, Captain G. R. Crqsfield, Messrs. Roger C, Parr, W. Peter Rylands, C. Jackson Holmes, J. H. Smethurst, Henry Roberts and F. W. Monks.—He explained that the necessity for appointing more trustees was pointed out to them a few weeks ago by Mr. Frederick Monks, who discovered that his name was the only surviving trustee's name on one of the investments of the institu- tions. He (the speaker) understood that in the case of several investments there was only one surviving
trustee. Mr. C. WitiTE seconded, and the proposition was carried.
NEW VICE-PRESIDENTS,

Mr. W. P. RYLANDS said a finance sub-committee had recently been appointed by the Board of Manage- ment for the purpose of going into the whole question of the finances of the institution and placing them on a more elastic basis. In order to enlist the sympathy of all who would be likely to render useful aid many outside the membership of the Board of Manggement were invited to serve on that sub-committee, amongst them being Messrs. W. H. Bleckly; J. J. Bleckly, ani Witham Carson. They were gentlemen of long stand- ing in the town, connected with prominent works, and he now proposed that they be appointed vice-presidents. Councillor H. ROBERTS seconded and the proposal was approved.
NEW BOARD MEMBERS.

On the proposition of Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH, seconded by Alderman BURTON, one of the rules was amended so that the Board of Management shall in future include 13 instead of 11 Rovernors. On the motion of Mr. J. H. SMETHURST, seconded by Mr. R. C: Parr, Messrs. F. W. Monks and J. A. Ransome were appointed to the vacancies on the Board of Management created by the alteration of rule.
Sir GILBERT GREENALL was thanked for presiding, on the proposition of Mr. C. Jackson Holmes seconded by the Rev. J. Yonge. •

COLBORNE STREET BAPTIST SALE OF WORK. A Sale of Work in connection with Golborne-street Baptist Church was commenced on Thursday afternoon and will he continued until this (Saturday) evening. The sale has bea promoted to clear away the deficit now resting upon the Church, and also if possible, to add to the funds for the building of a new church. The stalls were tastefully arranged and contained some very useful and ornamental articles. The following is a list of stallholders : FLOWER AND FRUIT STALL.—Mesdames Letheren, Starkey, Perkins, Baker, S. Rickers, and Misses Paul, Piing, on and Heywood. SUNDAY SCHOOL STALL.—Mesdames Bnckby, L. Heywood, G. Hall, and Misses Hankey, Dewar, P. Heywood, Tynan and Roberts. LADIES' STALL.—Mesdarnea Clatworthy, Jarman, E Wynne Jones"). S. Hughes and Barnett. REFRESHMENT STALL.—Mesdames Few, Edgar Balmford, J. Edward, Davies, Popper, Baker, Patrick, and Misses Hamer and Tynan. SWEET STALL.—Misses Mabel and Agnes Freeman. BROTHERHOOD STALL:—Messrs. W. T. Heywood. J. H. Pepper, W. Patrick, S. Rickers, T. Rickers, J. Worrell, and T. Davies. There was a fair attendance at the opening ceremony. The Rev. R. E. Letheren presided and was supported by the Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mr. J. W. Scholefield J.P. (Liverpool) Mr. James Kenworthy and Mr. J. Jarman. The Chairman welcomed all who were there that afternoon and especially Mr. Scholefield who was the ' president for this year of the Lencashire and Cheshire Baptist Association. Heanight perhaps ray partly for his sake, as well as for those who might be strangers, that that sale ef work had a sort of natural relation- ship to the Bazaar which they held in March last. All of those who knew the conditions of the church would realise that a handful of people as they had there could not make such an effort without feeling it and since that period their own finances had gone down under the strain. If by the providence of God they were able to go forward with their new building in the spring they would naturally need some temporary building and they also hoped to clear the deficit and also get a balance out of the sale of work. It was now nearly two years since he had been called to take over that church and it was then in a state of ruin. If the speeches were enthusiastic enough for them to stamp their feet no doubt the floor would give way, or if they clapped perhaps the roof would come down. (Laughter). The place was not at all safe for anybody to be in and the state of the premise? called for something to be done and to be done quickly. (Applause.) They thought that by far the cheapest and the most efficient way would be for them to build a new chapel altogether. (Applause.) At this period Mrs. Kenworthy rendered "Abide with me " very tastefully and effectively. Mr. SCHOLEFIELD said that the only effective_open- ing of a sale of work was for the ladies to sell and for the gentlemen to begin to be sold. (Laughter.) Although he had not been in Warrington for some time he could claim to have a very deep and special interest in churches situated as they were. They had in Liverpool a number of places where no man would think of putting up a Baptist Church, but the churches were there and they had done their work. Some which had been built to serve the outskirts were now serving the centre of the great city. He said that it was a stimulus to wk under difficulties and there was a saying that " Difficulties are the despair of fools and the opportunities of wise men" He was sure that Mr. Letheren would have that wisdom abundantly and also courage. If he were to have that wisdom and courage they must have wisdom and courage too. It was no use putting everything upon the leaders. As long as they had that place to worship, and no- other, they would make the very best of it and they would also let it be a spur to get ready for a better place. He had been a Nonconformist and Baptist for over 40 years. In all those years the one thing that he had pressed more than anything else in all their congr 6 gationa was worship. Wherever one worshippe whether it was in a barn or in the ver latest kind of gothic church that was possible he had always longed that there should be a clear recognition that worship was the basis of the church. (Rear, hear.) He was brought up in the Church, and perhaps he had got some ritualism in him, but he shrank Irons the eaay-going public worship,and a desire for mere fine singing and eloquent preaching. He had much pleasnre in declaring the sale opeu. (Applause). On the proposition of Mr. J. JA.RMAN, seconded by Nlr. B. Fnw. a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Scholefield and Mrs. Kenworthy.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. -41. R. WILLIAMS.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. -41. R. WILLIAMS.

Another familiar ani respected figure has been removed by the death of Mr. Joseph Rigby Williams, chartered accountant,who passed away at his residence, 69, Manchester-road, on Tuesday. For several months Mr. Williams had been in failing health but it was only thought necessary to summon medical aid a fortnight ago. It was then found that he was suffering from consumption. Mr. Williams who was fifty-five years of age, was a native of War- rington and received his early education at the Roman Catholic school in Bewsey-street and afterwards at the Newton-street school. As a youth he weot to the late Mr. Joseph Davies, Bewsey Chambers, to learn accountancy and remained with him for many years. He held seveial other appointments and in 1885 he passed his final examination as a Chartered Accountant. In 1891 be commenced business on his own account in Sankey- street and carried it on with success up to the time of his death. Mr. Williams never took any prominent part in public affairs. He was a devout Roman Catholic and worshipped at St. .Itary's Church, Buttermarket- street. The funeral took place quietly at the Cemetery yesterday, the Rev. Father Mawson officiating. The mourners were: Messrs. J. W. Haslehurst (nephew), John Rigby and Henry Rigby (cousins), Thomas Hasle- burst, J. H. Houghton, Henry Houghton,John Eckersley, J. A. Magrath (secretary of the Warrington Catholic Philanthropic Society,of which Mr. Williams was a mem- ber for many years and also an hon.auditor),Henry Rigby, jun.,T. P.ltighy, E. Rigby and W.Rig'oy.Amongst otArs present at the graveside were: Alderman Bennett, Messrs. P. Bennett, T. Lonsclin (borough surveyor), W Walker, A. S. Wright, L. Bolton, W. Dilworth, F. It Pierpoint, F. Magian and P. Maginn (representing the Alliance Box Co., Ltd„ of which Mr. Williams was the auditor). Floral tributes were placed over the grave from: sister, brother, and nephew; Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Houghton, Mr. and Mrs. Henry Houghton, and Alder- man Bennett.

div.head: LECTURES ON " TENNYSON."
div.p: LECTURES ON " TENNYSON."

The Rev. W. L. Schroeder delivered the second of his course of lectures on " Tennyson ; his art and personality" in the Assembly Room at the Conserva- tive Club on Wednesday evening. Dealing with the relation of art and morality, the lecturer said the artist simply as an artist did not primarily concern himself with ethics or religion. His work might have the highest moral significance for the world, but its appeal was effected by virtue of its art. If merely good moral intention made good poetry, tiara he imagined that newspaper poetry was among the best and the highest. (Laughter). It was notorious that hymns were not as a rule the highest poetry; if they were good poetry they were often not very singable, because the tune did not fit. (Laughter). The moral and spiritual appeal of the artist was best secured in the perfection of the art. It was signifi- cant of the charactistics of English poetry that Voltaire should say that no nation had treated in poetry moral ideas with more energy and depth than the English nation. With Tennyson the artistic impulse wa4 predominant, but it moved through the medium of strenuous morality and lofty spiritual thought, and therefore his work held that ethical and religious significance which aroused the anger of the " art for art's sake " critics. Despite an element of preaching, the greater part of Tennyson's work was prevailingly artistic and morality as a fundamental motive had very little to do with it. Not by the execution alone, but also in the choice of subject was the true artist known. We demanded from him the revelation which by reason of our blindness and lack of feeling remained undiscovered until the master poet, painter or musician made it clear to our souls.. Tennyson in both capacities as maker and chooser claimed position in the first rank of artists. He had chosen the great themes of immortality, of friendship, of the strife between the soul and sense, and had handled them in a masterly, artistic fashion. From the ordinary lives of men and women he had taken phases of pathos, thought and action, and had presented them in a poetic setting. He had proved his possession of the eye that saw artistically and if we

were inclined to doubt his power of dealing with the mightiest forces of our day we dare not deny that as an artist in words he stood almost supreme. Tennyson once said that simple poems, with simple thoughts and in simple language, were .the most difficult to write. He set before himself the high ideal of poetic craftsmanship and. wrought faithfully to attain the highest ends. He had the scientific habit of keen observation. We had only to open his works at any page to find how close and realistic he was in his observation of nature. Tennyson could paint what he had seen ; he could bring together in his imagination elements of experience, and fashion out of them similes that lightened his narrative with rare touches of beauty, but he had not the power of pictorial creation. The lecturer showed how one word or brief
melodious phrase that flashed unbidden through Tennyson's brain would inspire a poem. For instance the words "Some one had blundered" formed the
nucleus round which he wrote " The Charge of the Light Brigade." There was very little deliberate imitation of other poets in Tennyson, but. there were

signs of poetic influences which 'linked him up with Chaucer, Spenser, Sydney and Keats and in some senses with Shelley. Tennyson was supreme as a lyrist, as a singer of undying songs. We had cause to thank God for his artistry and the spiritual influence and moral power made possible by virtue of such perfected art.

div.head: ROLLER SKATING.
div.p: ROLLER SKATING.
THE PALATINE RINK,

The Gymkhana held at the above Rink oft Thurs- day was a pronounced success. These events being the first of their kind to be held in the town the man- agement were sceptical as to the result, but their fears were groundless, the races proving a source of amusement and at times were of an exciting descrip- tion. Several of the lady competitors displayed con- siderable agility. Musical chairs provided the " Tit-bit "of the evening and evoked considerable amount of mirth amongst the spectators. Miss Parker the winner was undoubtedly very clever. Miss B. Cotterill won the Balloon Race, Miss J. Cooper the Potato Gathering Race; and Mr. J. Davies the Obstacle Race. Owing to insufficient time the finals for the Egg and Spoon and Hoop Races were adjourned until Thursday next. A "Grand March " was introduced during the evening, the various evolutions of the skaters, wheel- ing and counter-wheeling from an onlookers point of , view was very interesting and pretty. The management are introducing novelties in their weekly programme. Next week it is intended to hold a whist drive and the two finals above mentioned will he decided. Events already fixed are : The Measured Mile Championship of Lancashire • Mile Championship of Warrington and district ; Ladies Hockey Match. With the introduction of the sur- facing machine, the lighting and decorative scheme to be placed in hand the, management will leave very little to be desired for the pleasure and comfort of ' patrons. A hockey match between the Palatine and Wigan clubs attracted a large gathering of spectators to the Palatine Rink on Monday night, the game ending in a draw of two goals each. The Palatine team was : A. Whittle, goal; Davies, back; Whitehouse, Wadsworth and Whittaker, forwards. Mr. Arthur Ashton was the referee. Whittaker and Wadsworth were the scorers for the Palatine. THE EMPIRE RINK.

Another highly successful carnival was held at this handsome new rink on Thursday evening. There were no fewer than 350 skaters, many of whom were picturesquely costumed, and the scene was one of brilliance and animation. The spectators, to the number of between 400 and 500, spent a very pleasant time watching the evolutions of the devotees of the graceful pastime. Handsome prizes were offered for competition, and the judging was undertaken by Messrs: A. Booth and J. Harvey. The Winners were: Best dressed lady, Miss Fairclough (" Cleopatra ") ; best dressed gentleman, Mr. Henry Walton (" Seaside Sultan ") • most up-to-date costume (lady), Miss Plinston (" Lady Scout ") ; most up-to-date costume (gentleman),Mr. Naden ("Aviator"); most humorous costume, " Donkey Girl." Before distributing the prizes, Mr. W. Boothroyd announced that on the recommendation of the judges an addi- tional prize to those announced on the bills had been given. No one in connection with the management had been allowed to compete; otherwise a prize would have been awarded to the Hungarian Huzzar." The judges had been entirely independent and the manage- ment hoped their awards had met with the approval of public and competitors alike. (Applause.) They thanked them for their kind services. During the evening the band, under the conductorship of Mr. Jack Payne, played a special selection of music which was much appreciated. On Thursday evening next a grand gymkhana will be held when a variety of prizes will be competed for. Other events in prospect are : —The one mile amateur championship of Warrington and district and various other races including the amateur championship of England. _ _

(in Monday evening last the Empire hockey team played their second match of the season when Wallasey defeated them by five goals to three. A good crowd of spectators watched a capital game. The Empire team was :—Madeley, goal; Berry, back; Johnson, Jackson (captain) and Bowcock, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.

A special meeting of the members of the Town Council was held last evening to consider the tenders received for the construction of Warrington bridge. Twenty firms have tendered and it was decided to send the designs, specifications and other papers, with the exception of the tenders, to Ur. J. J. Webster, who has been appointed engineer, to adjudicate thereon.

LYMM. • (Continued from Page 11.) HIGHER-LANE BAPTISTS.—A social evening was held on Thursday in the Baptist schoolroom, Higher-lane About 50 people assembled to hear the various items of interest which consisted of songs, recitations, etc. Mr. Richards was the chairman of the evening and spoke very well. The meeting was in every way a success and is likely to be the forerunner of others. Thanks are due to Mrs. S. Moss who helped to make the room attractive and comfortable with plants etc. CONGREGATIONAL GUILD.—The second meeting of the Congregational Guild was held on Thursday evening in the schoolroom, and took the form of a devotional service. Mr. J. 11. Holt conducted the service, speaking from the words "The Hidden Treasures," his address being appreciated. The lesson was read by Mr. Sidney Miller. The soloist was Mrs. C. Lewisonho rendered the hymn" Pleading for Thee." The meeting was very well attended, about 40 being present.—Next week's meeting should be intermting, as a discussion on Women's Suffrage will be intrcduced by Mr. J. D. B. Smith.

div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
N.S.L. Meeting at Latchford.

CAPTAIN CROSFIELD AND GERMANY'S INTENTIONS. A public meeting arranged by Miss Sylvia Broadbent in support of the proposals of the National Service League was held in the Parish Room, Latchford, on Thursday evening. Captain G. R. Crosfield presided over a largo attendance and the principal speakers were Colonel the HA. M. G. Talbot, Colonel Eales and the Rev. Canon Blogg. The Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) was present. The following letter which Miss Broadbent had received from Lord Roberts was read "Dear Miss Broadbent,—l am very glad to hear you are getting up a National Service League meeting at Latchford, for I cannot but feel that the more the principles of the League are spread the better it will be for the country. These principles will be explained by the speakers and I trust the audience will give their most careful atten- tion to their remarks, and that the meeting may result in a great accession of members and associates to the League. The reception given to the Bill for Universal Training, which I introduced in the HOLM of Lords, was most encouraging, and I trust that the question of the acceptance of principle may be one of those to be put before the people at the next General Election. Australia has set the mother country a splendid example and I hope it will be followed.—With all good wishes for the success of the meeting, believe me, yours sincerely, ROBERIS." Captain Crosfield, after briefly outlining the proposals of the League, said many people objected to compulsion but the N.S.L. was trying to show tbat its proposals were necessary, just and advantageous and that they could not possibly get them as long as they stuck to the voluntary principle, because they could not get manufacturer a to let his men go off for four months unless manufacturer b was obliged to do the same thing. That was why the scheme must be compulsory; it was the only fair and just system. Lord Roberts in his letter referred to the desirability of bringing forward the N.S.L. proposals at the next general election. He (Captain Crosfield) was afraid they would all be too full of the Budget, tariff reform, and one thing or another to think very much about national defence, although it was far and away the most important matter. They had to take politics as they found them and pre- pare the ground for the election after the next one, and then they would go in a body to both candidates and bring them tangible evidence of public opinion on this great question. (Applause.) Col. the Hon. M. G. Talbot, a member of the Executive Committee of the League, said that during the last two years the self-governing colonies had awakened to the fact that it was now time for them to take part in the defence of the Empire. The reason for that was that the naval situation of the world had changed very much—and very much to our disadvantage. He did not suppose even the bitterest opponent of the present Government would accuse them of exaggerated fears of attack or excessive preparations to meet it. Yet, in spite of the fact that the navy was still ruled by the Admiral who a few years ago told us that we might sleep peaceably in our beds without any fear for the morrow, we now found that practically the whole of our battle fleet had been drawn in from abroad and concentrated round our shores in order to protect them. This withdrawal of our flag from places where it used to be seen had naturally made our self- governing colonies realise that they could no longer depend upon the British Navy for their protection,that they had got to wake up and do something for, them- selves and the most satisfactory symptom about this awakening was that there had not been any complaint on their part that they had been deserted by the British cation. On the contrary they had manfully accepted the task not only of defending themselves but also of contributing to the defence of the Empire. All this agitation had naturally led in Australia and New Zealand to even greater enthusiasm in the cause of universal military service. It was being taken up by politicians of every class of opinion in Australia, but hitherto financial difficulties bad stood in the way. Ho had no doubt that before long those difficulties would be removed and legislation introduced to put their ideas into practice. Meanwhile, all our self-governing colonies bad realized that it was desir- able, and some of them that it was essential that the boys of their codntries should receive military training. Hero there were many people who called it barbarous and demoralizing. A great deal was being done in this country, but in our usual haphazard way by private effort. An immense amount of physical and moral training was given in our various brigades of boys, but the bulk of the nation was left untouched. The National Service League concluded the speaker, wished to promote peace, and they said peace was best secured by our being so strong that nobody would attack us. (Applause). Col. Eales, who has recently been visiting Germany gave some of his impressions of that country. He said the average general level of education was a great deal higher in Germany than it was in this country. We in England were a little bit too individualistic; too mu ch was left to private effort. He was much struck by the organization of the Germans, and the quickness with which they picked up information. Germans had said to him in conversation: "You English have a wonderful history but you are beginning to take it a little bit easy, and you are very jealous of us because •we make a little progress. Why should we not make progress. We are better educated, particularly in chemistry." The Germans knew themselves to be fine, virile men. They said "With our GO millions, why should not more of the world belong to us ? We feel ourselves to be great and strong. Therefore we are perfectly justified in basing a big navy." The Germans would have respect for us so long as we were strong. Colonel Eales spoke in favour of military drill for boys and said the reason why our sailors were the finest in the world was because they were taken in hand when they were very young and trained to the sea life. The League did not cant the Territorials to be utilized by any statesman as an object of offence, but simply for *home defence pur- poses. The voluntary system, be contended, penalised patriotism. (Applause). Captain Crosfield said the Garman nation had gone ahead to an enormous degree./ What he would point out was that compulsory military training did not seriously interfere with trade or the German nation could not have made the phenomenal progress it had done in the last thirty years—in fact, business people in this country were beginning now to realise that it was very largely because of the military training that business people in Germany were making such extraordinary progress. He was delighted to see that the Leeds Chamber of Commerce had passed a resolution which they were going to bring up at the meeting of the Associated Chambers of Com- merce to the effect that for industrial purposes, quite apart from any fear of invasion, it was necessary that the men of this country, the rich and the poor alike, should have some military training so that they might be able to perform their cork more efficiently. The Rev. Canon Blogg said he was the son of a soldier. His father was for forty years in the Indian Cavalry and commanded a regiment during the Mutiny, and he (the speaker) was the proud possessor of his Mutiny modal. The speaker proceeded to commend the soldier's life on the grounds of cleanliness, self- respect and obedience. He said they wanted to break down the prejudices that existed in the minds of a great many people against the Army and military service in general. When he had said to a fond mother "Why don't you put your boy into the army ? " the reply had been "I would sooner see him dead." He (the speaker) said "My good woman, that just shows your ignorance. You could not do a better thing for your son than put him in the army." There was an extraordinary idea in the minds of a great many people that if a boy went into the army he was not only lost to sight but went from bad to worse. That was not his (the speaker's) experience of the army and he wanted to break down that strong and foolish prejudice against the service. He urged his hearers to look at the matter from the highest and purest view of responsibility to God. A number of cinematograph pictures illustrating an invasion were shown, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. J. Parkinson. Captain Crosfield, in a final address, said he had not the slightest hesitation in saying, although they mi4ht think he was a bit of a fanatic, that national, service was the most important question that was before the country to-day. If our country were defeated, what would be the good of all these social reforms upon wbich they were engaged at the present Limo? Defeat would mean at the least a war indemnity of 2,000 millions,the smashing up or taking away of our Navy, the breaking up of our Empire. It would mean that we would simply become a Holland or a Belgium. As to the possibilities of invasion, we had Europe thoroughly armed on land and now she was arming at sea. We were armed at sea, but we were not thoroughly armed on land, and as long as that went on there was a danger. Why was Germany building her navy at this extraordary speed? Why was she building a navy which in five or ten years, if we strained every nerve, would be equal or nearly equal to our own? She was not an island. We were dependent on food- stuffs from over the seas ; Germany was not. Germany lived on the land. Why was she acting as be had described? He asked his hearers to think over the auestion for themselves. A vote was then taken, and only two held up their hands against the principle of compulsory training.

div.head: Welsh Church Crosfield-street.
div.p: Welsh Church Crosfield-street.

The annual tea party and concert took place on Thursday when a good muster were present to enjoy the good things provided. A very enjoyable pro- gramme was taken part in by Miss Silcock who sang beautifully, Mr. W. Hughes, a rising tenor, and Mr. McArthur, bass, whose., powerful voice was heard to great advantage in his choice of songs Miss Corney was the elocutionist and she gave great pleasure to her audience. Councillor H. Roberts, J,P., fulfilled the duties of chairman in his usual thorough manner. The singing of the Welsh and English National Anthems brought the evening's entertainment to a close.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, NOVEMBER IST, 1909. TO THE ELECTORS OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been requested by the St. John's Ward Liberal Committee and by many personal solicitations to offer my services in the interests of the Ward and the town generally, I have consented so to do. I do not desire to make any specific promises as to what I shall do if elected your representative,but all matters arising in the Council proceedings which demand the thoughtful and serious consideration of its members, shall, upon the merits of the question, have my careful judgment and vote. Any interest exclusively affecting St. John's Ward would certainly have my special care and attention. I firmly believe that the trust committed to your representatives is a responsible one, and their duty is not only to see to the material requirements of the people they serve, but to carefully watch over all matters that would facilitate the improvement of the moral and social condition of the Electors they desire to represent in the Council. Having lived and laboured in your midst for over 50 years, I trust that the confidence and honour I solicit, may be shown by electing me your representative on Monday next. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JAMES SHAW. 83, L3thgoes lane, Warrington.'

The Committee invite applications from fully quali- fied Medical Practitioners for the appointment of MEDICAL OFFICER to the workmen. Membership upwards of 2,000.
